News.title: Girl, 6, dies days after Shoreham sea tragedy killed three family members
News.content:
A six-year-old girl has died in hospital after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex, in an incident which also killed her father, mother and sister.

Saja El-Khawas, a British Palestinian from London, was pulled from the sea by emergency crews on Tuesday.

Her father Hassan El-Khawas, 55, mother Zeina Alayn, 37, and 14-year-old sister Sara, died despite the efforts of paramedics at the scene.

Emergency services were called to the sea off Shoreham Fort at about 14:40 BST on Tuesday to a report of four people in difficulty in the water.

News.title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
News.content:
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than at any point in the last nine years, new data shows.

Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.

In 2017, it was closer to one in five.

The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.

Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.

For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.

Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.

News.title: Burnham economic adviser O'Neill rules out government job
News.content:
The economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer, was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, he said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

"I've decided to not take a formal role," he said.

"It's not because of any policy disagreements. I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

"I'll continue to, hopefully, maintain an informal relationship with the PM and his team," he added.

He said he did not want "the constraints of a blind trust and all the constraints that would be necessary".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.

Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.

The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.

The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.

Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.

Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.

News.title: GTA 6 leaks - a nightmare or a blip for the biggest video game of the year?
News.content:
Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

Vermeij believes it's possible to overstate the significance of the leaks.

"I think the vast majority of gamers aren't really on the internet, hunting down these clips," he says.

However, Vermeij accepts there is a "very small subset" of hardcore fans desperate for any new information they can get their hands on.

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and that it doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

News.title: 'Quiet, quiet, quiet!' - What triggers Trump to shut down reporters?
News.content:
President Donald Trump has been lashing out at reporters, often female journalists, when confronted with questions he does not like to answer.

The BBC's Tom Bateman takes a look at what triggers these public insults, and what are the questions the president doesnât want to be asked.

News.title: Under-fives and pregnant women told to avoid runny eggs when eating out over salmonella risk
News.content:
Vulnerable people are being warned not to eat under-cooked or runny eggs when they are eating out because of the developing salmonella outbreak.

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) told the BBC the under fives, over 65s, women who are pregnant and those with health conditions should avoid them along with freshly-made products that might contain uncooked eggs, such as mayonnaise, souffle and hollandaise sauce.

But the FSA said well-cooked eggs in restaurants, cafes and from takeaways were fine to eat.

It comes after the UK Health Security Agency declared a national outbreak of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds more fell ill.

It is thought imported eggs or dishes containing them are behind the outbreak.

FSA chief scientific adviser Ian Young said: "If people are eating out or consuming eggs or egg-containing products from cafes and restaurants then for those people in particular who are young, elderly, pregnant or vulnerable, it's important to make sure that any eggs or egg products that you consume in those settings have been very well cooked."

He described the outbreak as "unusually large and rapidly increasing", and added that "people need to be careful".

But he reiterated the message that it was fine for people to buy British eggs from supermarkets as chickens bred here are vaccinated against common strains of salmonella.

"There is no link to those eggs to this current outbreak," he added.

Mark Williams, chief executive of the British Egg Industry Council, said eggs from Britain were safe to eat when runny, even for vulnerable people, and were widely available in restaurants and cafÃ©s.

"Customers who want to enjoy a runny egg should simply ask whether British Lion eggs are being used," he said.

News.title: Prince Harry and six others face privacy case legal bill of up to £34.5m
News.content:
Prince Harry and six other public figures face paying up to Â£34.5m to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional order for legal costs over their failed privacy case.

The seven claimants, also including Sir Elton John and Liz Hurley, must pay an initial Â£9.54m by Friday of next week to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL).

The judge ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before trial, criticising how they presented their claims as "unreasonable to a high degree".

On 7 July, Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the claims of unlawful information-gathering, which ANL denied.

The Duke of Sussex and the other six claimants have until 2 October to attempt to launch an appeal.

Those other claimants are Sir Elton John and his husband David Furnish, former Liberal Democrat deputy leader Sir Simon Hughes, racial justice campaigner Baroness Lawrence, and actresses Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley,

They had insurance to cover up to Â£16.2m of Association Newspapers' costs in the event of losing the case - but Friday's ruling means the newspaper group could now try to recover up to the Â£34.5m that it said it had to spend to defend itself. This means the duke and others could face a bill of some Â£18m.

Justice Nicklin said: "I regard a claim for costs in excess of Â£34 million as, on its face, excessive and as giving rise to real concerns as to whether all of the costs now claimed by Associated were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount."

But he added he had "decided not to impose a ceiling on Associated's recoverable costs", as it would "be too broad-brushed, would risk unfairness, and would be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary".

The judge also ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, which is more favourable to the publisher in terms of the amount it can recover, aside from where orders had already been made.

He added it was "striking" that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group of seven claimants.

He said: "That matters. Serious allegations of criminality or grave impropriety cannot properly be left hanging over individuals in that way.

"If a party no longer advances such an allegation, or no longer has a proper evidential basis for advancing it, the allegation should be withdrawn clearly and in terms.

News.title: Brief break from rain as sunshine returns for weekend
News.content:
After the spell of showery weather earlier this week, a strong area of high pressure is set to bring bright and sunny weather to much of the UK this weekend.

Daytime temperatures will feel pleasantly warm - though a long way off from the record heat experienced earlier this month.

Nights are expected to be mostly clear, leading to a significant temperature contrast from morning lows to afternoon highs.

While Saturday and Sunday will bring a brief break from the rain for many, unsettled weather will return early next week.

News.title: Murder probe after wildfire uncovers body in park
News.content:
A murder investigation is under way after human bones were uncovered at a west London park following a wildfire, the Metropolitan Police said.

Emergency services were called to Bedfont Lakes Country Park in Hounslow at about 18:35 BST on Wednesday, 12 August.

A police spokesperson said the remains were found by a member of the public after the wildfire affected an area of woodland known as The Pits.

Following a post-mortem examination, police said the bones belonged to a woman aged between 25 and 45. They said it was not clear how long the remains had been there and officers were still working to identify her.

News.title: Arran ferry evacuated over 'bomb threat' by passenger rescued from sea
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has been arrested after a ferry service on Scotland's west coast was evacuated over a bomb threat.

Operator CalMac said a passenger was reported overboard on the MV Caledonian Isles 16:40 service, carrying 329 people from Brodick on the Isle of Arran.

The BBC understands that after being pulled from the sea by the ferry's rescue boat, the man then told crew that there was a bomb on board.

All passengers were removed on foot at Ardrossan so the vessel could be searched. Police Scotland said it was established that the threats "were not credible".

The passengers and others waiting at the port were taken to a nearby supermarket car park by police while the search was carried out.

After this was complete, officers allowed people back on board to collect their vehicles.

News.title: Ofcom investigating Sky News over Farage harassment claims
News.content:
Ofcom would not comment on any investigation but said it treated complaints in strict confidence and would not "publicly confirm the identities of individuals concerned".

Farage claims reporters from Sky News approached his daughter's home while he was out of the country.

Sky News says it did not interact with his daughter, and was trying to ask Farage about a Â£5m gift he received from cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne before he entered Parliament in July 2024.

A parliamentary standards investigation into whether the gift broke any rules resumed earlier this month after Farage was re-elected as MP for Clacton following a by-election he triggered that was boycotted by the other major parties.

Upon returning to the country, Farage was questioned by Sky News over the undeclared gift, to which he responded: "You tell your bosses, you harass my family any more, there will be serious consequences, that's what your organisation has done this morning, now go away."

When pressed on the donation again, he said: "Did you not hear me? You have broken all the rules, Leveson and everything else, cut."

At the time, Sky News said in a post on X: "Sky News was not at the property at 7.41am. As has already been acknowledged, and as shown in the footage from 10.19am, Sky News was outside a property where Mr Farage was registered to vote at the last election.

"Sky News did not interact with Mr Farage's daughter.

"On a single occasion, we approached the property without a camera operator, identified ourselves as Sky News and the adult occupant chose not to engage. We were seeking to contact Mr Farage to ask questions about the gift he accepted from Mr Cottrell.

"This is a well-established and routine journalistic practice when reporting on matters of legitimate public interest.

"The footage clearly demonstrates that Sky News did not 'hound' or pursue Mr Farage's daughter.

"At no stage did we seek to speak to anyone other than Mr Farage in connection with this story."

The BBC has contacted Sky News for comment.

Ofcom says it aims to conclude fairness and privacy complaints within 90 working days.

News.title: Men admit trying to tunnel into jewellery shop
News.content:
Three men who were caught trying to tunnel into a jewellery shop from a neighbouring massage parlour have admitted conspiracy to commit burglary.

Ioan Asafeti, 39, Laurentiu-Daniel Nitisoara, 38, both of no fixed address, and Sergiu Plastin, 42, of Portadown, County Armagh, were behind the attempted raid on Mitcham Road in Tooting, south London, in the early hours of 17 July.

Kingston Crown Court heard how body-worn camera footage captured Nitisoara being arrested in a nearby alleyway, while Asafeti was found hiding on a rooftop.

Plastin was tracked down using mobile phone data and arrested later that day at Stansted Airport as he tried to board a flight to Ireland.

News.title: Man denies charge over Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
A man has denied failing to disclose information in relation to the Manchester synagogue attack.

Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim appeared before Westminster Magistrates' Court and pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity.

The 49-year-old, of St James Road in Higher Broughton, Salford, spoke only to confirm his name and indicate his plea. He was remanded into custody to appear at at the Old Bailey on 25 September.

Worshippers Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October.

He then began attacking with a knife, while wearing a fake suicide belt, before being shot dead by police outside the synagogue.

News.title: Body recovered in search for man fallen overboard on cruise ship
News.content:
A body has been recovered in the search for a man fallen overboard from a cruise ship in the North Sea off the east coast of Scotland.

The man was reported missing at 08:35 on Ambassador Cruise Lines vessel MS Ambition, about 36 nautical miles from Arbroath.

Lifeboats, coastguard crews and aerial support were launched as part of a search operation before the ship docked in Dundee.

Police Scotland said formal identification was still to take place, but the missing man's family had been informed.

The ship was on its return journey to Dundee from a solar eclipse cruise, with stops in Iceland and the Faroe Islands.

It docked in Lerwick before returning to the city on Friday.

BBC Scotland News understands that the passenger's luggage was still onboard and his bed had not been slept in.

News.title: French becoming more effective in stopping small boat crossings, UK says
News.content:
French police tactics are becoming more effective in stopping small boats in the English Channel from reaching Britain, the Home Office has said.

It credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.

Footage released by French police shows officers racing across a beach in jeeps to intercept a launch. Once the boat is abandoned, an officer slashes it lengthways with a knife.

The Conservatives described the announcement as a "joke" and said Channel crossing preventions were "down by half over the past year".

Migrants can be seen throwing objects at the officers, one of whom appears to respond with pepper spray.

While Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, thousands of illegal migrants are getting through with 250 arriving on Monday.

In late July a record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat with Border Security Command pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on 23 July.

The Home Office, citing French police figures, said that since it struck a deal with France three months ago which included additional funding for authorities, 61% of small boats have been intercepted - a five per cent increase compared to last year.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the "UK-France deal is already having a real impact".

The UK-France Border Security deal agreed in April under the Starmer government, includes Â£501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and Â£161m for new approaches.

Previously the French authorities allowed most dinghies to head towards the UK once they had launched, because of the risk of intercepting them in deep water, while loaded with people.

Of the 12 dinghies stopped so far at sea, three interceptions took place in the last two weeks.

The techniques being used have not been disclosed by the UK or France.

Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at the Border Security Command, told the BBC that "last Thursday alone, the French prevented all three of the boats that tried to cross".

Speaking to the BBC at the Western Jetfoil facility in Dover used to process migrants, he said: "Two of those they prevented at sea, and one they prevented on land."

News.title: Why Kate will be a key figure in Harry and Meghan’s return to the UK
News.content:
The Princess of Wales is likely to be a "peacemaker" between families when the Duke and Duchess of Sussex return to the UK with their children, a former royal butler believes.

Speaking exclusively to The Independent, Grant Harrold explained that he believes Kate will be trying to look for the positives in the situation, and reassure the Prince of Wales.

Mr Harrold, who worked closely with Prince William and Prince Harry until 2011, has also warned that William would likely be “furious” with his brother’s return after their public fallout, following Harry’s barrage of accusations against him, Kate, the King and Queen Camilla in his memoir, Spare.

Every week in the 1990s, Gillian Anderson would throw on a sensible, well-pressed pantsuit and face off against a parade of extraterrestrials and boogeymen. Being a famous woman of the Nineties, Anderson also found herself somewhat inevitably facing off against the era’s IRL boogeymen, such as Harvey Weinstein, the huffing, puffing uber-producer who shaped the film industry back then. He’d always want her to star in “scary things” for him, she once recalled, as if TV’s most prolific monster magnet would want nothing more than to replicate her day job on the big screen, too.

“I mean, he’d try to get me to do his films, period,” Anderson, 58, says today, with the cool, husky drawl of a Wild West gunslinger. She’s famously bidialectal, due to her upbringing between London and Grand Rapids, Michigan, and today is on a video call from France – a neutral ground, maybe, but one she’s chosen to speak with an American accent in. Anyway, she remembers her interactions with Weinstein always involving “a kind of bribery” with an element of quid pro quo. “He’d say, ‘if you do this for me, I’ll do that for you.’ That kind of thing.” She leans her head to her right, before firing off a very Dana Scully-coded roll of the eye. “I didn’t buy into that at all.”

Weinstein is invoked early in Anderson’s new erotic thriller, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a glowy, sultry celebration of the slasher movie, which also doubles as a bit of a meta commentary on Anderson herself. Playing Billy Presley, a horror icon famed for a starring role in a B-movie film franchise, Anderson tells the prodigious young filmmaker (the actor and comedian Hannah Einbinder, of the acclaimed Hacks) hoping to work with her that she doesn’t scare easily – after all, Billy says, she auditioned for The Burning, a real-life Friday the 13th knock-off that served as Weinstein’s first producer credit.

Anderson’s casting in Camp Miasma is in tribute to writer and director Jane Schoenbrun’s early love of The X-Files. “That show took up probably 50 per cent of my imagination as a kid,” Schoenbrun tells me. “Gillian was always in my life back then, so there was this ephemeral feeling while working with her of having always known them, even though I’d just met them.”

Financiers want to hear a sob story. They always want a minority filmmaker to talk about how their life has been hard, and why they’re dysfunctional Jane Schoenbrun

Plus there’s the sex of it all. Camp Miasma is about horror, but it’s also about orgasms. The earliest thoughts of sexual longing felt by Kris, Einbinder’s character, came as she watched archetypal horror heroines flee from masked men – usually while dressed in their underwear, occasionally right before they were horribly butchered. It’s the kind of fantasy that would make Freud’s eye twitch, but also not trouble Anderson in the slightest. She’s about to publish her second collection of erotic fantasies, crowdsourced online. One woman wrote to her about wanting to be tied down by her own dentist; another admitted she craves the sexual freedom that would be instigated by her husband’s demise. In Camp Miasma, it is Billy who grants Kris the freedom to voice, then indulge, those fantasies of hers. It’s as if Anderson took her brilliantly frank sex therapist from Netflix’s Sex Education, drenched her in blood, then sent her overseas to save the world’s libidos one person at a time.

Upon receiving the Camp Miasma script, Anderson began to see the parallels. “It made perfect sense for me to play Billy,” she says, “because of how many layers of the role aligned with what I’ve been talking about quite avidly over the last years.” She gleefully stepped into what she terms “the meta world” of the film. “How bizarre that this would come into my life at this very moment,” she adds. “I felt like I had to do it.”

open image in gallery Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson in ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ ( Mubi )

It is May, and we’re speaking a few hours before Camp Miasma’s Cannes Film Festival premiere – where it would go on to earn raves, and ultimately take home the event’s Queer Palm award. Next to a glamorously coiffed Anderson is a groggy Einbinder, 31, who is valiantly persevering through a press junket despite being struck down with flu. Like Anderson, she saw herself in Camp Miasma. She identifies as bisexual, with Kris’s “emotional journey” mirroring hers as a young woman. “You start with discomfort, then shame, then liberation,” she says. “I related to it enormously.”

Kris, too, shares parallels with Jane Schoenbrun, who at 39 is the most exciting millennial filmmaker working today. They specialise in work that is spooky and nerdy and lightly otherworldly, rooted in pop culture ephemera and body horror both literal and supernatural. Their commercial breakthrough was 2024’s breathtaking I Saw the TV Glow, about two outcast teenagers drawn together by their shared love of a fictional supernatural drama called The Pink Opaque, which starts to bleed into reality.

Like Schoenbrun and their dysphoric 2021 thriller We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, Kris’s character in Camp Miasma debuted with a tiny independent film that was warmly received at the Sundance Film Festival – a remake of Psycho told from the perspective of the shower curtain. Also like Schoenbrun, who was sought out to direct a reboot of the flagging Leprechaun franchise (the 1993 original saw a terribly bewigged Warwick Davis chase around a pre-fame Jennifer Aniston), Kris is asked to take the reins of the long-dormant Camp Miasma movies (think an even grimier version of the Friday the 13th series). But unlike Schoenbrun, Kris accepts the movie offer, sending her down a rabbit hole with Billy that unlocks her own psychosexual malaise.

open image in gallery Jane Schoenbrun, Anderson and Einbinder attend the LA premiere of ‘Camp Miasma’ in July ( Getty )

Making Camp Miasma, Schoenbrun experienced a similar blossoming. They grew up watching horror movies that cast genderqueer or trans characters as sickos and deviants: think Psycho, The Silence of the Lambs, or the fascinatingly offensive Friday the 13th copy-paste Sleepaway Camp. “I knew that if I was to develop a more positive relationship to sex and to my own body, I had to return to those Buffalo Bills or Norman Bateses, who I loved as a young person but who also probably f***ed me up.”

Today, Schoenbrun stands alone in the Hollywood ecosystem, as the only out trans filmmaker commanding high budgets (relatively speaking, anyway) and major studio backing. It’s no exaggeration – even with The Matrix and Bound as her calling cards, Lilly Wachowski said this month that no one is willing to fund her $10m new indie. It’s a fact that Schoenbrun finds daunting. “The thing I’ve learnt is that financiers want to hear a sob story,” they explain. “They always want a minority filmmaker to talk about how their life has been hard, and why they’re dysfunctional.”

You basically have to fake it until you make it, Schoenbrun explains. “I’ve kind of mastered the language of the pitch meeting. I wouldn’t be sitting here if I hadn’t.” So in those rooms selling Camp Miasma, they leant into the critical acclaim they’d received for TV Glow, the fact that they’re a Sundance Film Festival fave, and that general audiences would love the big, attention-hogging idea of Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder as lovers covered in blood. “It’s a process of making your work understandable to the world of capital, and that’s a very different process to actually making the thing,” they say. “They’re not going to care that much about gender transgression in the history of the horror film…”

open image in gallery Ian Foreman in Jane Schoenbrun’s star-making 2024 movie ‘I Saw the TV Glow’ ( A24 )

It explains why Camp Miasma is two films in one – the first is an easier-to-sell slasher satire with severed heads and impalings, the second is a tender, sexy love story flush with queer existentialism. Schoenbrun Trojan-horses us, essentially. “It’s a story of queer liberation,” they say, directly inspired by their own gender journey. I Saw the TV Glow was conceived in a period of trauma at the very beginning of their transition, which explains its occasional fatalism. Camp Miasma, comparatively, is the product of a period of joy. “I often compare transition to getting on an antidepressant,” they joke. “You deal with all of the s****y side effects first, and it takes a couple months before the good stuff starts. This movie was made from a place of full enjoyment with the good stuff – the joy, sex and euphoria of becoming myself.”

Schoenbrun cast Anderson because of The X-Files, and Einbinder because of the physicality she saw in her stand-up specials (“she commits her whole body to performance and not only performance but, like, weird performance”). But there’s also a cool, understated muscle to both actors that makes them evenly matched on-screen, as evidenced by Anderson’s run of steely, impervious women (she’s played everything from Margaret Thatcher in The Crown to A Streetcar Named Desire’s Blanche DuBois at the Young Vic), and in Einbinder’s off-camera activism. Einbinder is currently one of the most high-profile Jewish anti-Zionists working in Hollywood, with her continued advocacy for Palestine – as well as her leftist politics generally – earning her repeated drubbings from conservatives. She says that the industry is set up in a way that makes it consistently difficult to navigate ethically.

open image in gallery Anderson and Einbinder in ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ ( Mubi )

“Life under capitalism implicates an individual in systems that are evil,” Einbinder says. “End of story, you know what I mean? It’s something that torments me on a daily basis.” How does she get through it? “The way I make sense of it is just to continue to act in a way that is in line with my morals. So I do speak to those things and put action behind them. But it’s not straightforward, and it does eat me up.”

For Anderson, she doesn’t think her own story has involved any real fighting, even when I suggest it probably wasn’t easy to use her X-Files clout to make something like her dazzling adaptation of Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth, and not whatever Weinstein had in mind for her.

“I’ve never allowed anyone to force me into anything that I didn’t want to do,” she says. “It’s more been about choosing to step away for a period of time, or do theatre, or do an indie film, as opposed to whatever your trajectory is meant to be.” As she says this though, she starts to have second thoughts... “It’s funny, only sometimes in retrospect does one realise there might have been a divine plan all along. I think I’ve always stayed on a path that makes sense for me at any given time. And ultimately you get to a point where you feel like, yes – this does represent who I am.”

“This”, at the moment at least, being Camp Miasma – a bloody, profound and sapphic love story soaked in weirdness and joy. It just feels right that Dana Scully found a home there, doesn’t it?

‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ is in cinemas

News.title: Are narcissists born or made? The answer might surprise you
News.content:

Narcissists are everywhere these days. Narcissism has become a social media buzzword, with checklists of traits to cross-reference and tools to help you manage the narcissist in your family, friend group – or relationship.

But while received wisdom is that it’s a trait that is produced largely by parenting, a new report has found that narcissism is, in fact, 50 per cent genetic, with the other half attributable largely to environmental experiences that aren't shared within families. In fact, the report “Narcissism Runs in Families Due to Genetics: An Extended Twin Family Analysis”, published in Sage Journals, found that parenting styles may have no impact on whether you, or your children, end up as narcissists.

If you, like me, suspect quite a few narcissists are lurking in your extended family tree, then this news might send you into a tailspin. If you had a difficult, manipulative parent with narcissistic traits, you might now worry that you will be the same or that - worse - your children will be, even if you parent them lovingly and listen to them and their feelings.

Does narcissism run in families, as seen in HBO’s Succession, in which the Roy family is headed by a ruthless patriarch, Logan (Brian Cox), who showcases narcissistic traits of grandiosity, lack of empathy, and intense manipulation on a constant loop, as do his children?

In which case, what power do we have over stopping the family dysfunction?

open image in gallery Miranda Priestly in ‘The Devil Wears Prada’ exhibits strong traits of grandiose narcissism that is studied in the new report ( 20th Century Studios )

Most of us carry some traits of narcissism, including a need for admiration, self-centredness, and sensitivity to criticism and empathy.

But a narcissistic personality, in which narcissistic behaviours are commonly seen on a daily basis, is something different. On a more extreme end of the spectrum is Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD), in which narcissism is ever-present, incurable – and intolerable.

A 2014 study of 304 twin pairs found that “grandiose narcissism” was about 23 per cent heritable, and “entitled narcissism” about 35 per cent heritable, with most of the rest linked to life experiences and environmental influences that were unique to each person.

This new study offers vastly stronger evidence on the influence of genetics, despite previous theories placing most of the emphasis on parenting and family environment.

Dr Claire Hart is Associate Professor of Social and Personality Psychology at the University of Southampton, specialising in quantitative research on interpersonal relationships, empathy, and narcissistic dysfunction. She explains that although there does appear to be a substantial genetic component to narcissism, it’s important to understand what that 50 per cent figure in the new study means.

“It doesn’t mean that half of an individual's narcissism comes from their genes,” she says. “Or that a narcissistic parent has a 50 per cent chance of having a narcissistic child. Instead, when we look across lots of people and ask why some people are more narcissistic than others, genetic differences appear to explain around half of that variation.”

In other words, there isn’t a single narcissism gene that you either inherit or don't. “Lots of genetic influences are likely to be involved, alongside our experiences and environments,” she says. “Genes can influence our predispositions towards certain personality traits, but they don’t determine an individual’s personality.”

But where the new research is especially interesting, she says, is that parents and children in the study were similar in their levels of narcissism, but that similarity appeared to be explained by genetic rather than shared environmental transmission.

open image in gallery Dr Claire Hart: ‘Genes can influence certain personality traits, but they don’t determine an individual’s personality’ ( Supplied )

“That challenges the simple idea that narcissistic parents necessarily ‘make’ their children narcissistic through the way they parent.”

That is not to say that parenting doesn’t matter. “Previous longitudinal research has found that parental overvaluation – seeing and treating a child as more special or entitled than other children – predicts increases in children’s narcissistic traits over time.”

She also makes the point that children growing up in the same family don’t necessarily experience the same parenting. “If parents treat their children differently, parenting can actually form part of the ‘non-shared’ environment rather than the environment siblings have in common,” she says.

Dr Craig Malkin is a lecturer in Psychology at Harvard Medical School. He is also the author of 2015’s Rethinking Narcissism, in which he defines narcissism as running along a spectrum from healthy to unhealthy. “This new study puts another nail in the coffin of the idea that parenting style alone creates extreme narcissism,” says Malkin, who has been giving a rough estimate of the 50/50, genetics and environment for years. “The genetic evidence is now impossible to dismiss.”

While some people seem to be born with more of a tendency toward narcissistic traits and are more attention-seeking, dominant, dramatic, or difficult to manage from an early age, there’s still “a tremendous amount” we can do as parents, he says.

“We don’t have complete control over who our children become, but how we respond to more difficult temperaments can help determine whether a child gets knocked further up the narcissism spectrum or stays in a healthier range.”

open image in gallery Mad (narcissistic) Men: Don Draper is a textbook example of a man with a grandiose idea of himself ( AMC )

He cites research by psychologist Phoebe Crane that showed that early narcissistic tendencies are less likely to develop into unhealthy narcissism when parents are warm and responsive while also providing structure and limits; something psychologists refer to as authoritative parenting.

“They were instead more likely to develop healthier forms of confidence and self-regard,” says Dr Malkin. “Giving children healthy limits ... and combining those expectations with warmth, support, and empathy may be the best protection we can provide against a child with a genetic vulnerability moving toward destructive narcissism.”

He adds that research contradicts the popular idea of “once a narcissist, always a narcissist”.

“Longitudinal studies find that narcissistic traits change over time and, on average, decline with age, even though people who are more narcissistic than their peers tend to remain relatively more narcissistic than their peers.”

I do appreciate the authors doing this work; personality does have a genetic element, but complex constructs like narcissism take in more territory than just a handful of the components Dr Ramani Durvasula, author of ‘It’s Not You: Identifying and Healing from Narcissistic People’

Dr Ramani Durvasula – a leading expert on narcissism and author of It's Not You: Identifying and Healing from Narcissistic People, says the new study is flawed and “may not be as much doom and fatalistic gloom” as it first appears to be.

“The way they measured narcissism is really focusing on a relatively narrow band of the construct,” she says. “I do appreciate the authors doing this work; personality does have a genetic element, but complex constructs like narcissism take in more territory than just a handful of the components.”

While it does appear that traits like status seeking, attention seeking, perception of one's own specialness, and capacity to control others has a heritable component, she says, we need replication science and broader measures of narcissism to say narcissism is inherited.

“This study does not necessarily support that other key elements of narcissism, such as low empathy and selfishness, as well as the associated behaviours, are heritable,” she says, pointing out that it only focuses on grandiose traits and not vulnerable/covert ones. “More research would be needed.”

When it comes to recovery from narcissistic parenting, she says that genetics don't really matter. “Selfish, manipulative, invalidating, emotionally harmful parents do real damage to their children – and you recover by fostering other healthy relationships, seeking out therapy, doing the hard work of breaking out of self-blame and guilt cycles.”

open image in gallery Professor Sam Vaknin introduces the concept of ‘healthy narcissism’, a building block of self-worth in early life ( Supplied )

Professor Sam Vaknin is the author of Malignant Self Love: Narcissism Revisited, the first book on narcissistic abuse published in 1999. He agrees that the report doesn’t add up. “[It] absolutely fails to establish that genes cause narcissism, parenting doesn't matter, and narcissism is genetically predetermined,” he says.

He explains that narcissism is a cluster of traits, and, like all psychological traits, it is hereditary. “This includes ‘healthy narcissism’, an integral part of personal growth and maturation and is at the core of self-esteem, a stable sense of self-worth, and even social functioning.”

However, environmental factors may mutate healthy narcissism into the pathological or even the malignant kind. “It is very likely that certain people have a genetic predisposition to develop pathological narcissism given a dysfunctional environment, a specific life history, and certain adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). However, at this stage, we have no body of rigorous, serious studies in any field to support such a claim.”

How we respond to more difficult temperaments can help determine whether a child gets knocked further up the narcissism spectrum or stays in a healthier range Craig Malkin, author of ‘Rethinking Narcissism’

On the other hand, he says there are “thousands upon thousands of rigorous studies”, which highly correlate childhood abuse and trauma with later-life pathological narcissism.

“There is childhood abuse or trauma in the personal histories of literally all people diagnosed with NPD. ‘Abuse’ and ‘trauma’ in this context is any disruption to the formation of an individuated, separated, integrated, and constellated self. An overprotective or smothering parent is therefore being as abusive as an incestuous or bullying one.”

Psychologist Kathleen Saxton and author of 2025’s My Parent The Peacock: Discovery and Recovery From Narcissistic Parenting says that while the genetic evidence in the new study is important, there is no way on earth that your parental upbringing does not impact the way that you are shaped.

“Genes may create vulnerability or temperament, but relationships help shape how that vulnerability is expressed,” she says. What she repeatedly sees in her consulting room is that children adapt to narcissistic environments in very different ways.

open image in gallery Psychologist Kathleen Saxton says there is no way parental styles don’t impact narcissism ( Supplied )

“One may become perfectionistic, another invisible, or highly anxious and people-pleasing, while another may replicate some of the narcissistic defences themselves, “ she says. “So the question is not simply whether narcissism is inherited, but what happens to a child who has to organise themselves around a narcissistic parent.”

The take-home message from the new research is that narcissism can run in families, but genes are not destiny. That is a huge relief. “I think the most useful message is therefore not to worry about trying to eliminate narcissism in a child because it exists somewhere in the family,” adds Dr Hart.

“Instead, focus on the things that support healthy development more generally: warmth, empathy, responsiveness, appropriate boundaries and recognising the child's needs as distinct from the parent's own needs.”

News.content:

A collection of 688 handwritten reflections by Mahatma Gandhi has sold for £1.2m at an auction in India, setting a record for an Indian historical document sold at auction.

The handwritten messages were addressed to Anand T Hingorani, a close associate of Gandhi and a fellow participant in India’s independence movement.

They were written over almost two years, from 20 November 1944 to 10 October 1946, and were later compiled into a book called A Thought for the Day, according to auction house Saffronart.

The circumstances in which they were written were deeply personal; Hingorani’s wife Vidya had died, and he shared his loneliness and grief with Gandhi while undergoing nature-cure treatment for deafness, according to the Hingorani family.

Gandhi responded by writing him a thought each day, turning a private act of consolation into one of the most extensive surviving records of their relationship.

“Gandhi responded by setting aside time each day to write a personal thought. What began as a personal exchange soon evolved into a collaborative project,” Minal Vazirani, co-founder and president of Saffronart, told The Indian Express.

open image in gallery The handwritten messages were addressed to Anand T Hingorani, a close associate of Gandhi and a fellow participant in India’s independence movement. They were written over almost two years, and were later compiled into a book called A Thought for the Day ( Saffronart )

“While Gandhi authored each reflection, Hingorani became the recipient, organiser and transcriber, ultimately preparing the writings for publication,” she said.

The 688 entries cover many of the subjects that occupied Gandhi throughout his life, including truth, ahimsa or non-violence, brahmacharya (self-control), non-possession, fearlessness, religious equality, prayer, service, labour, duty, silence, conscience, self-realisation and the search for God.

A group of nine letters from 1930 and 1931 concerns Anand and Vidya Hingorani’s marriage, including parental opposition, financial independence, reconciliation within the family and Gandhi’s views on self-restraint and domestic obligations.

The wider collection was preserved by the Hingorani family across generations and was offered as an 86-lot sale by Saffronart under the title Gandhi: From the Collection of Anand T Hingorani.

open image in gallery The 688 entries cover many of the subjects that occupied Gandhi throughout his life, including truth, ahimsa or non-violence, brahmacharya, fearlessness, religious equality, prayer, labour, self-realisation, and the search for God ( Saffronart )

The reflections, which were the auction’s standout lot, had been estimated at Rs 150m (£1.1m) to Rs 250m (£1.9m) before the sale and eventually fetched Rs 162m (£1.2m). Saffronart said the result set a world record for an Indian historical document sold at auction.

Among the other notable lots was Message on God, a group of three manuscript and correspondence items documenting Gandhi’s reflections on God and the Bhagavad Gita, which sold for Rs 16.8m (£128,518). His peti charkha, a portable box spinning wheel, accompanied by two letters about the spiritual discipline of spinning, fetched Rs 10.2m (£78,040).

A signed presentation photograph of Gandhi writing fetched Rs 7.8m (£59,678m), while a collection of his letters, telegrams and postcards relating to economic independence sold for Rs 5.8m (£44,376m).

open image in gallery Gandhi’s peti charkha, a portable box spinning wheel, along with two letters about the spiritual discipline of spinning, sold for Rs 10.2m ( Saffronart )

“What makes this collection particularly compelling is the opportunity to see one of the most significant figures in India’s history through the lens of a close, personal relationship,” Dinesh Vazirani, co-founder of Saffronart, said in a statement.

He added that the reflections showed “how Gandhi lived the principles he advocated publicly”, describing them as a valuable record of his “thought and practice”.

The buyer has not been identified publicly; Saffronart has confirmed they are from within India, and the manuscript will remain in the country.

News.title: What to know about Alex Jones' Texas court win and more than $1 billion in damages he still faces
News.content:

Conspiracy theorist Alex Jones is still under orders to pay more than $1 billion over his false claims surrounding the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School massacre despite a Texas court reducing some of the money awarded to families.

For the bombastic Infowars founder, the ruling that saves him more than $40 million was still a legal victory amid multiple punishing financial judgments that forced him and his company, Free Speech Systems, to file for bankruptcy.

Sandy Hook families have yet to collect any money from Jones, who has left his Infowars platform amid numerous ongoing legal battles but is still broadcasting on other websites.

He still faces a defamation judgment of $1.25 billion in a Connecticut lawsuit and the nearly $6 million that remains in the Texas case.

What to know about Jones, Infowars and his legal cases:

How Jones lawsuits got here

Several relatives of the 20 first graders and six educators killed at Sandy Hook sued Jones and his company, Free Speech Systems, in Connecticut and Texas for defamation and inflicting emotional distress for saying the shooting was staged by “crisis actors” to win more gun control.

Victims’ relatives testified that followers of Jones subjected them to death and rape threats, in-person harassment and abusive comments on social media.

Jones argued there was no proof that linked him to the others’ actions. He did concede under oath that the shooting did happen.

The Connecticut case produced a judgment against Jones of more than $1.4 billion in damages, which was reduced by about $150 million during appeals. In Texas, Jones was hit with nearly $50 million in damages.

On Friday, a state appeals court threw out most of the Texas award because it vastly exceeded the state's legal cap on punitive damages. The ruling reduced that portion from more than $40 million to $1.5 million, leaving about $6 million intact.

Only one judgment impacted

The Texas court ruling did not throw out the finding of defamation against Jones. He still called it a major victory for free speech and vowed to continue his appeals.

“I got lawyers who are good constitutional lawyers, and they are not backing down,” Jones said.

The Texas ruling has no impact on the bigger Connecticut case, where Jones was found liable for $1.25 billion. That judgment still stands, and Jones' appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court last year was denied.

“The families care not at all about this irrelevant ruling which affects only two of the 19 claims they all share. Jones still faces over a billion dollars of liability, so this changes absolutely nothing. All it does is highlight the absurdity of Texas law,” said Mark Bankston, an attorney for the families in the Texas case.

How Infowars became a media empire

Jones pushed many conspiracy theories over the last three decades, including that the U.S. government was behind or failed to stop the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing and the 9/11 attacks.

As the outlandish nature of his false claims grew, so did his presence across radio stations, his Infowars website and social media.

After getting fired from an Austin radio station in the mid-1990s, he began broadcasting from home on his Infowars website. He bought the domain name for $9.

In 2004, he had two employees and a tiny office. By 2010, Jones had over 60 employees. By 2024, he had four studios in Austin and a warehouse for the products he sells.

Jones filed for bankruptcy in 2022 as the judgments against him mounted. The liquidation of assets forced him to surrender his Infowars platform.

He still broadcasts on new websites, social media and streaming platforms, and he continues to sell merchandise, including dietary supplements and clothing that bring in millions of dollars a year.

The Onion steps in the take over Infowars

Sandy Hook families have been prevented from collecting any money from Jones while he pursues lengthy appeals in state and federal courts.

The satirical website The Onion has moved to take over Jones’ Infowars platforms and turn his bullhorn of conspiracy theories into parody sites.

Jones took Infowars off the air in April. A proposed licensing deal that would give The Onion temporary authority to use Infowars’ trademarks, copyrights and intellectual property has been put on hold during Jones' appeals.

Still, The Onion has set up its own Infowars webpage on its website, running videos of shows parodying Jones. The webpage replaced the “o” in Infowars with an onion and sells products under that logo including T-shirts, tote bags and coffee mugs, with some proceeds going to the Sandy Hook families.

___

Associated Press writer Dave Collins contributed from Hartford, Connecticut.

News.title: Arsenal play like the champions they are as title defence starts with a bang
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to the Emirates Stadium, where the Premier League champions begin the defence of their title. Or, as Mikel Arteta prefers to put it, their “attack” on a new season. A classic Arteta-ism.

The assault starts tonight against Coventry City but our understanding is that Arsenal will be without new £75m midfielder Bruno Guimaraes. We believe the Brazilian has picked up an injury, and it’s not currently clear how severe it might be. Clearly, this is a blow for Arteta. But they should still have enough to get past promoted Coventry… shouldn’t they? We’ll find out soon enough.

Meanwhile, Arteta has said he and his players should relish being Premier League title favourites and the role of the hunted rather than the hunter.

“In the last three seasons, at some point we were first and at some point we were chasing. And you never know what is better,” Arteta said. “But if you give me the choice, I want to be first. I want to be hunted, and I want to be in control of our future, rather than depending on somebody else.”

Arteta called on his players to retain the hunger they had last season.

“We start from scratch, from zero, and we’re going to have to prove we are at the level to go back to that position again,” he said. “We need to show that desire and the ambition to be better than what we were last season, a month ago, a week ago.”

This is Coventry’s first Premier League campaign since they suffered relegation in 2000-01, and they were led to the Championship title by Frank Lampard. They scored the most goals in the Championship and conceded the fewest, and could face one of their former players tonight in Viktor Gyokeres.

Full team news as and when we get it.

News.title: Russell takes Dutch GP sprint pole as Antonelli struggles to fifth
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for sprint qualifying for the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix from Zandvoort. This is the last time the race will be on the F1 calendar for the foreseeable future, having been reintroduced in 2021 after a 35-year absence. It will be a shame to see it leave again, but never rule out it coming back, especially with Max Verstappen signing a lengthy contract extension with Red Bull.

What of the competitive action this weekend? As it is a sprint weekend, there is not a lot of preparation time, with just one practice session before sprint qualifying. In that it was a fairly close fight at the top, and it was Kimi Antonelli, the championship leader, who was fastest of all. Behind him was the McLaren of Lando Norris who was 0.121sec adrift then George Russell, who will be looking to kickstart his title campaign here, a further 0.004sec behind him.

Then came the two Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton (0.190sec) and Charles Leclerc (0.289sec) before a fairly significant gap of 0.659sec to Oscar Piastri in sixth. Verstappen was down in 11th, nearly 1.4sec off Antonelli’s ultimate pace but 0.5sec or so ahead of new (and old) team-mate for the weekend, Liam Lawson.

It was a tricky session for the drivers, though, as it began damp on a showery and blustery day by the Dutch seaside. Several drivers ran wide and off the track, though they all avoided anything more serious than gravel rash. The rest of the day looks to be drier but there are still a few showers around and the wind is all over the place, as it often is here.

Sprint qualifying starts at 3.30pm BST and we will be here for all of the updates for the nearly hour-long session.

News.title: Root delivers perfect riposte to captaincy doubters as England hammer Pakistan
News.content:
There was no attempt to be a Ben Stokes tribute act by Joe Root, just a measured captaincy performance very much in his own undemonstrative style.

Root, ever the team man, pushed his bowlers forward to lead England off at the end, recognising the match-winners in a walkover against Pakistan, who were bowled out for 135 in under two sessions.

Victory by an innings and 103 runs inside three days marked a perfect return to the job and put the smile back on England faces for the first time in a long while. The chants of “F--- the ECB” from Trent Bridge, after the New Zealand regime-toppling loss, were replaced by the Yorkshire faithful’s “Roooot”.

There was plenty of scepticism around rebooting the Root captaincy, but he was the only realistic choice. Harry Brook’s batting here was more sensible and at a tempo in the captain’s mould. “He is still learning the art of Test cricket,” Root said. Thrusting Brook into the job would have put more pressure on him, he may well have felt he needed to make risky statements with the bat. Now he can mature under Root and Stephen Fleming.

Tactically, Root was astute and showed enough to suggest he is going to be different this time. The old Root would not have whipped Jofra Archer off after two overs of the Test, but it was a prod that worked as he bowled quicker and more accurately to strike twice with the second-innings new ball, using his new-found skills with a scrambled seam to good effect.

It also showed his bowlers he wanted a fuller length and, from that first hour, they controlled the match and did not let their grip slip.

Root promised to keep the good aspects of Bazball and apply common sense. He continued Stokes’s leg-slip tactic and it paid off with the wicket of opener Azan Awais, and urged Ollie Robinson to bowl with the keeper standing up. England batted at 4.5 an over – a touch quicker than the Bazball years – but it was never reckless, just a calm tempo, with no ramps or scoops.

News.title: Officials selling yellow fever certificates to unvaccinated travellers
News.content:
Officials in Malawi are selling yellow fever certificates to unvaccinated travellers for around $20 and sending them on their way, a Telegraph investigation has found.



The passport-sized, yellow document, officially called the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP), is supposed to provide proof of vaccination against yellow fever, a mosquito-borne virus that kills tens of thousands of people every year.

The jab provides lifelong protection, beginning 10 days after vaccination. Most countries in Africa and Latin America require them for entry, either for all travellers or for those arriving from risk areas.



Yet travellers leaving Malawi through two major airports can get hold of the certificates without ever being vaccinated, according to interviews with multiple travellers and an undercover investigation.



Several passengers who travelled recently from Malawi to destinations including Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia and China said they had obtained yellow fever vaccination certificates at airports or public hospitals without receiving the vaccine.



One traveller, who recently flew to Uganda for work from Kamuzu International Airport, which serves the capital, Lilongwe, said he was initially told it was too late to get vaccinated because his departure was less than 10 days away.



“When I asked the health officials if I could get vaccinated at the airport, I was told it was too late because I needed to be vaccinated ten days before my trip,” he told The Telegraph.



“But then they offered to arrange the certificate for me for roughly $21,” said the traveller, who asked not to be named. “I had to pay because I could not postpone the trip.”

News.title: Congo gambles on ‘old’ vaccine as new Ebola virus spirals
News.content:
Nearly half of all those infected have gone on to die.

Dr Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine partnership, earlier this week said to beat the outbreak “we must deploy every tool at our disposal”.

She went on: “To avoid this becoming the worst recorded Ebola outbreak in history, it is critical that all effective countermeasure options are brought to bear.

“We have a tool that could help save lives while we wait for [Bundibugyo]-specific vaccines to become available.”

Previous clinical trials have shown that Ervebo is safe, but its effect on other strains is unknown.

The World Health Organisation said in a statement that while it was not known if Ervebo may protect against the Bundibugyo virus, “early laboratory and animal data suggest it may provide some protection”.

Medics told the Telegraph of anecdotal claims that health workers who had been given Ervebo to protect them during an outbreak of the Zaire strain in 2018 to 2020 had not fallen ill during the current Bundibugyo outbreak.

Health workers are at extreme risk of catching the disease because they come into contact with highly-contagious blood, vomit and diarrhoea from dying patients. When they fall sick themselves, they frequently go on to infect their own families.

Giving health workers vaccine jabs to protect them as they tend the sick is a cornerstone of Ebola responses.

The WHO said the vaccine allocation includes 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus. The remaining 50,000 doses will be used for front-line and health workers as recommended by WHO experts.

Dr Nishtar said: “Having already been licensed for the Zaire strain, we know that Ervebo is proven to be safe.

“And while the signs are that it may not stop transmission – which is essential for ending the outbreak - it could well save precious lives and reduce suffering.”

Health officials warn that the Bundibugyo outbreak centred on DRC’s Ituri province is easily outpacing relief efforts.

The virus is thought to have been spreading for months before an outbreak was finally declared in mid-May and medics have been unable to make up the head start.

An analysis by the Africa Centres for Disease Control meanwhile warned the current outbreak dwarfed all others on record

The current outbreak had almost ten times more cases than any other previous outbreak at a similar stage.

News.title: Soaring welfare bill pushes national debt to almost £3tn
News.content:
Britain’s soaring welfare bill forced John Healey to borrow more to balance the books last month.

The gap between tax receipts and spending unexpectedly resulted in a £1.8bn deficit in July, taking the national debt to within a whisker of £3tn.

Economists had predicted the Government would borrow nothing and blamed the deficit on the rising welfare bill.

Figures published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) this morning show total debt rose to £2.985tn in July.

Benefit payments also climbed by 7.2pc, or £2bn, to £30bn last month.

The Chancellor now faces another tax-raising Budget in October, even as strong receipts from self-employed workers provide some respite.

The ONS also said Mr Healey spent £7.7bn on debt interest in July alone, almost 10pc higher than a year ago.

Ashley Webb, at Capital Economics said: “The weak performance was mainly due higher social payments.”

Monthly borrowing was slightly higher than the Office for Budget Responsibility and markets expected, meaning the Government has borrowed £56.7bn this financial year to plug the gap between tax receipts and public spending.

Julian Jessop, an independent economist and IEA economics fellow, said: “The latest official data highlight the fragility of the public finances as John Healey prepares his first Budget. Government borrowing was £2.3bn above forecast in July, and £0.7bn higher than in the same month a year ago.”

July is traditionally a strong month for receipts from the self-employed, with self-assessed income tax receipts last month coming to £17.1bn, about £1.7bn more than a year earlier.

However, higher inflation triggered by the Iran war means Mr Healey will be forced to use the Budget to find billions of pounds to repair the public finances.

Mr Healey said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of our UK economic stability and national security which is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules, with a buffer against global uncertainties.”

The Resolution Foundation warned that the Chancellor’s headroom against his fiscal rules - self-imposed guardrails to guide public spending - has shrunk from around £24bn in the Spring Statement to less than £8bn today.

The think tank called on the Chancellor to use his first Budget on Oct 28 to put the nation’s finances on a more sustainable path.

Elliott Christensen, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said: “The Chancellor’s margin against his fiscal rules is now razor thin.”

News.title: Brook falls agonisingly short of Headingley hundred again as England continue to dominate
News.content:
“Yeah, of course I did,” said Cox, when asked if he was frustrated to miss out on three figures. Cox was caught behind off spinner Ali Usman, but believed he had hit his pad with his bat, not the ball.

“Once I got to fifty, I moved to sixty quickly, and thought ‘there’s a chance here’. Just keep being disciplined, ball by ball. I had it at the back of my mind, thinking you have worked so hard, do not give this opportunity up. That is exactly what I do in county cricket. I get to fifty, see how many runs I need to score, and work down from there.”

Asked if his team-mates were feeling the same emotion, he said: “Oh yeah there is. Every team, every player wants to score Test hundreds. Four of us got fifties, so we were hoping one would kick on, and instead of making it just a hundred, make it 150 or 170.

“I am thrilled. I would have taken it at the start of the Test match. I let myself down a tiny bit, but at the end of the day, you take 70.”

Cox resumed on day two on 23, then was dropped by the bowler Khurram Shahzad on 57. In the course of his innings, he was compared to AB de Villiers by the former England captain Michael Vaughan.

Cox is likely to get a good run across formats. England had hoped to call on Sam Curran for the third Test of this series, but his summer is over due to a groin injury. Curran will undergo surgery on Friday.

It is likely England will be without Curran, Bethell and Tom Banton for September’s white-ball series against Sri Lanka, which should mean greater opportunity for the likes of Cox and Sussex’s James Coles, and could even see a recall for Zak Crawley, who made an assured 81 for Kent against Middlesex on Thursday. Will Jacks is currently sidelined with appendicitis, but is expected to have recovered in time for the series.

Sports.title: Julian Alvarez would light up Emirates and make Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard ‘go up a level’, claims Gary Neville
Sports.content:
GARY NEVILLE has urged Arsenal to go all out to get Julian Alvarez to complete Mikel Arteta’s title-challenging attack.

The Argentine striker has been on the Gunners’ shortlist throughout the window.

But navigating a deal for his services with Atletico Madrid has proven difficult, with Barcelona reported to be his preferred destination.



But Neville told the North London outfit that he could be the difference maker in European competition if they want to go one better than their final defeat to Paris Saint-Germain last season.



Neville was on Sky Sports punditry duty for Arsenal‘s 3-0 win in their opener against Coventry City, but he felt something was still missing from the side.

He said: “We think that Alvarez wants to go to Barcelona, but if Arsenal could get Alvarez somehow that is going to light this place up, because then you have a world class striker to go with all the other world class defenders and midfield players.

“They’d become not just Premier League title winners, but you’re then thinking that they can go that extra step and win the Champions League as well.



“He does need that little bit of magic up front that when you don’t play well they’ll go and win a big game for you. Has he got enough of that? I’m not sure.”

Neville’s appreciation for the star extends beyond what he can bring to the team in terms of goals, but to how he can get the best out of his fellow stars.

He explained that the versatile forward could be the key to unlocking the full potential of Martin Odegaard in midfield.

The Norwegian technician was awarded man of the match for his performance against Coventry, which saw him score his side’s third to seal the result.

Neville added: “I think that, and I’m being respectful to Havertz and Gyokeres, but if there was an Ian Wright up front for Arsenal who made those little runs all the time, he (Odegaard) would be even better.

“I actually think that if Arsenal were to get an Alvarez, I think he would go up a level himself, because I think that would be perfect for the style of play.”

If Arsenal are to make a final push for the World Cup winner, they have just days left in the window to do so, and will still have to find a way to leapfrog Barca on his list of priorities.

Sports.title: Why Wrexham football shirt sales leapfrog Arsenal and Man City at UK airports revealed
Sports.content:
WREXHAM football shirt sales have leapfrogged Arsenal and Manchester City at the UK’s largest airports group.

The Disney series about the Welsh club co-owned by Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney has helped shirt sales finish third behind Liverpool and Man United, according to MAG, which owns Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands airports.



Shirt sales at JD Sports outlets across the three were up 19 per cent year-on-year.

Andrew Macmillan, at MAG, which handles 66million passengers a year, said: “It’s not surprising to see multiple Northern teams represented in the Manchester league table.



“The airport serves a catchment of 22million people across the whole of the North.

“It’s also no surprise to see United, City and Liverpool featuring heavily in all parts of the country given their global appeal and recent success.



The rise in Wrexham shirt sales is astonishing and partly reflects the club’s growing domestic fan base.

Especially in the case of Manchester, which is its primary international airport.

“But it also demonstrates how impactful the behind-the-scenes documentary was for the club’s profile, coupled with its A-list ownership.

“That will have driven a high volume of sales with the tens of millions of tourists who use Manchester and Stansted in particular as their gateway to the UK as a whole.”



Wrexham kicked off their Championship campaign with a 1-1 draw against Cardiff City.

They are set to play Watford next.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta gives update on Bruno Guimaraes after star signing is denied Arsenal debut against Coventry with injury
Sports.content:
MIKEL ARTETA gave a positive update on Bruno Guimaraes’ fitness after the Brazilian missed Arsenal’s season opener due to injury.

Guimaraes, who joined Arsenal for £75million this summer, was ruled out of the Gunners’ 3-0 win over Coventry with a groin issue suffered in last week’s Community Shield.



The midfielder was spotted with ice on his leg after being substituted during the victory over Manchester City last Sunday and was unable to be part of the matchday squad against Coventry.

Initial reports had suggested that Guimaraes could be sidelined for up to six weeks with the issue, but Arteta has reassured fans that is not the case.



Asked if his new signing could be out for weeks, Arteta replied: “No, no. We don’t expect that to be weeks at all.

“Let’s see how he evolves this week. He didn’t even want to stop. He wanted to carry on.



“Now we start to understand the character of the player, but I don’t expect that to be a big issue.”

Guimaraes, 28, is expected to play a significant part in Arsenal’s season after his big-money move from Newcastle.

Arsenal have already been forced to dip into the market to sign a new centre-back after losing William Saliba to a back injury.

The Gunners announced the arrival of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa on Friday, parading him out on the pitch ahead of kick-off against Coventry.

Sports.title: EFL star rushed to hospital after playing with chest infection as manager gives health update
Sports.content:
BLACKPOOL defender Jordan Brown was rushed to hospital after playing through a chest infection.

Brown, 25, was subbed off in the first half of the League One opening weekend draw with Wycombe after struggling with an issue.



And manager Ian Evatt has revealed that things got worse in the following days.

Speaking ahead of his side’s clash away to Stockport on Saturday, he said: “He’s had a rough week.



“I don’t really need to share too much of what happened post-game, but it was quite serious.

“A lot more serious than what it first looked when he came off.

“He’d been suffering with a chest infection, I had it as well a few weeks,ago but he had continued to play through.

“That infection had obviously caused some reaction, which left him hospitalised for a period.”

Englishman Brown, who joined Blackpool from Leyton Orient last summer, lasted 40 minutes before getting taken off.

His team were 1-0 down at the time but Evatt is hopeful things are set to keep improving.



He continued: “Thankfully he’s out now, and all of the tests and scans he’s had are clear, but now he’s in the process of building himself back up again to be able to play.

“There’s one or two more tests he needs to tick off, and he’ll have those tomorrow (Saturday).

“Hopefully by the end of next week he’ll be back available. It was pretty scary for a period.”

Evatt admitted that the situation escalated mid-match.

He added: “While the game was happening it was quite serious, so we weren’t privy to the information until after the game.



“It was pretty scary for him and his family, first and foremost. And we must always put them to the forefront of our minds.

“But thankfully now he’s recovering and he’s out of hospital. Things are looking more positive.”

Sports.title: Michael Carrick reckons Man Utd have a ‘good spine’ as his side launch Premier League title assault
Sports.content:
MICHAEL CARRICK reckons Manchester United have a “good spine” as his side launch a Prem title assault.

The Red Devils aim to show they have the backbone to challenge for a first crown since 2013.



Boss Carrick has added central midfielder Youri Tielemans to his spine of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, centre-back Harry Maguire and skipper Bruno Fernandes.

Ahead of Saturday’s Prem opener at Hull, Carrick said: “If you look at all the top teams over the ears, all the great teams, the spine is really strong.



“So we’re conscious of that, and I think we’ve got a good spine right now.

“The foundation of the team is important to be consistent — through one game from start to finish and over a period of time.



“You need that solid foundation through the middle of the team. We are in a good place.”

Carrick has brought in £35million Tielemans, 29, and 22-year-old Andrey Santos in a deal worth £50million.

Brighton’s Carlos Baleba, 22, is set to follow in a £150million midfield rebuild following the departure of Casemiro and a long-term injury to Manuel Ugarte.

United have missed out on main targets as rivals Manchester City splashed out £116million on Elliot Anderson, while Tottenham forked out £85million on West Ham’s Mateus Fernandes.

Sports.title: Man City’s Phil Foden enjoys caravan park break with family ahead of season alongside Sun readers on our £9.50 holidays
Sports.content:
FOOTIE ace Phil Foden and his family have enjoyed a caravan park break along with Sun readers on our amazing £9.50 holidays.

The £230,000-a-week Man City and England international took his partner and kids to the coast before the new season starts.



Foden, 26, Rebecca Cooke and children Ronnie, seven, True, five, and Phil Jnr, two, enjoyed rides, the penny arcade and even won teddies on a grabber machine at Lyons Winkups Holiday Park in Towyn, North Wales.

And Phil was happy to pose for pictures with fans who were delighted to see him enjoy a down to earth holiday, despite having millions in the bank.
