World.title: FRSC elevates 7472 personnel, reinforces professionalism, leadership and road safety delivery
World.content:
The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has approved the promotion of 7,472 personnel comprising 2,134 Officers and 5,338 Marshals, in a major career progression exercise designed to reward merit, strengthen professionalism and inject renewed energy into the Corps’ leadership and operational structure.

The promotion, which forms part of the Corps’ continuing commitment to human capital development, recognises the dedication, competence, discipline and years of service of personnel who have distinguished themselves in the discharge of their responsibilities to the nation. The elevation of the affected personnel is therefore not merely a change in rank, but a renewed call to greater responsibility, higher standards and more impactful service to the Nigerian motoring public.

Under the new arrangement, Heads of Departments, Corps Officers, Heads of Special Units and Commanding Officers have been directed to decorate the newly promoted personnel under their respective commands from Wednesday, 26 August to Friday, 28 August 2026, in accordance with the Administrative Instruction on the Decoration of Newly Promoted Officers and Marshals.

The Corps Marshal, Shehu Mohammed, mni, described the promotion as both a reward and a responsibility, stressing that every new rank must translate into a higher level of professionalism, accountability, leadership and service delivery.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, the strength of FRSC is not measured only by its patrol vehicles, technology or enforcement architecture, but fundamentally by the quality, character and commitment of the men and women who stand between road users and the consequences of unsafe road behaviour.

He congratulated the newly promoted personnel and charged them to see their elevation as a mandate to do more, lead better and serve with greater distinction, reminding them that every additional stripe, pip or insignia represents increased expectations from the Corps, the Federal Government and the Nigerian people.

The Corps Marshal further emphasised that promotion in FRSC must continue to serve as an instrument for building a professional, responsive and performance-driven institution capable of meeting the evolving demands of road safety management in Nigeria.

He urged the newly promoted Officers and Marshals to justify the confidence reposed in them by demonstrating discipline on and off the road, treating members of the public with dignity, upholding the integrity of the Corps and remaining uncompromising in the pursuit of safer roads.

The promotion also comes at a time when the Corps is intensifying its operational, technological and public enlightenment interventions towards reducing road traffic crashes and improving compliance with traffic regulations nationwide. The Corps views a motivated and professionally developed workforce as central to sustaining these interventions and delivering measurable improvements in road safety outcomes.

The newly promoted personnel are expected to carry their new responsibilities with renewed purpose and to remember that, in the FRSC, rank is not merely worn, it is earned, entrusted and ultimately measured by service.

The Corps congratulates all the promoted Officers and Marshals and wishes them greater success as they assume their new responsibilities in service to the nation.

World.title: Dangote to sell 30% shareholding of new refinery to East African countries – Report
World.content:
Dangote Group, the empire of Africa’s richest man Aliko Dangote, has offered a 30 per cent holding in its proposed 700,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery to nations in East Africa, the region where the mega crude-processing plant is to be located, Bloomberg reported Friday.

Kenya, where the new refinery will be sited at the southeastern coastal town of Lamu, will take a 10 per cent stake estimated at around half a trillion dollars, David Ndii, a top economic adviser of President Ruto, told Bloomberg.

“The total for the region is about $1.5 billion. I don’t actually see a challenge in doing that, and if some of them are not off-taking we will backstop,” Mr Ndii was quoted as saying at a capital market conference in Nairobi on Thursday.

Ethiopia and Rwanda are said to have indicated willingness to participate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Dangote is turning to business-friendly Kenya and other promising markets in East Africa to expand his multi-billion dollar empire after facing an avalanche of resistance from his home country Nigeria in bringing a refinery of similar capacity to completion.

The Nigerian refinery, situated in the outskirts of Lagos and initially projected to be completed in 2016, did not see the light of the day until eight years after, held back by logistic delay, infrastructure constraints and COVID-19 lockdowns.

The magnate, who has built his fortune around cement, sugar and a couple of fast-moving consumer products, accused international oil companies of sabotaging efforts at getting the refinery running seamlessly in its early days.

He claimed that the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority, which serves as the top watchdog for the midstream and downstream segments of the oil industry, issued new licences to some players to import “dirty fuel” as part of a broader conspiracy to frustrate his push to wean Nigeria off its longstanding dependency on fuel imports.

In the heat of the crisis, Farouk Ahmed, the CEO of the regulator at the time, resigned his appointment, while Mele Kyari, the immediate past managing director of state oil company NNPC Limited, whom Mr Dangote accused of surreptitiously running a fuel blending plant off the coast of Malta, was shown the exit door.

“I knew there would be a fight. But I didn’t know that the mafia in oil, they are stronger than the mafia in drugs,” he told an investment conference in June 2024.

A private placement, which raised $2.5 billion ahead of the Nigerian refinery’s planned $5 billion initial public offer scheduled for October, valued the refinery at $40 billion.

The private equity capital raise was 3.7 times, drawing interest from African institutional investors and institutional investors from outside the continent.

The groundbreaking of the Kenyan refinery is expected to kick off next month.

That puts the company on course to achieve the ambition of doubling its refining capacity to 1.4 million bpd in the next three years, with processing capacity at the refinery in Lagos already upped to 700,000 bpd from its original 650,000 bpd.

The planned refinery in Kenya is expected to cost $15 billion to $17 billion.

World.title: Tinubu suspends three permanent secretaries over fresh fake agency, orders alleged promoter’s arrest
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has ordered the suspension of three permanent secretaries over the discovery of a new fake agency.

The phoney agency, known as the National Brands Development and Made in Nigeria Special Project Office, was said to be operating within the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation.

The suspected permanent secretaries are M.S. Danjuma, Nadungu Gagare, and Richard P. Pheelangwah.

The president also ordered the immediate arrest of the alleged promoter of the fake agency, George Buchi Nwabueze.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The chairman of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Musa Aliyu, who disclosed the developments to State House correspondents on Friday, said Mr Nwabueze “was discovered to also operate under four other variations of names.”

The four other name variations are “George Nathan, George Nathan Nwabueze, Hon. George Buchi Nwabueze, Prince Geroge Buchi Nwabueze and George Nwabueze.”

“I have briefed Mr President comprehensively on these new developments. ICPC will continue with its investigations,” the ICPC chairman said.

The discovery of the new fake agency was an offshoot of ICPC’s investigations into the alleged fictitious Presidential Foreign Investment Promotion Council (PFIPC).

The ICPC chair had disclosed after briefing President Tinubu on 6 August on the commission’s interim report that the probe discovered two additional fake agencies.

Mr Aliyu said he submitted the interim report on 6 August, exactly 30 days after the President ordered a probe into the matter.

Mr Aliyu said the commission recommended the prosecution of the self proclaimed Director-General of the organisation, Adeniyi Adeyemi, over alleged forgery, impersonation and related offences.

World.title: Kwara senator picks PDP ticket hours after quitting APC
World.content:
Senator Saliu Mustapha of the Kwara Central District has picked the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) ticket for the district, hours after resigning from the All Progressives Congress (APC).

Mustapha received the PDP senatorial ticket on Friday from the party’s Kwara State Chairman, Issa Bawa, formally making him the party’s candidate for the Kwara Central senatorial election in 2027.

The development follows his resignation from the APC amid a prolonged crisis within the ruling party in Kwara State.

Mustapha had run for the APC governorship ticket. Still, the party decided to give the ticket to the state’s northern senatorial district, eventually nominating the state House of Assembly speaker, Yakubu Danladi-Salihu.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The ruling party also nominated Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq as its senatorial candidate for the central district.

Mustapha announced his resignation on Thursday through statements shared on his verified social media handles.

In his resignation letter dated 14 August and addressed to the APC Ward Chairman of Gambari Ward 1 in Ilorin East Local Government Area, the senator said recent developments within the party, particularly under its leadership in Kwara, had eroded his confidence in the APC.

He said his decision followed weeks of consultations with his supporters, constituents and political stakeholders across the state.

Mustapha leaves APC

Mustapha said he joined the APC as a founding member because of his commitment to good governance, unity, and service to the people.

He, however, said the party’s leadership in Kwara had departed from the principles of unity and internal democracy on which the APC was founded.

“I believe political leadership must be anchored on integrity, competence, accountability, and a sincere commitment to the collective interest of the people,” he said.

“The current leadership of the party in Kwara State has fallen short of these standards, and this has eroded my confidence.”

The senator also assured his supporters that leaving the APC would not affect his commitment to Kwara Central and the state.

“To my constituents, supporters, political associates and stakeholders in Kwara State and beyond, I assure you that while my political platform may change, my principles, purpose, and commitment to the people remain unchanged,” he said.

His resignation came after months of disagreement between him and other aggrieved APC stakeholders, as well as the party’s leadership in the state.

From APC’s crisis to PDP’s

PREMIUM TIMES had earlier reported the growing tension within the Kwara APC following the party’s governorship primary and the subsequent controversy over its National Assembly candidates.

Mustapha was among the prominent aspirants who contested the APC governorship ticket but lost to Danladi-Salihu.

Governor AbdulRazaq is the APC candidate for the Kwara Central Senatorial District.

The developments fuelled speculation about Mustapha’s next political move.

He was also part of the G15 coalition of aggrieved APC stakeholders, which rejected the outcome of the party’s primary and demanded intervention from President Bola Tinubu and the APC national leadership.

Members of the group, including Mustapha, Deputy Senate Leader Lola Ashiru and Senator Ibrahim Oloriegbe, had publicly criticised the process through which the party’s candidates emerged.

At one of the protests in Ilorin, Mustapha called on President Tinubu to intervene.

“We are protesting because we are not happy with the way the party’s leadership handled the process that produced the candidates. We are not against anyone, but the process lacked fairness and inclusiveness,” he said.

The group had also warned that the internal crisis could undermine APC’s chances in the 2027 elections.

Defection was expected

The senator’s move to the PDP did not come as a surprise.

PREMIUM TIMES had previously reported the widening political options available to Mustapha and other members of the G15 as efforts to resolve the APC dispute appeared increasingly uncertain.

The PDP had also emerged as a possible platform for the senator to continue his political career after losing the APC governorship ticket and facing uncertainty about his senatorial seat.

The PDP’s decision to hand him its Kwara Central ticket now confirms those earlier political calculations.

His emergence also ends speculations over who would fly the PDP flag in the district.

The party had previously been linked with other possible candidates for the seat as political negotiations continued.

Fresh contest

Mustapha’s emergence sets up a direct contest with Gov AbdulRazaq, who is seeking the Kwara Central Senate seat on the APC platform after completing his second term as governor.

The contest is likely to attract significant attention because both men are prominent figures in Kwara politics and have previously operated within the same political platform.

Mustapha was elected to the Senate in 2023 on the APC platform.

ALSO READ: Kwara senator Saliu Mustapha resigns from APC

His departure means that he will now challenge the party under which he currently holds the seat.

The development could also reshape the broader political landscape ahead of the 2027 elections, particularly in Kwara Central and among members of the G15.

Wider implications

The senator’s defection comes at a critical point for the APC, which has been attempting to contain the fallout from its primaries.

The party’s governorship candidate, Danladi-Salihu, has acknowledged the grievances and said a reconciliation committee had been established to address them.

The APC leadership has maintained that its candidates emerged from primaries conducted in line with the party’s guidelines.

The Emir of Ilorin, Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, has also publicly endorsed the APC candidates, praising AbdulRazaq’s administration and praying for their success.

Mustapha’s departure, however, means that APC’s reconciliation efforts now face a more difficult test.

His move to the PDP could also encourage further realignment among politicians and party members who were dissatisfied with the outcome of the APC primaries.

For the 2027 Kwara Central senatorial contest, the immediate consequence is clear. Mustapha will seek another term in the Senate under the PDP, while AbdulRazaq will attempt to secure the seat for the APC.

The contest is therefore likely to become one of the closely watched political battles in Kwara ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: Deepening Public Procurement Reform: How BPP and perm secs are resetting governance, By Ismail Omipidan
World.content:
Change is inevitable. But implementing it always meets resistance from within and outside. Since assuming office about two years ago, the Director-General of the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), Dr Adebowale Adedokun, FCIPS, has faced that resistance head-on with a reform agenda aimed at transforming Nigeria’s procurement ecosystem.

He came in at a time when confidence in the Bureau was low. It was gathered that before his appointment, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had considered shutting down the BPP, noting that it had “outlived its usefulness.” The period leading to 2023 was widely described as an era of “anything goes” at the Bureau.

This was captured by former BPP DG, Dr Emeka Eze, at the inaugural edition of “The Procurement Evolution” in June this year. Dr Eze, now Chairman of the FCT Civil Service Commission and pioneer DG of BPP from 2007 to February 2016, said he was the subject of numerous petitions during his tenure for blocking improper benefits from the procurement system.

“For nine years that I was DG, there were petitions flying everywhere. Fireworks everywhere. But after I left, for another eight years, no petitions, no fireworks,” Dr Eze said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He added: “The moment the current DG (Dr Adedokun) resumed, I noticed the fireworks and petitions have resumed again. It means there is something we are doing right which some people do not want. After I left office, I met one of those behind the petitions and asked why he had gone quiet. He said, ‘You blocked us from chopping.’”

Like every reformer, Dr Adedokun knows the journey demands courage, consistency, and collective resolve. Undeterred by naysayers, he has pressed ahead with reforms, backed by President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda.

Re-engaging Permanent Secretaries

To align Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) with the reforms, the BPP revived the Permanent Secretaries’ Retreat after a four-year break.

The 2026 edition, themed “Strengthening Procurement Leadership and Accountability for Effective Budget Execution and National Development,” held from Thursday, July 9 to Sunday, 12 July 2026, at Four Points by Sheraton, Ikot Ekpene, Akwa Ibom State, was declared open by Vice President Kashim Shettima.

Addressing participants, Dr Adedokun described public procurement as “one of the most powerful instruments of governance” and “the bridge between budget approval and service delivery.”

He disclosed that BPP has initiated 23 key reforms to align Nigeria’s system with global best practices. These include: Proposed amendment of the Public Procurement Act, 2007, Development of a National Procurement Strategy Framework, Revised procurement thresholds, Community-based procurement, Contractor classification and categorisation, Full rollout of Electronic Government Procurement (e-GP), and the Nigeria First Policy among others.

He also announced that BPP helped the Federal Government save about ₦1.1 trillion in 2025 through improved price intelligence and budget evaluation, with weekly savings averaging ₦8 billion since January 2026.

“Roads are constructed through procurement. Hospitals are equipped through procurement. Schools are built through procurement. Therefore, the quality of procurement determines the quality of governance,” he said.

Stressing that Permanent Secretaries, as Accounting Officers, bear ultimate responsibility for compliance with the Act, Dr Adedokun said BPP has introduced administrative sanctions for erring procurement officers and a Debarment Policy to blacklist contractors who violate due process.

He urged MDAs to publish contract awards on their websites and the BPP portal, and to comply with circulars on budget implementation, contract variations, and agreements.

Dr Adedokun added that Nigeria’s reforms are gaining global recognition, citing the Sustainable Procurement, Environmental and Social Standards Enhancement Project (SPESSE) as an evidence. Under SPESSE, specialised undergraduate degrees in Sustainable Procurement have been established in six universities: Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria; University of Lagos; University of Benin; Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University, Bauchi; Federal University of Technology, Owerri; and Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi.

“Development partners and multilateral institutions have acknowledged Nigeria’s strides in institutionalising transparency and accountability in public procurement under President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda,” he said.

“A budget is a covenant with the people. But procurement leadership is how we keep the covenant. Countries are developed by spending rightly. Only an accountable procurement system can guarantee that,” the BPP DG, added.

What Leaders Said

Representing the Vice President, Prof Tunji Olaopa, Chairman of the Federal Civil Service Commission, said procurement is now “a strategic instrument for economic growth, a driver of industrial development, a tool for promoting local content, and a mechanism for ensuring value for money.”

“It is an instrument of public trust. When procurement works, government delivers. When it fails, development suffers. The task before us is not just to comply with procedures but to strengthen procurement leadership, because no procurement system can outgrow the leadership behind it, “ he told participants.

Representing President Tinubu, SGF Senator George Akume, through his SSA, Prof Bernard Babatunde, said effective budget implementation depends on disciplined financial management and a procurement system that delivers value.

He lauded BPP’s reforms under Dr Adedokun and assured the Bureau of the SGF’s full support, adding that anyone involved in procurement fraud would be prosecuted.

The Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Mrs Didi Esther Walson-Jack, noted that procurement sits at the centre of governance.

“When procurement works well, Government delivers. When procurement is delayed, weak or poorly managed, citizens feel the consequences,” she said.

She urged Accounting Officers to insist on due process, value for money, and timely delivery, adding: “Creativity must never replace compliance, and innovation must never weaken accountability.”

The Takeaway

At the end of the retreat, which featured sessions on budget implementation, procurement planning, leadership, and institutional coordination, the consensus was clear: procurement must be seen as a strategic tool for economic growth, job creation, and national competitiveness.

* Omipidan, an author, journalist and media consultant writes from Abuja.

World.title: Football in Nigeria and the Teslim Balogun’s enduring legacies (1927-1972)
World.content:
Teslim Balogun

By Hon. Femi Kehinde

Harold Macmillian, the British Prime Minister, and his wife visited Nigeria in 1960 on the threshold of it’s Independence, to bid Nigeria farewell from the Union Jack. After the national reception and discussions in Lagos, he visited Ibadan, the seat of the Western Region. At the state dinner held in his honour at the Lafia Hotel, Apata, Ibadan, the Honourable Premier, Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola, rose after dinner to propose a toast to the Prime Minister and made a superb and exhilarating speech. That speech, featured the anecdote about an Alaafin of Oyo who was invited to be the guest of honour at a football match in Oyo and after watching the match patiently, he spoke to the resident:

“my friend, why are they fighting over one ball? Why didn’t they ask me to buy more balls for them, so that they may each have his own?”

Akintola’s extempore speech, was no doubt, apocryphal, but he brought the house down into tremendous laughter and applause. In the electrically charged atmosphere, Harold Macmillian rose to reply. Brushing aside his prepared speech like Hon. Akintola had done, he made a memorable response. His speech that evening took on a worldwide significance, for it was then that he served notice to all, “that the wind of change was blowing all over Africa,” which to him may simply mean, that wise men and educated elites were now taking over governance and Samuel Ladoke Akintola was one.

Players fight for the ball in football match (soccer) because retaining or winning possession is the most direct way to control the game, dictate the match’s tempo, and create scoring opportunities. Whoever controls the ball ultimately dictates the flow of play, shifting pressure onto the opposing team.

In the 50s, when Chief Obafemi Awolowo was the Premier of the Western Region, there was a football match at the Onikan Stadium, Lagos between the Western Region Football Team and another Regional Team. Chief S.L Akintola- the Deputy Leader of the Action Group and then serving as Federal Minister and Leader of the Opposition in the Federal House of Representatives National Assembly, Lagos and some other ministers in the Western Regional Cabinet joined the Premier- Obafemi Awolowo from Ibadan to watch the football and encourage the Western Regional Team to clinch the Trophy. The match eventually was breathtaking and confounding. The Western Regional team could not match the soccer wizardry of the other team. Despite the home advantage, the match towards the end of the day was still a 0-0 and there was a need for an extra time.

Obafemi Awolowo in demonstration of altruistic leadership and sagacity, stood up at the VIP box waving a white handkerchief to encourage his men. The premier was instantly joined by other leaders of the Action Group on the VIP podium, also waving at the Western Regional Team with their own handkerchiefs too. Behold, there was an instant reversal with the Western Regional Team. The Western Regional Team who had almost lost the Match, began to score -1-eeeeh!, 2-eeeeh!, 3-eeeeh!- in quick succession and eventually won the match.

The Late Alaafin of Oyo, Oba Lamidi Olayiwola Adeyemi III, then a student of St Gregory’s College, Lagos, living in the household of Sir Kofo and Lady Oyinkan Abayomi watched this football match and personally recounted this episode to me in one of our several private and intellectually engaging chats before his demise. Iku Baba Ye Ye. Leadership prompts success even in football!

The World Cup had come and gone, but its lessons are phenomenal. A sitting president of the United States of America USA – President Donald Trump, at a point intervened on the side of America during the recent World Cup placing a call to the FIFA president – Gianni Vincenzo Infantino to leave the suspension on Folarin Balogun to participate further in the match. Perhaps, this was the first presidential intervention in the FIFA record. In this instance, Donald Trump was not bothered whether Folarin Balogun was an indigenous Nigerian Yoruba Name.

In this season of anomie, perhaps it is now worthy of engaging our emotional investments on Soccer, rather than the murky waters of an endangered Nigerian politics. In encapsulating this emotional investments, perhaps football in Nigeria may be better captured through the life and times of one of its early pathfinders – Teslim Olawale Ayinde Balogun alias Thunder (1927-1972). Here is the story of a life of this soccer genius:

In this clime, it is better to remember with fondest and affectionate memory those people who had made us happy, and had impacted into our lives and essence, through their God given talents.

Tesilimi Olawale Ayinde Balogun was one. He lived a 45 years that was laced and filled with Soccer. After all, the Nigerian firmament is replete with stories of unsung heroes in commerce, politics, law, enterprise, education, sports, medicine, traditional institutions and so on. Football is arguably the world’s most important game. Football, that round leather ball, is mankind’s most beloved sporting game and ingenious invention. Its love, transcends religion, ethnic or political divides. This was the game that Teslim Balogun devoted his entire life to serve.

In the beginning

Teslim Balogun was born in Lagos in 1927. He attended St. Patrick’s Primary School, Oke-Awo, Lagos and St. Mary’s Catholic School, Port Harcourt, after which he moved back to Lagos to navigate his life, future and career growth.

His father- Oseni, was an international cricketer, but soccer was in his blood. His soccer ingenuity was noticed in his elementary school days in Lagos and Port Harcourt.

According to Teslim – “it must be because I even have to force myself to walk along the street ordinarily and not jog along, as if I had a ball at my feet “.

It was this urge that developed a footballer in Teslim. According to him-, “I not only wanted to kick things; many lads do, I wanted to be able to control things with my feet.

“I was a lad in Lagos long before I knew what the game was about, before I had even seen a football.

“I didn’t have a ball, so I got a hard unripe orange and tied it to a piece of string, then in any spare moment, even when I was walking across the road, I would dangle the orange in front of me and juggle it from one foot to the other.”

At the Saint Mary’s Primary School in Port Harcourt, his love for soccer became more than an interest but an obsession. His bow legs aided his skills as a footballer.

Club Career

At an impressionable age of 18 years, Thunder entered big football competition in 1945, when he played for the PWD second team and the defunct Apapa Bombers that won the second division Championship that year. Early in the next season, he transferred to the UAC, and later Lagos Marine, where he was quickly spotted out as a prospective great centre forward. He was from 1948-1950, Centre Forward for the Railway Club.

He was the live wire of the club, a forward line that knew no retreat. During that period, the club won all championship trophies. He had an outstanding feat. He scored a hat-trick against the Police Athletic club. This decided his soccer position as a centre forward. The match had an effect on Teslim’s football career. Referring the game was the Chairman of the Railway club, who recommended him as a member.

At this time, Teslim was an apprentice electrician, for a hobby. He took up printing, he became more interested in printing than in things electric, and was more interested in football than in anything. To an average Nigerian soccer fan, Teslim Balogun means the undisputed centre forward king, and the largest crowd puller of modern soccerdome. Teslim was quickly nicknamed “Thunder” and “Balinga,” the names that followed him around in the whole of his footballing career. To school children, he was “baba ball.”

The Nigerian Football Association was formed in 1933; a Daily Times Article of 21st August 1933 invited people to the NFA meeting held at the Sports Health Office, on Broad Street, Lagos and was open to a football interested public.

As of the 1938-1939 football season, the NFA, had been recognised by the Football Association of England. The NFA was not formally inaugurated until 1945, when a national team was put together.

In 1942, a cup competition, a world Memorial Challenge, limited only to Lagos based teams was started. The World Memorial Challenge was won by Zik Bombers in (1942), Lagos Marines, (1943,) Lagos Railways in (1944 and 1945) respectively. The NFA later inaugurated the Governor’s Cup to replace the World Memorial Challenge. The new competition became a national competition, and the first winners were Lagos Marine.

How he became a member of the first national football team at 22

The star players in the national team were Dan Anyiam (Lagos UAC)- a skillful player, who plays with his head as well as his feet. Anyiam was born in Nkwerre in the Eastern Region of Nigeria, in 1927. He had captained his primary school football team at the age of 12 years. Others were- Peter Anieke and Teslim Olawale Balogun (both of Lagos Railway).

Nigeria’s first National Team was named UK Tourists and after a few unofficial warm up games, went to the UK.

The team boarded the RMSS Apapa on 16th August 1949, for a playing tour of England and arrived Liverpool 13 days later. The players who made the trip were – Goalkeepers, Sam Ibiam (Port Harcourt), Isaac Akioye (Hercules, Ibadan); Defenders: Justin Onwudiwe (Lagos Railway), Olisa Chukwura (Abeokuta), ATB Ottun (Lagos Marine), Isiaku Shittu (Lagos UAC), John Dankaro (Jos), Hope Lawson (Lagos Marine), Dan Anyian (Lagos UAC), Okoronkwo Kanu (Land & Survey); Forwards: Mesembe Otu (Lagos Marine), Peter Anieke (Lagos Railway), Titus Okere (Lagos Railway), Etim Henshaw (Lagos Marine) and Edet Ben (Lagos Marine). Etim Henshaw was the team captain, making him our first ever national team captain. Teslim Balogun was the star. The team had no shoes.

Nigeria’s first ever official game was against Marine Cosby, which it won 5-2. During the next game, against an Athenian League XI, the English refused to play if the Tourists didn’t wear boots. The Tourists wore boots and lost, 8-0. The third game, which was generally agreed as the best, was a 2-2 draw with a Corinthians League XI. At the end of the tour of nine games, the team’s record was P9, W2, D2, L5. All five losses were with boots on.

After the tour, Teslim Balogun was signed by Peterborough United, becoming the first ever Nigerian football export. On the return voyage home, the UK Tourists took on the new name- Red Devils and stopped in Freetown, Sierra Leone. During the stopover in Sierra Leone, Nigeria played her first official game against another country, defeating Sierra Leone 2-0 on the 8th of October, 1949. Interestingly, one of the members of the UK tourists, Olisa Chukura, a native of Asaba in present day Delta State, veered off football, read law, practiced law in Ibadan, became a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, and died on the 3rd of September, 2001. He had a successful law practice.

One of his most outstanding cases was the 1983 Governorship Election Petition, between Bola Ige and Omololu Olunloyo. He was Bola Ige’s Attorney.

In the 1949 football tour of the United Kingdom, the English Soccer writers did not fail to see the qualities and soccer wizardry in Teslim Balogun. The Daily Graphics Sports Editor – Edgar Kail, remarked about him thus – “their 22 year old six foot three bow legged, giant centre forward, is a real artist and strange as it may seem in modern football, he holds the ball and uses it well.”

After the successful London trip, he wanted to play soccer off shore and also, learn more about printing.

He even as a spare time printer, ran into big trouble, when he sent a Nigerian 5 pounds note, to a printer in England and asked him to quote on printing 100,000 of them.

Going professional abroad

Teslim Balogun approached Mr. Darby Allen, the Secretary of the Nigerian Football Association and asked him if he could help him to join a football team in England. Allen, introduced Teslim to the Peterborough manager-Mr. George Swindin, the former Arsenal goalkeeper.

Mr. Swindin gave him a trial and signed him up. He became a professional footballer in 1955.

A coloured man in English soccer was a novelty!

According to Teslim, “I didn’t score. But the fans were pleased with me, and perhaps more important so, was manager Swindin. The goals were to come later, quite regularly. In fact, I finished the season, top scorer with Peterborough’s reserves.

“I thoroughly enjoyed the season-and not only because I was top scorer; the club did all they could to help me settle down in England, and I got a job with a local printing firm.

“I wanted to learn more about printing. On my return, I wanted to do two things: teach football and set up my own printing business. In fact, I wanted to combine the two and run my own football magazine.”

“I arranged to study at the London School of Printing. This meant living in or near London. Peterborough is over 75 miles away. So I got accommodation in London. To keep trim, I used to work out at the Paddington Recreation Ground.

There I met a Queen’s Park Rangers supporter. He suggested I should contact the club. I thought this is a good idea”.

“Soon afterwards, I got a letter from the Queens Park Rangers manager, Mr. Jack Taylor, asking me to go along for a trial. I was accepted. My ambition was realised. I was to play in the English League football.”

Not only was I to play, I was to score a goal in my first match against Watford.”

Retirement, return to Nigeria to begin coaching career

Thunder Teslim Balogun relocated back home in 1961 and became the first African to qualify as a professional coach. He was a coach for Nigeria at the 1968 summer Olympics. He was a member of the Nigerian National side for 12 years.

The 1954 edition, of Governor’s Cup, was renamed the FA Cup, in sync with the mood of the moment, after Anthony Enahoro had, in 1953, moved a motion for independence for Nigeria, at the Nigerian Parliament.

The 1954 edition of the renamed FA Cup was won by Calabar FC, who beat Kano Pillars 3-0 in the final. Meanwhile, the Red Devils were still active, playing a series of friendlies against Ghana, including a 7-0 loss in 1959. The NFA finally joined CAF, then followed this up by joining FIFA, a year later as Nigeria approached independence.

In 1960, Nigeria played against Egypt in a qualifying game for the Rome 1960 Olympic Games, its first ever international competition. In that game against Egypt, the Egyptians trashed Nigeria. The team was made to wear green, rather than the red, they used to wear. It was from that moment that the name of the team was changed from Red Devils to Green Eagles. Also, in 1960, as independence approached, the FA Cup was renamed the Challenge Cup. The 1960 edition of the Challenge Cup was won by Lagos ECN who beat Ibadan Lions 5-2 in the Final.

Impact on Nigerian football

This development was spurred by our first major triumph. Nigeria won the gold medal at 1973’s All Africa Games, which she hosted. In Teslim’s soccer career, there was a funny tale of a goal keeper, who died after trying to stop Thunder Teslim’s shot, that was usually as acerbic, as a Thunderstorm.

The likes of Christian Chukwu, Emmanuel Okala, Muda Lawal, Segun Odegbami Sam Ojebode, Christian Madu, Joe Apiah, Kunle Awesu, Best Ogedegbe, Haruna Ilerika and many others, broke into the National team in the 1970s, the new generation of players, qualified Nigeria for the Second AFCON, which was hosted by Ethiopia in 1979.

His demise

Teslimi Olawale Ayinde Balogun died in his sleep, on the 30th of July 1972 at the age of 45 years and left 8 children- Kayode, Tunde, Tokunbo, Olamide, Jibola, Iyabo, Bioye and Oluwole. He was married to Mulikat- a Table Tennis Player. Mulikat recalled that in the early hours of the 30th of July, 1972, she spoke and chatted with her husband, till about 2:30am, without an inkling of an unfortunate death. He was hale and hearty, without any untoward medical history. The Queen of England, sent a condolence letter, when he died.

As a befitting memorial and remembrance, the Teslim Balogun stadium in Surulere Lagos is named in his honour. The Teslim Balogun Stadium was officially opened in 2007, by the Government of Babatunde Raji Fashola as Governor of Lagos State.

The stadium, conceptualized in 1984, under the Administration of Military Governor Gbolahan Mudashiru, crawled and suffered so many hiccups, for about 23 years. As recently as 2006, it was occupied by homeless people and area boys. The stadium, with the capacity of 24, 325 people, sits adjacent to the Lagos National Stadium, Surulere Lagos.

The Teslim Balogun Foundation was also founded after his death, to assist the families of Nigerian former international footballers, who may have suffered financial distress.

Teslim Olawale Ayinde Balogun, may your soul continue to play soccer yonder, and also continually, find peaceful repose with the Lord.

Hon (Barr) Femi Kehinde, Former Member, House of Representatives National Assembly, Abuja, Representing Ayedire/Iwo/Ola-Oluwa Federal Constituency of Osun State, (1999-2003) & Principal Partner Femi Kehinde & Co Solicitors.

World.title: Return our IDPs to their homes before ranching, Benue leaders tell FG
World.content:
Plateau State Governor, Caleb Mutfwang

By Peter Duru, Makurdi

The three major socio-cultural organisations in Benue State have kicked against the Federal Government’s proposed pilot ranching scheme in Benue, state, insisting that the safe return and resettlement of displaced persons in the state must precede any land allocation for ranches.

Read Also: Plateau to return IDPs to ancestral homes when safe — Mutfwang

The leaders, who are the Presidents General of the Mzough U Tiv (MUT), Ochetoha k’Idoma, OKI and Omi Ny’Igede, ONI, said while they were not opposed to modern ranching, the policy must not be imposed on communities or implemented at the expense of displaced farmers and food production.

President General of MUT Worldwide and Chairman of the Benue Socio-Cultural Organisations, Air Commodore Titus Agbecha (retd), stated this at a press conference attended by President General of Ochetoha k’Idoma, Prof. Yakubu Ochefu, and President General of Omi Ny’Igede, Daniel Omeno.

Agbecha said the organisations received the Federal Government’s ranching proposal with “mixed feelings,” noting that ranching could help reduce herders’ incursions and improve food security if properly implemented.

He however, said the peculiar security and humanitarian situation in Benue made it inappropriate to embark on large-scale land allocation for ranches before displaced communities were returned to their ancestral homes.

According to him, “We currently have over 500,000 Benue people living in Internally Displaced Persons, IDP, Camps across Benue state. They have no home to return to, no shelter, no farms and no livelihood.”

He described it as unjust to discuss new land use for ranches when “the owners of the land are still refugees in their own state.”

The retired Air Commodore also alleged that several Benue communities had remained under siege for more than five years, with villages attacked and residents killed or displaced.

“Establishing ranches under this atmosphere will be seen as rewarding violence and dispossession,” he warned, calling for comprehensive mediation, restoration of occupied communities and justice for victims before the scheme is introduced.

The socio-cultural organisations further cautioned that large-scale land acquisition could threaten food production in Benue, which remains one of Nigeria’s major food-producing states.

“Benue remains the food basket of the nation. Any programme that involves large-scale land acquisition must not undermine food production,” Agbecha said.

The groups consequently urged the Federal Government to make the safe return and resettlement of all Internally Displaced Persons a priority, insisting that “peace must precede policy.”

They also demanded genuine consultation, consent and compensation for host communities before any ranching project is undertaken.

“We are not against modern ranching, but it must be voluntary, community-driven and must not displace food production,” Agbecha said.

He appealed to Benue residents to remain calm and law-abiding, assuring that the socio-cultural organisations would continue to engage relevant authorities through dialogue.

“Benue is the food basket of the nation. For Nigeria to be food secure, Benue farmers must first be secure on their land,” he added.

World.title: ‘Gunmen went from house to house, killing people who were sleeping’ – Survivors of Plateau night of horror
World.content:
File: Governor Mutfwang in an armoured vehicle during a condolence visit.

*Over 24 dead, homes burnt, farms destroyed in, Mangu

By Golok Nanmwa, JOS

It was another night of fear in Mangu Local Government Area of Plateau State.As residents of Bin-Per community in Kombun District went to sleep on Monday night, August 17, few could have imagined that heavily armed attackers were already closing in on their homes.

By about 11:30pm and into the early hours of Tuesday, August 18, the community was plunged into terror as gunmen reportedly opened fire on local vigilantes before splitting into groups and moving from house to house.

By the time the attackers withdrew, at least 24 persons had been killed, according to community sources, while others sustained injuries.

Several homes were reportedly burnt and farmlands and crops destroyed, leaving families devastated and a community struggling to comprehend the scale of the tragedy.

The victims were later given a mass burial.

But beyond the figures, the horror of Bin-Per was captured in the stories of survivors who watched loved ones disappear in the darkness.

For many residents, the most painful part was that the attacks took place inside homes, where families had sought refuge from the violence and expected to be safe.

An eyewitness, Daniel Musa, said the attackers moved from house to house, forcing their way into homes and attacking residents who were asleep.

“Our village came under attack in the early hours of today, Tuesday, by heavily armed persons.

“They were moving from house to house, opening the doors of people who were sleeping and slaughtering them,” he said.

Eight family members killed

The extent of the carnage became even more disturbing as residents recounted how entire families were wiped out.

A resident, Mr Fangwsak James, said eight members of one family were killed in a compound, leaving behind only a two-year-old child who survived the attack despite sustaining gunshot wounds to the leg and hip.

James said the child was left for dead before being discovered.

Another resident, Shedrack Ayuba, said he lost his wife and four children in the attack.

According to Ayuba, he was keeping watch over the community with other vigilantes when they suddenly heard gunshots from different directions.

“I was with some of my co-vigilantes keeping watch over the community when we heard shooting from all over,” he said.

Ayuba said he attempted to escape through a building but was shot in the leg.

“I managed to escape through a maize farm. My wife and children were not spared.

“They went into my house and opened fire on them while they were sleeping.

“I was taken to the hospital. It was the next day that I discovered that my wife had been killed,” he said.

Another resident said a man lost three children in the attack, further highlighting the devastating impact of the violence on families.

Residents said the attackers appeared to have carefully positioned themselves around the community to prevent people from escaping.

“They positioned themselves strategically and scattered themselves so that nobody would escape,” one resident said, adding that some people attempting to flee were also attacked and killed.

“They did not spare anyone. They killed everyone,” another resident, Tongret Rogo, said.

Vigilantes overrun

Ronbak Maxwell, another resident, said the attackers first opened fire on vigilantes before gaining access to the community.

He said the incident started at about 11:30pm and that about two vigilantes were killed before the attackers advanced into the community.

According to him, the gunmen divided themselves into groups and began moving from house to house.

“We called for help but the response was not fast,” Maxwell said.

He added that most of the casualties were women and children.

The attack also destroyed the economic foundation of many households.

Women protest killings

As the community buried its dead, women of Bin-Per took their grief to the streets.

Carrying leaves, the women staged a peaceful protest against the killings and demanded urgent action from the government.

They lamented the loss of husbands, children, relatives, neighbours and friends, saying the attack had left families traumatised and livelihoods devastated.

One of the protesters, Mrs Ladi Joshua, said the women were devastated by the killings and demanded an end to recurring attacks on the community.

“The scale of destruction is not merely an attack on individuals but an attack on an entire community, its dignity, livelihood, and future,” the women said.

They questioned how heavily armed attackers could repeatedly penetrate vulnerable communities and inflict such destruction.

The women also expressed concern over the effectiveness and responsiveness of the existing security architecture, saying communities were increasingly being forced to rely on themselves for protection.

According to them, the intervention of youths helped prevent the death toll from becoming even higher.

“Citizens should not have to become their own soldiers before they can sleep safely in their homes,” they said.

However, they stressed that community self-defence could not replace the responsibility of government to protect lives and property.

They called on Governor Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang and the Federal Government to urgently reassess security arrangements in vulnerable communities.

They demanded improved intelligence gathering, proactive deployment of security personnel and effective rapid-response mechanisms.

Assembly raises alarm

The Plateau State House of Assembly has also raised concerns over the attack and its wider implications.

During plenary, the member representing Mangu South Constituency, Dr Matthew Sylvester Kwarpo, raised a Matter of Urgent Public Importance over the attacks.

Kwarpo said more than 25 people were killed in Bin-Per, while another person was killed in attacks on Jwak and Murish communities.

He disclosed that 38 houses were burnt, while several hectares of farmlands, barns containing stored grains and other valuables were destroyed.

The lawmaker warned that the destruction of farms and stored food could worsen the hardship facing residents and threaten food security.

He urged the Assembly to convene a critical stakeholders’ meeting to examine the implications of the attacks on affected communities and Mangu Local Government Area.

Kwarpo also called for proactive security measures, stronger intelligence gathering, improved surveillance and timely deployment of security personnel to vulnerable locations.

He appealed to the Plateau State Government, State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA, humanitarian agencies and well-meaning individuals to provide relief materials, food, medical assistance and shelter to victims.

Governor orders intensified security

Following the attack, Governor Mutfwang directed security agencies to intensify surveillance and patrols in Bin-Per, Kombun District and other vulnerable communities in Mangu.

The state government condemned the attack and described it as a disturbing development capable of threatening the peace and security being consolidated across the state.

The governor sympathised with the victims and their families and urged residents not to embark on reprisal attacks.

He also called on residents to provide credible and timely information to security agencies to assist in identifying and apprehending the attackers.

Police vow arrests

The Plateau State Police Command has also moved to reassure residents.

The Commissioner of Police, CP Ayodeji Faniyan, visited Bin-Per for an on-the-spot assessment of the situation.

Faniyan commiserated with traditional council elders, the local government chairman and residents of Mangu and delivered the condolence message of the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu.

The CP vowed that the perpetrators would be identified, arrested and prosecuted.

“The Command will do everything within its constitutional powers to identify, arrest and prosecute those responsible,” he said.

Faniyan said security had been strengthened in Bin-Per and surrounding communities to prevent further attacks and restore confidence among residents.

He urged residents to provide accurate and timely information that could assist the investigation.

He also warned against jungle justice, saying taking the law into their own hands could further escalate tension and undermine efforts to bring the perpetrators to justice.

Attack rekindles old fears

The Bin-Per attack did not occur in isolation.

It came barely days after gunmen reportedly attacked Juwak Mai Tunbi community in Mangu, where properties, including tin sheds, places of worship and a chemist, were reportedly destroyed.

The latest violence has therefore revived concerns over the vulnerability of communities in Mangu and the wider security situation in Plateau State.

The attack has also attracted condemnation from political actors.

A scribe of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, in Plateau State, Hon. Jude Eli Dakur, described the killings as “barbaric, senseless and unacceptable.”

Dakur mourned the loss of innocent lives and condemned the destruction of homes, farms and property.

He said the killing of people who were asleep in their homes represented a grave assault on the sanctity of human life.

He called on security agencies to immediately mobilise and go after the perpetrators, while demanding intensified intelligence gathering and surveillance across Mangu and other vulnerable parts of Plateau State.

He also called for effective rapid-response mechanisms capable of responding promptly to distress calls.

The Plateau Initiative for Development and Advancement of the Natives, PIDAN, Central Zone, has called on the Plateau State Government to declare a state of emergency on security following the killing of more than 20 persons in Mangu Local Government Area.

PIDAN made the demand while reacting to the latest attack on Binper community in Mangu, where more than 20 persons were reportedly killed and buried on Tuesday.

In a strongly worded statement signed by its Chairman, Central Zone, Alpha John Dakwak and made available to newsmen on Wednesday , the group said the recurring attacks across Plateau had become intolerable and demanded urgent, decisive measures to protect vulnerable communities.

PIDAN said the latest massacre, coming amid a series of deadly attacks in the state, demonstrated that government could no longer afford to respond to killings with condolences and condemnations alone.

“Condolences are no substitute for security. Expressions of grief cannot resurrect the dead. What the people need now is decisive action, not another cycle of condemnation and condolences,” the group said.

It declared: “Enough is enough,” insisting that the magnitude of the security crisis required “extraordinary, immediate and unequivocal action.”

The group specifically urged the Plateau Government to declare a state of emergency on security in affected and vulnerable communities and take all necessary measures to protect lives and property.

PIDAN also called for the equipping, training and proper coordination of local vigilantes to complement conventional security agencies, particularly in remote communities.

The organisation further demanded a review of the current deployment of military personnel in communities.

It called on the National Assembly to urgently fast-track the passage of the State Police Bill, saying the move would strengthen community-based policing and improve security across the country.

PIDAN further urged security agencies to become more proactive through improved intelligence gathering, early-warning systems and rapid-response mechanisms capable of preventing attacks before they occur.

“The people of Plateau State deserve to live in peace, farm their lands and raise their families without the constant fear of being attacked,” the group said.

While expressing solidarity with the victims, their families and affected communities, PIDAN demanded accountability and decisive action from government.

“This is no longer a time for condemnation alone. It is a time for action the group declared.

World.title: 2027: Obi lists five critical questions that should shape polls, begins campaign in Onitsha
World.content:
By Vincent Ujumadu & Henry Umoru

TWO days after the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, removed the lid, 2027 Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Mr Peter Obi, yesterday, commenced campaigns in Onitsha, his homeland in Anambra State, in style.

Read Also: Governor Adeleke’s victory: Nigerians must replicate Osun experience in 2027 — Lawyers, activists

Obi, who said Nigeria can work and must work, unveiled his agenda in critical sectors and listed five critical questions that should inform the choice of voters in the election.

“Are Nigerians better off than they were four years ago? Can they afford food, education, and healthcare? Can businesses produce, expand, and create jobs? Can young people find productive work? Can farmers work safely and get their produce to market?These are the measures that matter” he said.

Addressing newsmen at his Onitsha residence to mark the commencement of his campaign, Obi promised that he and his running mate, Dr Rabiu Kwankwaso will defeat insecurity, pull people out of poverty, drastically reduce hunger and the number of out-of-school children, as well as improve education and healthcare and build growth that serves everyone, especially the most vulnerable.

He said that as the campaigns begin, all candidates for the election must be willing to present their credentials, defend their records, and subject their vision to open scrutiny.

“No candidate should hide behind the high walls of power, send proxies or surrogates to the hustings, and expect Nigerians to entrust them with the leadership of the country.

“Every candidate seeking the presidency must have the courage to come before the people, answer their questions, defend their records, and subject their vision to public scrutiny.

“True leadership requires presence and empathy. No one can lead from the front without standing with communities across Nigeria devastated by banditry, criminality, terrorism, and flooding. You cannot truly lead people you are unwilling to visit, listen to, and understand”, he said.

He expressed clear commitment that he and his running mate will take their message directly to Nigerians.

“We will listen to them, understand their concerns, and engage them openly. We will not delegate this duty to proxies. We will answer questions, defend our record and character, and present our plan to rebuild Nigeria.

“Any presidential candidate who lacks the resolve to travel across the country, meet the people, and respond to their questions lacks the capacity to govern it”, he added.

Obi said further: “I commit to commencing the journey of resetting Nigeria by uniting it, securing it on the path of economic and inclusive growth, and moving our country from consumption to production.

“The campaign period gives every citizen an opportunity to join the national conversation. I urge Nigerians to examine each candidate’s record and proposals, ask tough questions, and demand evidence behind every promise.

“We should debate ideas without hatred, compete without violence, and disagree without weakening the bonds that unite us. When Nigerians make their choice, that choice must be respected.

“Democracy does not end on election day. Citizens must continue to demand transparency, accountability, and results from those entrusted with the mandate to govern.

“Nigeria’s challenges are real, but so are its opportunities. We have the people, resources, enterprise, and creativity to build a safer, more productive country. Our task is to turn these possibilities into results. We have the credentials, experience, and record to collaborate with Nigerians on this transformative journey.

“Our journey will be harder if we do not unite as one people and one nation. A united Nigeria, guided by shared purpose and a commitment to fairness, justice, and equity, will make transformation easier, strengthen our institutions, and help us hold our leaders accountable.

“The 2027 election must be guided by capacity, competence, compassion, character, and commitment. Our campaign will focus on the urgent concerns of Nigerians and not on ethnicity or religion. Nigerians must reject and disregard any campaign driven by propaganda, ethnicity, religion, elitism, or cronyism.

“As my team and I travel across the country, we will listen to Nigerians, understand their needs and concerns, and assure them that we have the competence, character, and compassion to lead and reset Nigeria for the benefit of all.”

On the state of the nation, Obi said sustainable development requires more than reactive reform, adding that reform is not the goal, but that better lives are.

According to him, the World Bank’s April 2026 Nigeria development update made it clear that Nigeria’s challenge is how to turn economic reform and stabilisation into improved livelihoods, stronger human capital, wider opportunities, and inclusive growth.

“We will pursue practical reforms that deliver lasting results, combining fiscal discipline with productive investment, as Senator Kwankwaso and I have demonstrated.

World.title: Six months of Tunji Disu: Will he write his name in gold?
World.content:
IGP Disu

By Austen Yong

On August 25, Nigeria’s Police Chief, Inspector-General of Police Olatunji Rilwan Disu, will clock six months in office. Six months is certainly not enough time to measure the full performance of a public servant, particularly the head of an institution as large and complex as the Nigeria Police Force. But in policing, six months is long enough to reveal direction. Indeed, in security, 30 seconds can sometimes make the difference between life and death.

When Disu assumed command of the Nigeria Police Force on February 25, 2026, he appeared to understand that he had been handed more than a powerful office. He had been handed an opportunity. In his maiden speech, he said the confidence reposed in him was one he would “neither squander nor take lightly.” Those words provide an appropriate yardstick for assessing his first six months.

Has he used the opportunity? The answer, at least for now, appears to be yes.

Confronting the State Police question

One of the most significant things Disu did almost immediately was to confront an issue that several of his predecessors approached with considerable caution: State Police.

At his inaugural conference with senior police officers on March 4, barely a week after assuming office, Disu inaugurated a Steering Committee, headed by Prof. Ogunsakin, on the establishment of State Police. The committee was mandated to examine policing models, community security needs, recruitment, training, standards, resource allocation and accountability mechanisms.

That was an acknowledgement that Nigeria’s security architecture is changing and that the Nigeria Police Force cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while the country debates its future.

If State Police eventually becomes a reality, as it is wont to be, the Federal Police will have to lead by example through professionalism, national standards, impartiality, intelligence capability and institutional integrity. Disu appears to understand this.

The end of police impunity?

His second defining feature has been accountability within the Force. From the beginning, he directed senior officers to lead by example and strengthened the Complaints Response Unit and X-Squad.

Then came a significant demonstration of intent.

Following the extrajudicial killing of a suspect in Delta State, Disu publicly described the action as unlawful and announced that the officers involved had been dismissed from the Force, while the case was forwarded for criminal prosecution.

That sent a powerful message: the uniform does not place anyone above the law. It soon became a defining mantra of the Complaints Response Unit under Iniedu Inietie, now Force Public Relations Officer, that the era of police impunity had come to an end.

The principle is simple. The police cannot demand respect for the law from citizens while appearing unable or unwilling to discipline officers who violate it. If Disu can sustain this principle, he may eventually change one of the most damaging perceptions surrounding Nigerian policing.

Building policing capacity

Accountability is only one side of professionalism. The other is capacity. The first six months have also produced measurable operational activity. In April alone, according to the Nigeria Police Force, intelligence-led operations resulted in the arrest of 28 suspected terrorists, 85 suspected kidnappers, 62 armed-robbery suspects, 51 murder and culpable-homicide suspects and 54 suspected cultists.

The Force also reported the rescue of 189 kidnapped victims and the recovery of 140 firearms and 1,074 rounds of ammunition.

The establishment of the Violent Crime Response Unit is another institutional development deserving attention. It represents an attempt to provide a specialised response to serious and violent crimes rather than relying exclusively on conventional policing structures.

The same thinking is visible in counter-terrorism. Disu approved additional Counter-Terrorism bases in Madagali, Adamawa; Ikot Odo in Cross River; and Ode-Remo in Ogun State, alongside additional CTU personnel. These initiatives suggest an IGP trying to move the Force towards specialised, intelligence-led and proactive policing.

Policing with the people

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the Disu administration, however, is that it has not treated policing merely as a contest of arrests, weapons recovered and suspects paraded. There appears to be a conscious effort to reconnect the police with the people.

In six months he has engaged the leadership of the Police Community Relations Committee, a record three times. This is significant. In April, while receiving the PCRC leadership, Disu described the organisation as an important partner in intelligence gathering and grassroots security. He has also directed Commissioners of Police to strengthen town-hall engagements with traditional rulers, religious leaders and community groups, while making their contact details accessible to community leaders.

His engagement with young Nigerians on August 20 at the Police Resource Centre, Jabi, Abuja, further demonstrated this philosophy. This was the occasion of the National Youth Leadership and Security Dialogue, organised by the Nigeria Police Force as part of the 2026 International Youth Day programme, built around the United Nations theme, “ Different Contexts, Common Aspirations.”

Disu’s message was clear: young Nigerians must not allow themselves to be used as instruments of violence, particularly political violence, as the country moves towards the 2027 elections.

Politicians contest elections, but young Nigerians live with the consequences. Political actors may reconcile after an election, but ordinary Nigerians can lose their lives through electoral violence.

His warning therefore, extended beyond thuggery to carrying weapons for politicians, misinformation, digital intimidation and other forms of political violence. This is the philosophy of modern policing.

Sir Robert Peel’s famous principle that the police are the public and the public are the police is not merely a quotation for police academies. It is a practical security doctrine.

The police cannot secure communities that distrust them. Communities, on the other hand, cannot expect sustainable security while treating crime prevention as somebody else’s responsibility.

That is why Disu’s emphasis on community intelligence, public engagement and policing by consent may ultimately prove more important than the number of suspects arrested.

The human side of policing

There is also a human side to Disu’s leadership that deserves recognition. Despite the enormous demands of his office, he has demonstrated personal concern for officers and people beyond operational statistics. His visit to an ailing Assistant Inspector General of Police and his earlier conduct as Commissioner of Police in Rivers State, including his personal visit to one of the surviving pioneer women police officers, reflect a conception of policing that sees the human being behind the uniform. That matters. It shows that a police organisation is ultimately made up of human beings. An IGP who understands compassion, welfare and institutional memory is more likely to understand that officers cannot be expected to give their best to the country when the institution does not care for them.

His approval of the promotion of 17,952 junior police officers is another indication of attention to the human-resource dimension of policing.

There has also been emphasis on professional development, strategic communication and modern policing methods, with the administration pushing intelligence-led, evidence-based and technology-driven policing.

The 2027 test

Then there is the electoral question. Disu has already had important tests in Ekiti and Osun. The Osun experience, in particular, demonstrated how quickly political violence can become a policing crisis.

Disu personally intervened, ordered a crackdown on political thuggery and insisted that perpetrators and sponsors of violence should be arrested and prosecuted irrespective of political affiliation.

This is important because 2027 will be the real examination. The police must not only secure elections. They must convince Nigerians that they are professionally neutral before, during and after the ballot.

That will be one of the defining tests of Disu’s tenure.

Not yet Uhuru

But the IGP cannot solve Nigeria’s security problems in six months. Nobody honestly expects him to. However, he has established a direction. He has confronted the State Police question. He has spoken firmly about accountability. He has created new operational structures. He has pursued intelligence-led policing. He has paid attention to community partnerships. He has shown concern for police welfare. He has demonstrated a willingness to engage stakeholders outside the traditional police establishment.

Most importantly, he appears to understand that public trust is itself a security asset.

But expectations must now rise. The PCRC should expect deeper institutional partnership. Civil society should demand greater accountability. Police officers should expect better welfare, but also higher professional standards. Victims should expect investigations. Communities should expect responsiveness. And Nigerians should expect a police force capable of saying no to political pressure.

A test case for Disu’s legacy

The statistics of arrests, weapons recovered and suspects prosecuted will always matter. But they are not the ultimate measure of policing. The ultimate test is whether Nigerians begin to feel safer. Can a woman travel at night with less fear? Can a community report suspicious activity without fearing retaliation? Can a young Nigerian walk into a police station and expect to be treated with dignity?

Can a police officer refuse an unlawful political instruction, as outlined in section 137 of the Nigeria Police Act 2020? Can the police conduct the 2027 elections without becoming an instrument in the hands of politicians? These are the questions that will eventually determine Disu’s legacy. His six-month anniversary, therefore, should not be treated merely as a celebration. It should be treated as a checkpoint

The IGP does not need to be remembered as the man who solved every security problem in Nigeria. That would be an impossible and unfair expectation. He should strive instead to be remembered as the man who left the Nigeria Police Force better than he found it. He has been given the opportunity. He has shown evidence that he understands its importance. The remaining question is whether he can sustain the momentum.

Nigerians are hoping. And they are beginning to expect a different Nigeria Police Force. If he continues in the direction he has begun, history may eventually give him something every public servant craves but very few attain: a name written in gold.

World.title: 2007: PDP, ADC battle for opposition relevance, as US-linked IRI weighs in
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike

The significance of the recent engagements between the US linked International Republican Institute, IRI, and two opposition parties lies less in the courtesies exchanged than in the messages each chose to put before the same international election assessment mission.

Read Also: Governor Adeleke’s victory: Nigerians must replicate Osun experience in 2027 — Lawyers, activists

At the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, national headquarters in Abuja, National Chairman Abdulrahman Mohammed presented a party that was ‘fully ready’ for the 2027 general election. Two days later, at the African Democratic Congress, ADC, National Chairman David Mark was speaking about something else: the conditions under which that election would be fought, insisting that it must not become a ‘war or a do-or-die affair’.

PDP’s message: We are still standing

Mohammed’s pitch was built around structure, reach and voters. Receiving the IRI delegation at Wadata House, he stressed that the PDP remained a nationwide organisation with structures across the 36 states, the Federal Capital Territory and the 774 local government areas.

“But I want to assure you that the PDP is fully ready for the election,” he said.

It was more than a declaration of preparedness. By emphasising the party’s nationwide spread, Mohammed was putting organisational weight behind the PDP’s claim to continued political relevance.

His choice of Osun as supporting evidence was equally revealing. The recent governorship election, he argued, had demonstrated that Nigerians were willing to participate when given the opportunity to choose their leaders.

“You can attest with the outcome of the election,” Mohammed told the IRI team, pointing to the turnout and determination of Osun voters to make their choice.

ADC changes the question

Mark took a different view of the same political landscape.

The message was telling: the PDP was not merely describing its preparations; it was asserting that the party still possesses the national reach expected of a major opposition force. For the ADC, the emphasis was different: whether citizens could trust the electoral process itself.

There was little emphasis on party machinery or organisational reach when he received the IRI delegation. Instead, the former Senate President focused on the rules of the contest: peaceful elections, free choice, institutional neutrality and protection against manipulation.

“Elections should not be treated as war or a do-or-die affair,” Mark warned, arguing that citizens should be allowed to choose their leaders without violence, intimidation, manipulation or abuse of state institutions.

For the ADC chairman, the credibility of the 2027 election was ‘non-negotiable’

The PDP is presenting itself as an established political structure with the reach and capacity to contest nationally. The ADC, meanwhile, is using the language of electoral integrity to define the kind of opposition politics it wants to represent.

Both messages are aimed at a political constituency that will ultimately decide which party or platform can best carry the opposition challenge into 2027.

Osun exposes the fault line

The recently concluded Osun governorship election brings that difference into sharper focus.

For Mohammed, Osun demonstrated voter participation. For Mark, it demonstrated the dangers that could undermine an election if violence and intimidation become part of the process.

Mark referred to reports that no fewer than 30 people were killed in connection with the recently concluded election, using the episode to underline his warning that elections must not be reduced to contests in which political actors fight for victory at any cost.

The PDP can point to citizens who turned out to vote. The ADC can point to the circumstances surrounding that vote. One emphasises the willingness of Nigerians to participate; the other emphasises the need to protect that participation from forces that could distort it.

The same election has therefore become evidence for two competing political narratives.

IRI listens, but does not choose

And hovering over both arguments is the IRI mission.

African Regional Director Jenai Cox explained that the organisation was consulting political and other stakeholders to understand the pre-election period, preparations by political parties and issues that could require attention ahead of 2027.

The mission had also observed the Osun election and visited Ekiti, while its delegation included IRI President Dan Twining and former US Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazier.

Cox made no endorsement of either party’s interpretation. She said the mission would present preliminary findings and recommendations to stakeholders after considering its meetings and observations.

That gives the separate meetings a wider significance. Mohammed and Mark were not addressing precisely the same questions, but both were placing their political narratives before an organisation assessing the environment in which the 2027 election will be held.

The opposition question behind the meetings

For the PDP, the message was one of continuity and capacity: despite the turbulence surrounding Nigeria’s opposition politics, it remains a party with national structures and an established claim to the electorate.

For the ADC, the emphasis was different: opposition politics must also be about the credibility of the process through which power is contested and transferred.

The contrast points to a larger struggle within Nigeria’s opposition space. Organisational machinery matters. So do alliances. But so does the credibility of the electoral ground on which those structures will operate.

The question hanging over the consultations is whether 2027 will be shaped by political machinery or by credibility, and which opposition platform can make the stronger case to Nigerians.

What the separate encounters with IRI show is that the parties are already making different cases for why their version of opposition politics deserves attention.

The louder battles of 2027 are still ahead. The quieter one over structures, narratives, credibility and who speaks for the opposition is already under way.

World.title: Governor Adeleke’s victory: Nigerians must replicate Osun experience in 2027 — Lawyers, activists
World.content:
A screengrab from the video of Osun electorate escorting a bus carrying election results to a collation centre.

By Dayo Johnson, Regional Editor, South West

During last Saturday’s governorship election in Osun state, a video trended online where some residents of Ward Okerewe 3, in Ife East Local Government Area of the state, on motorcycles, followed a minibus conveying election results to the collation centre. On noticing that the driver of the minibus was making phone calls while driving, the vigilant residents started yelling at him: “Drop that phone, you are carrying our votes and you are receiving calls. We are following you and monitoring you, end that call now”. The driver had no choice than to obey them. Another video surfaced online after the election showing a large number of Osun citizens as they trooped to the INEC collation centre in Osogbo, the state capital on Sunday morning at 2:00am to watch the process and protect their votes.

Read Also: How Federal might came to Osun and met the people, by Stephanie Shaakaa

The incumbent governor, Ademola Adeleke was later declared winner of the election by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC. Many people have hailed the resilience of Osun voters in the midst of violence and their vigilance to protect their votes and ensure their votes counted. As the nation prepares for a general election next year, activists, lawyers, and other stakeholders have therefore tasked the Nigerian electorate to emulate Osun voters and protect their votes, saying the Osun experience was a signal to tyrants and a profound lesson in collective action. They described what happened in Osun last Saturday as a vital democratic strength and warned against complacency. Citing Osun as a template for 2027, they urged citizens to stay engaged until results are officially declared. While acknowledging the importance of protecting ballot integrity, they however insisted that such oversight must remain peaceful and lawful.

A democratic awakening — Prof Okaba
