World.title: Liberia: Golden Touch Pushes Back Against MPR/APM Investigation, Says Dukuly’s Role Was Lawful
World.content:
Golden Touch said that description was inaccurate and insisted that Dukuly’s involvement with the company was neither improper nor unlawful. “There is nothing improper, unlawful, or fraudulent about Mr. Dukuly’s involvement with Golden Touch,” the company said.

MONROVIA — Golden Touch Health Care LLC has mounted a strong defense of its operations and the involvement of Sekou Dukuly, rejecting what it describes as inaccurate implications contained in an investigation published by MPR News and APM Reports.

The healthcare company issued its response Friday, four days after the August 17 publication, maintaining that it has operated with a commitment to providing stable and long-term care to Minnesotans with significant medical and behavioral health needs.

Golden Touch said the report prompted the company to clarify its position, particularly concerning claims surrounding Dukuly and his relationship with the healthcare organization.

At the center of the company’s response is its rejection of the characterization that Dukuly was “moonlighting” in Minnesota while simultaneously living and working in public service in Liberia.

Golden Touch said that description was inaccurate and insisted that Dukuly’s involvement with the company was neither improper nor unlawful.

“There is nothing improper, unlawful, or fraudulent about Mr. Dukuly’s involvement with Golden Touch,” the company said.

The company did not disclose additional details about Dukuly’s specific responsibilities in its statement but maintained that his involvement with Golden Touch should not be interpreted as evidence of wrongdoing.

Golden Touch also defended the structure of its Minnesota operations, emphasizing that it works to comply with applicable assisted living laws and regulations.

According to the company, licensed assisted living directors are present in Minnesota to oversee the care and supervision provided to residents at its facilities.

The company said those arrangements are intended to ensure that residents receive the necessary care and oversight required under Minnesota regulations.

Golden Touch further highlighted its history in the healthcare sector, saying it has provided services since 2017 to residents with complex medical and behavioral health needs.

The company said its work has helped some residents progress toward greater independence, while its directors, caregivers and nurses have remained responsible for providing services throughout the year.

“Our directors, caregivers, and nurses show up 365 days a year,” Golden Touch said, adding that it stands behind their professionalism and compassion.

Alongside its defense of its operations, Golden Touch expressed sympathy to families who lost loved ones while receiving care from the company.

The statement said the company recognizes the significance of those losses and extended condolences to affected families before addressing the issues raised by the MPR/APM investigation.

Golden Touch’s response also took issue with what it described as political implications arising from the report.

The company suggested that some individuals could attempt to use the report for political purposes, but it maintained that such considerations would not change its focus on healthcare delivery.

“It is unfortunate that some may seek political gain based on the inaccurate implications made in the MPR/APM report,” the company stated.

Rather than engage in what it considers political distractions, Golden Touch said it intends to continue concentrating on its healthcare responsibilities and the people who depend on its services.

The company’s statement places particular emphasis on its commitment to Minnesota residents, arguing that its primary responsibility remains providing quality care to people with medical and behavioral health needs.

The dispute highlights the broader importance of oversight, management and compliance within residential healthcare facilities, particularly those serving residents requiring specialized support.

Golden Touch said its continued operations are guided by Minnesota’s assisted living requirements and that licensed professionals oversee care at its facilities.

Golden Touch said it will remain focused on its stated mission rather than the controversy surrounding the report. “Golden Touch will remain focused on what it has always done: providing quality care to Minnesotans in need,” the company said.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-VP Howard Taylor Remains Hospitalized in Police Custody as Bong Residents Rally Behind Her
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County — In the streets, communities and political circles of Bong County, the detention Wednesday of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has opened a new chapter in a political story that stretches from the civil war years to the highest office in Liberia.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected] & Webster Clayeh

For a county that once gave Howard-Taylor two consecutive mandates to represent it in the Liberian Senate, later rallied behind the political ticket that carried her to the vice presidency and watched her influence produce other elected officials, her current predicament has been met with emotions ranging from disbelief and sadness to defiance, caution and demands for evidence.

Howard-Taylor, a native of Sanoyea District, is facing serious criminal allegations following her detention at Roberts International Airport on Wednesday as she attempted to travel outside Liberia.

Her arrest has placed one of Bong County’s most recognizable political daughters at the center of an investigation the government says is aimed at dismantling an alleged transnational narcotics trafficking network.

But the reaction from Bong County shows that the case is unlikely to be viewed simply as another criminal proceeding. For many residents, Howard-Taylor’s political history has created a deep emotional connection between the former Vice President and the county she represented for 18 years.

Her supporters argue that the allegations must be proven in court. Others are questioning the circumstances surrounding her detention and demanding that the government explain the evidence linking her to the alleged drug network.

Still others say the investigation should be allowed to proceed without political interference, while insisting that Howard-Taylor, like every other accused person, deserves due process.

Howard-Taylor’s political roots are firmly planted in Sanoyea District, where her journey into national politics began to take shape. In 2005, she won election as senator of Bong County by an overwhelming margin, establishing herself as one of the county’s most powerful political figures.

Her victory was not a short-lived political moment. In 2014, she successfully returned to the Senate, winning another nine-year term and reinforcing her position as a dominant force in Bong County politics.

Her two victories meant that for 18 years she was not merely a national political figure with connections to Bong County. She was one of the principal political representatives of the county in Monrovia.

That history has become central to the current reaction. Residents who once saw Howard-Taylor travel between Gbarnga, Sanoyea and Monrovia as a senator and later as Vice President are now watching as she faces detention and criminal charges. Now, she is an accused person in a major narcotics investigation.

The Taylor Legacy and Bong County

Howard-Taylor’s political story cannot be completely separated from the political history of Charles Taylor. Her former husband, Charles Taylor, used Gbarnga as a major base during Liberia’s civil war before eventually becoming President of Liberia. The Taylor movement’s presence in Bong County left a lasting political imprint.

Gbarnga became closely identified with Charles Taylor’s political and military rise, and the Taylor name subsequently carried substantial political weight in the county.

When Howard-Taylor entered politics, that historical connection formed part of the political environment surrounding her. But over time, Howard-Taylor developed a political identity of her own.

Her two Senate victories demonstrated her ability to maintain an electoral constituency in Bong County, while her later selection as George Weah’s running mate in 2017 elevated her from county-level political prominence to national executive power. Her political journey therefore became intertwined with both the history of Bong County and the evolution of Liberia’s opposition politics.

2017 Changed Everything

The 2017 presidential election became one of the defining moments of Howard-Taylor’s political career. George Weah selected her as his running mate on the ticket of the Coalition for Democratic Change, a political alliance that included Howard-Taylor’s National Patriotic Party and the Liberia People Democratic Change. The partnership proved decisive.

In Bong County, the CDC secured victory in both rounds of the 2017 presidential election. For supporters of Howard-Taylor, the result was evidence that her political influence had survived beyond her Senate years.

The former senator had helped position herself at the center of a political movement that eventually captured Liberia’s presidency. Her influence was also reflected in the political careers of other lawmakers.

Edward Karfiah won election as representative of District Five in 2011, while Josiah Marvin Cole later won election as representative of Jorquelleh District Three. Those victories contributed to the perception that Howard-Taylor’s political network extended well beyond her own campaigns.

For years, her supporters viewed her as one of the county’s most effective political mobilizers. Her detention therefore has consequences that extend beyond one individual.

A Sudden Turn at the Airport

The latest chapter began at Roberts International Airport. Howard-Taylor was stopped from leaving Liberia and subsequently taken to the headquarters of the Liberia National Police. The action immediately generated questions among supporters and political observers.

The government, however, says the action was connected to an ongoing investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. Following investigative procedures and a review of evidence presented by the Joint National Security Investigative Team, Howard-Taylor was formally charged.

The Justice Ministry said the charges include offenses under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act of 2023, Liberia’s Penal Law and the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law.

Seven Serious Allegations

Under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act, Howard-Taylor is accused of unlicensed importation of a controlled drug or substance, unlicensed sale, trading, administration, dispensation, delivery, distribution, dispatch in transit and transportation of a controlled drug or substance, and illicit trafficking of a controlled drug or substance.

Under Chapter 10 of Liberia’s Penal Law, she faces allegations involving criminal solicitation, criminal facilitation and criminal conspiracy.

She also faces a money-laundering allegation under the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law. The government has also announced charges in absentia against three alleged members or organizers of the network: Croatian nationals Nikolai Ivancic and Mihovil Vrlovac and Ukrainian national Tara Zaderieko.

Bong County Asks for More Than Headlines

For residents like Marvelene Lepukoi, the seriousness of the allegations makes evidence even more important. Lepukoi has called

on the government to demonstrate independent evidence connecting Howard-Taylor to the alleged narcotics operation. “If Sheikh Basirou is truly the government’s star witness, then the public deserves to know exactly what independent evidence corroborates his claims,” she said.

Her position is that the case should be determined through the courts rather than public accusations. “If there is credible evidence against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, present it before the court and allow it to be properly authenticated, challenged, and tested under the law,” she said.

Lepukoi’s remarks reflect a central concern among some residents: whether the public debate surrounding the case is moving faster than the evidence that will eventually be presented in court. She insists that communication with another person, without more, does not establish participation in an alleged narcotics organization.

He said: “Bring the evidence, establish the connection, and prove the allegations beyond reasonable doubt.”

Emmanuel Weah of Gbarnga said the opposition should not allow Howard-Taylor’s detention to distract from the larger questions surrounding the country’s narcotics investigation. He argued that Liberians still need answers concerning the drug case and that the government must not use prominent political figures to divert attention from unresolved questions.

“The government must not be allowed to shift public attention away from the central questions by turning political figures into scapegoats,” Weah said. His comments reveal a suspicion among some residents that the case could become politically charged because of Howard-Taylor’s history and continuing influence.

But Archie Gboe, a Bong County native residing in Monrovia, approached the issue from a democratic perspective. “What a sad day for Liberia’s democracy,” Gboe said.

He described the repeated emergence of what he considers political witch-hunts as damaging to Liberia’s democratic culture. Although he acknowledged that nobody should be above the law, Gboe questioned the manner in which the former Vice President was stopped at the airport. For him, the government could have used established investigative procedures to request her cooperation rather than allowing the detention to occur in such circumstances.

Ebenezer Gotolo offered another perspective. Rather than immediately defending or condemning Howard-Taylor, he urged Liberians to recognize that being questioned or charged does not amount to being convicted.

“If a former Vice President is invited by the police in connection with an ongoing drug investigation, the matter should be approached through the rule of law and due process—not immediately turned into a political battle,” Gotolo said.

He emphasized that the fight against drugs should not belong to either the government or opposition. “An invitation for questioning is not the same as a declaration of guilt,” he said. Gotolo urged investigators to conduct their work professionally while protecting the rights of everyone involved.

His position may represent the middle ground emerging from the county: support the investigation, but do not abandon due process. Among the strongest reactions has come from Howard-Taylor’s home district.

David Gorlormator, a native of Sanoyea District, questioned the circumstances of the former Vice President’s detention. He asked why Howard-Taylor was allegedly not formally invited before being stopped at Roberts International Airport.

He also questioned the government’s broader handling of the drug investigation and whether all individuals alleged to have connections to the case are being treated equally. For Gorlormator and others, the government must demonstrate that its investigation is not influenced by political considerations.

Dr. George Toto, a native of Totota now living in the United States, responded to the allegations from a deeply personal perspective. Toto said he feels ashamed as a son of Bong County hearing allegations of such magnitude involving a daughter of the county.

For a county that has celebrated Howard-Taylor’s political accomplishments for years, the allegations have created a difficult moment. Residents are now being forced to reconcile the image of the powerful political figure they know with the allegations being brought against her by the state.

Victor Tokpah, a Gbarnga resident and Bong County native, said the government’s announcement has raised questions that should be answered through the legal process. Tokpah said he was neither defending Howard-Taylor nor suggesting that she should be exempt from the law.

He asked what specific drug, quantity, transaction, agreement or alleged proceeds form the basis of the charges. He also questioned whether the case involving Howard-Taylor is directly connected to the approximately US$317 million cocaine investigation or whether that connection is being assumed because the developments emerged around the same period.

Howard-Taylor hospitalized

On Thursday, Former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor was rushed to GIMS Hospital in Sophie, Monrovia, after experiencing a medical emergency while in police custody.

Taylor was transported to the medical facility Thursday evening under heavy police escort after health practitioners reportedly observed a significant rise in her blood pressure.

The medical emergency occurred as authorities were preparing to transfer the former vice president to the Monrovia City Court, where she was expected to face proceedings stemming from allegations of drug trafficking and money laundering.

Medical personnel were called to the Liberia National Police Headquarters after concerns were raised about Taylor’s condition.

At the Gomez Institute of Medical Science hospital in Sophie Community, scores of individuals especially from the CDC along with her legal team visited the former Vice President.

Former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwel Saah Kemayah went to the hospital a visit former Vice President Taylor. While Kemayah was allowed entry, three lawmakers were denied.

Frank Saah Foko, Marvin Cole, and Eugine Kollie were prevented from entering the fence of the hospital. “I don’t know the reason for which they are denying me other people went and the police have them assets. But it is ok, at the appropriate time we will have asset,” Montserrado County District 9 Representative Foko said.

He added: “We are to make sure that transparency takes place, that is all we are asking for. We are also asking the citizens of Bong County to be on their alert, to remain peaceful, democratic. The strongest person is the law. We are going to invade the laws; it is our hope that all uphold the dignity of the law.”

While at the Hospital, her legal team issued a statement that it has requested additional time to gather information it says it needed to support the ongoing investigation involving the former vice president.

In the brief statement issued Thursday, August 20, Taylor’s lawyers said she remains at Police Headquarters while they seek additional time to prepare and gather information in connection with the investigation.

“Let it be known that the Former Vice President remains at the Police Headquarters as her counsels have requested additional time to gather information in support of the ongoing investigation,” the legal team said.

World.title: Liberia: First Group of 20 Third-Country Deportees Arrive In Liberia, Secretly Whisked From RIA as Five Reportedly Refuse Disembarked Plane
World.content:
Monrovia — Liberia’s controversial deportation arrangement with the United States took effect Thursday with the arrival of the first 20 third-country deportees at Roberts International Airport, but the transfer was overshadowed by a dramatic standoff after five of the deportees reportedly refused to leave the aircraft and were restrained by U.S. federal agents.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The five men were among the 20 deportees flown to Liberia under an agreement between the Liberian government and the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump that could see as many as 1,200 third-country nationals sent to Liberia over the next 12 months.

According to The New York Times, the five men resisted efforts by American federal agents to remove them from the aircraft after it landed at Roberts International Airport.

The agents reportedly restrained the men for several minutes and eventually forced them off the plane. However, the five were subsequently returned to the aircraft.

The men were reportedly later flown onward to Equatorial Guinea, although the circumstances surrounding their reported transfer remain unclear.

The Liberian government has not publicly explained what happened to the five men, whether they were formally admitted into Liberia, or why they were reportedly flown to another African country.

Neither Liberian nor U.S. authorities had, as of publication, provided a detailed public account of the incident.

The episode has intensified questions about the implementation of the deportation agreement, including the legal status of the deportees, their consent or otherwise to being transferred to Liberia, and what happens when individuals refuse to disembark.

Five Refuse to Deplane

The confrontation reportedly began after the aircraft carrying the 20 deportees landed at RIA.

According to The New York Times, five men refused to leave the plane when U.S. federal agents attempted to remove them.

The agents reportedly restrained the men for several minutes before forcing them off the aircraft. The five were later returned to the plane, according to the report.

Their reported onward flight to Equatorial Guinea has raised additional questions about whether Liberia was ultimately their intended destination and whether other countries are involved in the implementation of the U.S. third-country deportation arrangement.

The Liberian government has yet to provide an official explanation.

Deportees Secretly Moved from RIA

The drama surrounding the five deportees unfolded against a backdrop of secrecy surrounding the arrival of the 20-person group.

Airport and state security personnel restricted journalists from accessing the arrival area and prevented local and international media organizations.

including AFP and DW, from observing the deportees’ processing.

According to a FrontPage Africa reporter at the scene, security officers ordered doors closed and were deployed at entry points, restricting movement in and out of the area.

Journalists later discovered that the deportees had already been moved from the airport without media access to their departure.

The group was reportedly transported from the airport in a bus operated by the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission through a back exit, rather than through the main arrival hall.

No interviews were permitted, and journalists were unable to obtain photographs or video footage of the deportees.

The manner in which the group was moved out of RIA has fueled criticism over the government’s handling of the arrangement and its commitment to transparency.

LRRRC Tight-Lipped

Officials of the LRRRC, the government agency responsible for receiving the deportees, declined to provide details about the group at the airport.

Staff referred questions to the commission’s headquarters in Montserrado County but did not provide information about the identities, nationalities or immediate plans for the 20 deportees.

The government had previously stated that the deportees would include nationals of African and Western Hemisphere countries, with most expected to come from Latin American countries, including Venezuela, Cuba and Colombia.

Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah has said the deportees would be received “as guests” and would have the option to apply for asylum in Liberia.

Secretive Arrival Sparks Youth Anger

The secrecy surrounding the arrival has also triggered frustration among some Liberian youths, who argue that the government should prioritize addressing domestic unemployment and poverty before accepting deportees from other countries.

Youth advocate Levi Levala told FrontPage Africa that Liberia is already struggling with unemployment and inadequate social services.

“We, the youth in this country, have nothing right now. No job. No support. And now these people are being brought here? They say America will sponsor them, but Liberia is already suffering. This is not the partnership we need,” Levala said.

“My message to America is: take them back. Liberia is not a dump site,” he added.

Levala and other residents of Unification Town argued that Liberia’s economic challenges make the country ill-equipped to accommodate large numbers of third-country deportees.

How the Deal Came About

The Liberian government announced earlier this week that it had agreed to accept up to 1,200 people deported from the United States who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

The government has described the arrangement as “entirely humanitarian” and not a “quid pro quo,” while acknowledging that Liberia will receive U.S. support to manage the program.

The Ministry of Justice has not disclosed when the next group of deportees will arrive, although the government expects the full group of up to 1,200 to be accommodated over a 12-month period.

Rights Groups Demand Answers

The agreement has generated growing concern among human-rights advocates in Liberia and elsewhere in Africa, particularly over the prospect of countries accepting deportees who have no meaningful connection to them.

Liberian human-rights lawyer and activist Adama Dempster said the government must answer fundamental questions about the arrangement.

“The issue of deportations is raising many concerns that can’t be left unanswered,” Dempster said.

“What conditions will they be held in?” he asked, while questioning other aspects of the agreement.

The identities and backgrounds of the 20 deportees have not been publicly disclosed, making it unclear whether any have criminal records in the United States.

The lack of information has intensified calls for the Liberian government to publish the agreement and explain the legal framework governing the deportees’ arrival, stay and possible departure from Liberia.

A New Test for Liberia

Thursday’s events have placed the Boakai administration under renewed scrutiny over an agreement officials have defended as being in Liberia’s national interest.

But the refusal of five deportees to leave the aircraft — followed by their reported onward flight to Equatorial Guinea — has raised fresh questions about the humanitarian, legal and diplomatic dimensions of the arrangement.

It also remains unclear whether Liberia is simply the destination for the deportees or whether the agreement forms part of a broader U.S. arrangement involving multiple African countries.

As Liberia prepares for potentially hundreds more arrivals, pressure is mounting on the government to disclose the terms of the agreement, explain the treatment of the first 20 deportees and provide a full account of what happened to the five men who refused to disembark at Roberts International Airport.

World.title: Liberia: Townships Accuse MCC of Withholding Millions, Crippling Services and Exposing Residents To Public Health Risks As City Government Remains Tight-lipped
World.content:
Monrovia — A deepening revenue-sharing dispute between the Monrovia City Corporation and several townships in Montserrado County has erupted into a major local-government crisis, with township commissioners accusing the city authority of collecting revenues from their communities while allegedly failing to remit the agreed shares.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The commissioners say the alleged non-remittance has gone beyond crippling their administrative operations.

They warn that the financial squeeze is now threatening public health, as some townships lack the resources to sustain garbage collection, clean drainage systems and respond adequately to sanitation problems confronting densely populated communities.

According to the commissioners, the failure to receive their agreed percentage of revenues has left township administrations financially incapacitated, forcing them to struggle with basic operations while residents face growing sanitation challenges.

The dispute has placed Liberia’s decentralization policy under renewed scrutiny and raised serious questions about transparency, accountability and control over revenues generated within local communities.

At the center of the controversy is a revenue-sharing arrangement under which the MCC collects municipal revenues within several townships and is expected to remit an agreed percentage to the respective township administrations.

But commissioners interviewed by FrontPageAfrica alleged that the MCC has failed to honor the arrangement for extended periods.

Some say they have received less than two percent of the revenues collected within their jurisdictions, while others allege receiving less than five percent despite agreements providing for substantially higher shares.

‘MCC Is Crippling the Townships’

Commissioner Edward H. Lahai of Oldest Congo Town is calling for an urgent intervention by the National Government, saying the existing arrangement is no longer serving the interests of the people.

Under the arrangement cited by Lahai, Oldest Congo Town is entitled to 45 percent of revenues collected within its jurisdiction.

Yet, he alleged that for more than two years, his township has received less than five percent of the total revenues collected.

“We cannot allow resources generated from our Township to not impact the lives of our people,” Lahai stressed.

The commissioner said the alleged non-remittance has severely weakened the township administration and affected its ability to maintain office operations and provide services to residents.

But the consequences, he warned, are increasingly moving beyond administrative inconvenience.

Lahai said inadequate financial resources are making it difficult for township authorities to sustain community-development and sanitation initiatives, potentially creating conditions for worsening public-health problems.

Garbage Piles Up as Resources Dry Up

The commissioners say one of the most immediate casualties of the alleged revenue crisis is sanitation.

With township administrations struggling to access their expected revenues, garbage collection activities have become increasingly difficult in some areas.

Commissioners say the lack of resources affects their ability to maintain garbage-collection tricycles and trucks, hire or pay sanitation workers, and respond promptly to waste-management needs.

The result, they warn, could be increased accumulation of solid waste in communities already facing serious sanitation pressures.

The problem extends to drainage.

Without adequate funds for routine cleaning and maintenance, clogged drains can remain unattended, increasing the risk of stagnant water, flooding and other environmental-health hazards, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall.

For township officials, this is no longer simply a question of accounting.

They argue that failure to release revenues needed for sanitation can directly affect the health and safety of residents.

New Kru Town: Less Than Two Percent

Commissioner Robert B. Teah of New Kru Town said the situation has persisted for approximately a year since the MCC, according to him, stopped effectively implementing the revenue-sharing arrangement.

Teah said that since 2025, New Kru Town has received less than two percent of revenues collected within the township.

He described the situation as a major challenge to his administration.

The commissioner said the lack of revenue has affected the township’s ability to maintain garbage-collection tricycles and trucks and implement pending community-development projects.

He said sanitation services are among the areas suffering from the financial constraints.

When sanitation equipment cannot be maintained, and garbage cannot be regularly collected, he said, residents ultimately bear the consequences.

Teah also disclosed that township employees are owed one month’s salary, despite government subsidy being provided to the township.

He wants the MCC to settle the revenues he says are owed to New Kru Town.

Although he indicated that the outstanding amount is substantial, he declined to provide FrontPageAfrica with a definitive figure when asked to substantiate the exact arrears.

Garworlohn’s Revenue ‘Lifeline’ Withheld

For Rudolph S. Buima, Commissioner of Garworlohn Township, the situation is particularly alarming because his administration does not receive a government subsidy.

According to Buima, the revenue generated within Garworlohn is effectively the township’s financial lifeline.

Under the arrangement, Garworlohn was expected to receive 30 percent of revenues collected within the township.

But Buima said the township has received only a fraction of what it was supposed to receive since the arrangement took effect.

He described the situation as disheartening, saying his administration is expected to serve residents without having access to the financial resources generated from the community.

“The revenue collected is what the Township depends on for its operations,” Buima said.

He said the MCC collects the revenues, while the townships were expected to meet quarterly to discuss collections and the division of revenues.

According to him, those mechanisms have failed to produce the expected results.

The consequence, he said, is an increasingly cash-strapped township administration struggling to meet its obligations.

Public Health Threat Looms

The commissioners’ concerns are particularly significant because sanitation deficiencies can quickly become public-health problems in densely populated urban communities.

When garbage collection is interrupted, waste can accumulate around homes, businesses, streets and public spaces.

When drainage channels are not regularly cleaned, debris and solid waste can obstruct the flow of water.

The commissioners warn that the combination can create stagnant water, flooding and unsanitary conditions, increasing exposure to environmental-health hazards.

They argued that township administrations need predictable revenue flows to prevent these conditions before they become emergencies.

For communities already struggling with inadequate sanitation infrastructure, they say, withholding or delaying local revenues can compound existing vulnerabilities.

Development Projects Also Suffocating

Beyond sanitation, commissioners say the alleged revenue crisis is affecting community-development projects.

Lahai cited Oldest Congo Town’s career-development and national examination programs for students, vocational training for women and girls, job-creation initiatives, support to schools and needy students, disaster response, drug-awareness programs and fire-safety education.

He said such programs demonstrate what township administrations can achieve when they have access to resources.

But he warned that continued revenue shortfalls threaten the sustainability of those initiatives.

“The non-remittance of revenues collected from the Township has left the office of the Commissioner struggling with office operations and increased service delivery to the people,” Lahai said.

A Direct Challenge to MCC

The commissioners are now demanding greater transparency from the MCC.

They want detailed accounting of revenues collected from their respective townships, the amounts transferred, the balances outstanding and the basis for any deductions or delays.

They also want the National Government to review the entire revenue-sharing arrangement.

For Lahai, the issue is fundamentally about fiscal decentralization.

“True decentralization must go beyond policy discussions,” he maintained. “It must give local authorities the financial power, systems and capacity to make decisions and invest directly in the development of their people.”

The commissioners argue that it is contradictory to assign local authorities responsibility for sanitation, community development and other services while denying them access to predictable revenues generated within their own jurisdictions.

MCC Yet to Answer the Allegations

FrontPageAfrica repeatedly sought the MCC’s response to the allegations.

The newspaper contacted MCC Communications Head Varney Diggs, who initially appealed for time to prepare a response. Diggs subsequently indicated that he would respond to FrontPageAfrica’s inquiries at 10 a.m. on Thursday, August 20. However, despite repeated calls, text messages and WhatsApp communications, Diggs ultimately did not provide a substantive response to the newspaper’s questions by publication time.

As a result, the MCC’s position on the commissioners’ allegations remains unclear.

Among the questions awaiting answers are how much revenue has been collected from the affected townships, how much has been remitted, whether there are outstanding balances, and whether the MCC disputes the percentages and figures being cited by the commissioners.

The MCC has also not publicly explained whether delays in remittance are the result of accounting discrepancies, disagreements over the interpretation of the agreements, or other administrative considerations.

Boakai’s Decentralization Agenda Under Pressure

The controversy comes as President Joseph Nyuma Boakai continues to support decentralization and stronger local governance.

Lahai welcomed the President’s position but challenged local-government officials to demand more meaningful fiscal authority.

He said decentralization cannot remain confined to policy documents and public pronouncements.

For the commissioners, the current dispute provides a practical test.

If local governments are to become engines of community development, they must have predictable access to the resources necessary to perform their responsibilities.

Lessons From China

Lahai made his comments while visiting the People’s Republic of China, including Litong District in Wuzhong and Ningxin Community, where he is observing local governance and community-development initiatives.

He said the experience is providing useful lessons on how local authorities can be empowered to participate directly in development.

He believes Liberia can strengthen its own system by giving local authorities greater financial capacity, stronger accountability mechanisms and clearer responsibility for community development.

A Crisis Bigger Than Revenue

What began as a disagreement over percentages and remittances has now evolved into a broader debate over the effectiveness of Liberia’s local-government system.

For the commissioners, the issue is not merely how much money is owed.

It is whether townships can continue to provide services when they allegedly cannot access the revenues generated from their own communities.

The consequences, they warn, are already being felt through weakened sanitation operations, difficulties maintaining garbage-collection equipment, unpaid workers, delayed development projects and inadequate drainage maintenance.

If these allegations are substantiated, the dispute could represent a serious failure of fiscal accountability within Liberia’s decentralization framework and as garbage collection becomes harder to sustain and drainage systems remain vulnerable to neglect, the commissioners warn that the cost of the revenue dispute could ultimately be paid not by government institutions, but by ordinary residents through deteriorating living conditions and growing public-health risks.

The Government now faces pressure to determine exactly how much revenue is being collected, where the money is going, what townships are owed and whether the existing arrangement is capable of delivering the decentralization Liberia has promised its citizens.

In Monrovia, the signs of a city struggling with sanitation are difficult to miss.

Along busy streets and densely populated communities, heaps of garbage can become part of the urban landscape. Drainage channels are often overwhelmed by waste and silt. During heavy rainfall, blocked waterways can turn ordinary streets into stagnant pools, while residents in some communities contend with the consequences of inadequate waste collection and poor environmental management.

Behind the visible sanitation crisis, however, township commissioners say there is another problem receiving far less public attention: the money.

Three township commissioners are now accusing the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC) of failing to regularly remit agreed portions of revenues collected within their jurisdictions, leaving local administrations without the resources they say are necessary to manage their communities.

On the surface, it is a dispute over percentages, but beneath it lies a much bigger problem: who controls the money generated in Monrovia’s communities, who accounts for it, and who ultimately pays when that money does not reach the local authorities responsible for delivering services.

Workers and township operations face financial constraints. Development programs are being delayed. And local authorities say they are being asked to manage communities without reliable access to the revenues generated within those same communities. The commissioners are accusing the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC), headed by Mayor John Siafa, of failing to regularly remit agreed portions of revenues collected from their jurisdictions.

They want records.

From Revenue Dispute to Public Health

The stakes become even higher when sanitation enters the equation.

A city’s waste-management system is a public-health system.

When garbage is collected regularly, communities are safer.

When drains are maintained, rainwater can move more efficiently.

When waste is removed from public spaces, the risk of unhealthy environmental conditions is reduced.

But when local authorities cannot afford those services, the consequences can accumulate. Garbage may remain longer. Drains may go uncleared.

Flooding risks may increase. Communities may become less healthy.

The commissioners say that is why the MCC and the National Government should not treat the revenue-sharing dispute as a routine administrative disagreement. They believe it has direct consequences for the quality of life of residents.

Mayor Siafa’s MCC Under Pressure

The allegations place Mayor John Siafa and the MCC at the center of a growing accountability debate. The corporation is responsible for collecting revenues under the arrangements described by the commissioners. The townships, meanwhile, say they are entitled to agreed percentages. If the money is being collected, commissioners argue, there should be a clear and verifiable record showing where it goes.

If there are outstanding remittances, the reasons should be disclosed.

And if the commissioners’ figures are incorrect, the MCC should publish the records necessary to correct them.

World.title: Conflict Management Committee urged to be vigilant during post-election period
World.content:
Chilanga District Electoral Officer Stephen Malenga has urged the Conflict Management Committee to remain vigilant and watch for early warning signs of violence during the post-election period.

Mr Malenga explains that the period immediately after elections is often tense, as some electorates may react negatively to unexpected election outcomes.

During the Conflict Management Committee review meeting, Mr Malenga stated that minimising election-related violence can be achieved through public sensitisation on the dangers of engaging in violent conduct.

“Even after elections, electorates are still prone to engaging in violence due to unmet expectations of the election outcome,” he said.

He added that civic education should target communities, youth groups and political party supporters to promote peace and tolerance.

“Therefore, it is the duty of the Conflict Management Committee to be alert and look out for any possible violence during the post-election period,” Mr Malenga added.

Meanwhile, Chilanga District Conflict Management Committee Chairperson Bishop Richard Sikazwe implored the committee to engage and educate various political party leaders to refrain from violent behavior.

Bishop Sikazwe pointed out that political party leaders must take responsibility for the conduct of their members and supporters both during and after the election period.

He emphasised that peace and unity should remain a priority as the district moves forward.

Bishop Sikazwe also called on various stakeholders to support efforts aimed at maintaining stability in Chilanga.

World.title: ZAPD offices in Kasam nears completion
World.content:
Construction works for the Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ZAPD) offices in Kasama District in Northern Province have reached 90 percent completion.

Kasama Municipal Council Public Relations Officer Andrew Munthali has confirmed the development saying the project is progressing well and nearing completion.

Speaking in an interview with the media, Mr Munthali said the completion of the ZAPD office will provide a dedicated and conducive environment for the agency to effectively deliver services to persons with disabilities in the province.

Mr Munthali said the project will also improve access to disability related services and strengthen coordination of programmes aimed at promoting the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities.

And Dean Dash Enterprise, the company contracted to carry out the works, says the company will deliver the project soon.

Company Director Dean Mumba who toured the construction site to assess the progress of works said the company is currently attending to the remaining works to ensure that the office is completed to the required standard.

The development of the ZAPD office is expected to contribute to improved service delivery by providing appropriate infrastructure for the agency to carry out its mandate and respond to the needs of persons with disabilities.

The construction project is being implemented in two phases, with Phase One costing K350,000 and Phase Two valued at K830,176 under the 2025 Constituency Development Fund (CDF) for Kasama Central.

World.title: Three plead guilty to trafficking in cannabis
World.content:
Three men of Kasama District have pleaded guilty for trafficking in cannabis.

Before Magistrate Chapson Silwimba, were Victor Siniza, 23 of Chiba Village, Patrick Mutale, 41 of Simbeye Village, and Pethias Mutale 27 of Mulenga Hills, all of Senior Chief Mwamba’s Chiefdom in Kasama District.

This was in a matter that came up for plea in which the trio pleaded guilty to the charges.

The three were charged with the offence of trafficking in psychotropic substances contrary to Section 15 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act No. 35 of 2021 of the Laws of Zambia.

Particulars of the offense were that Mutale, on July 8, 2026, in Kasama District of Northern Province, trafficked in 50 grammes of a psychotropic substance, a herbal product of cannabis sativa without lawful authority.

In a separate case, Siniza pleaded guilty to trafficking in 250 grammes of a psychotropic substance, a herbal product of cannabis sativa on July 9, 2026, in Kasama District without lawful authority.

Meanwhile, Pethias Mutale also pleaded guilty to trafficking in 3.4 grammes of a psychotropic substance, a herbal product of cannabis Sativa on July 6, 2026, in Kasama District, without lawful authority.

The matters have since been adjourned to August 24, and August 25, 2026 for presentation of facts

World.title: CSAWUZ congratulates President Hichilema
World.content:
The Civil Servants and Allied Workers Union of Zambia (CSAWUZ) has congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election following the just-ended general election.

CSAWUZ General Secretary Teddy Muyenga says President Hichilema’s re-election is a significant demonstration of the confidence and trust that the Zambian people have in his leadership and vision for the continued development of the country.

Mr Muyenga said the Union remains confident that the president-elect will continue providing leadership that will promote national development and improve the lives of Zambians.

He has also commended Zambians for peacefully exercising their democratic right during the general election.

He said the conduct of citizens during the electoral process demonstrates their continued commitment to peace, democracy and good governance.

The CSAWUZ General Secretary has since wished President Hichilema wisdom, strength and good health as he continues leading the country.

Mr Muyenga further wished the President God’s guidance in his continued service to the nation.

This was contained in a press statement issued to the media in Lusaka today.

World.title: New dates unveiled for Mopani Challenge ‎
World.content:
Mopani Copper Mines has announced new dates for the 2026 IRH–Mopani Challenge Cup involving Super Division giants Nkana FC and Mighty Mufulira Wanderers.

‎

‎The annual pre-season tournament is now scheduled for Saturday, 5 September and Saturday, 12 September 2026.

‎

‎The competition brings together teams from Mopani-sponsored Nkana and Mufulira Wanderers, featuring the men’s Super League sides, Young Nkana and Young Mufulira Wanderers, as well as Nkana Girls and Mufulira Wanderers Queens.

‎

‎The first-leg fixtures will be played at Shinde Stadium in Mufulira on Saturday, 5 September.

‎The return fixtures are scheduled for Nkana Stadium in Kitwe on Saturday, 12 September.

‎

‎

‎The Challenge Cup forms part of preparations for the new season, while proceeds from the matches will be channelled towards charitable organisations in Kitwe and Mufulira.

‎

‎Speaking on the tournament, Mopani Copper Mines Chief Executive Officer Charles Sakanya challenged both clubs to use it to adequately prepare for the new campaign.

‎

‎“As the Challenge Cup is part of pre-season preparations, I urge both clubs to field their strongest teams to test their readiness to compete for the Super League honours and continental qualification in the new season,” Sakanya said.

‎

‎Sakanya added that the event also serves a community purpose.

‎

‎

‎“Through this event, we raise funds for charitable causes. All proceeds will be directed towards selected organisations and individuals working tirelessly to uplift vulnerable members of our communities,” he said.

‎

‎The tournament will provide both clubs with an opportunity to assess their readiness ahead of the new Super League season, while also raising funds for charitable causes in the two Copperbelt communities.

World.title: CROP congratulates President elect Hichilema on his re election
World.content:
The Consortium for the Rights and Welfare of Older Persons (Crop) has extended heartfelt congratulations to President-Elect Hakainde Hichilema on his victory in the August 13th, 2026, General elections.

Crop Team Leader, Geoffrey Chiyesu has stated that the outcome of the polls is a clear demonstration of the trust and confidence Zambians have placed in Mr Hichilema’s leadership.

In a statement delivered to ZANIS in Lusaka, he has described the President- Elect, as a leader who’s governance has been anchored on humility, selflessness, Godliness, wisdom, and determination to transform lives.

Mr Chiyesu praised Zambians for turning out in large numbers to exercise their democratic rights, particularly expressing pride in the participation of older citizens, some aged over 100 years, who actively took part in the elections.

He highlighted that their involvement reflects appreciation of the government’s fulfillment of campaign promises, especially through social protection policies such as social cash transfers, cash-for-work programs, and pension reforms.

Mr Chiyesu pledged older persons’ continued solidarity to President Hichilema’s national development agenda.

He further called upon all political leaders to uphold democratic principles by respecting the will of the people, stressing that elections are a race whose outcome must be accepted as part of Zambia’s chosen path of democracy.

“The willpower of the people to choose their leader must not only be respected but also be seen to be accepted,” he said, urging unity and continued peace as the nation moves forward.

Mr Chiyesu also commended the Electoral Commission of Zambia for managing the electoral process with distinction, noting the peaceful atmosphere that characterised voting.

And CROP Stakeholders Engagement Adviser appealed to President-Elect Hakainde Hichilema to remain steadfast in upholding justice, protecting citizens’ rights, and ensuring no Zambian is left behind as he carries out his second mandate.

He further called for stronger efforts in promoting social justice and inclusion, particularly for older persons.

Mr Chisanga noted that senior citizens should not be confined to social welfare support alone, but instead be integrated into programs that recognise their potential to contribute to national development.

He stressed that equitable distribution of resources must be prioritized to build the capacities of older persons, enabling them to add value to Zambia’s economic growth agenda.

“Older persons should be embraced in opportunities that dignify them as a sector that can add value to the much-anticipated national economic growth agenda in their diversity,’’ he said.

World.title: Government addressing empty grain bag shortage
World.content:
Chitambo District Commissioner (DC) Marjory Mwape has assured farmers that the government will address the shortage of empty grain bags which is affecting Food Reserve Agency (FRA) depots across the district.

Ms Mwape said the concern had been brought to the attention of the government through the Ministry of Agriculture and that efforts were being made to address the challenge.

She said this after visiting an FRA depot in Mpelembe area where farmers raised concerns over the shortage of empty grain bags.

The Chitambo DC observed that the shortage of empty grain bags was affecting the smooth purchase and collection of maize from farmers in various parts of the district.

“This is not only a challenge in Mpelembe but one that is affecting farmers across the district. We have brought the matter to the attention of the relevant authorities, including the Ministry of Agriculture, and we will continue engaging FRA to ensure that the bags are distributed to the depots so that farmers can sell their maize without unnecessary delays,” she said.

Ms Mwape noted that the government was concerned that the shortage of bags, coupled with transport challenges in distributing them to depots, was slowing down the maize marketing exercise.

She added that the government would continue engaging relevant stakeholders to address logistical challenges affecting the maize purchasing exercise and ensure that farmers are able to sell their produce without unnecessary delays.

The development comes as farmers in Chitambo continue delivering their maize to FRA following the commencement of the crop marketing exercise, with the availability of grain bags being critical to the smooth collection and storage of the crop.

World.title: Lwandamina demands hard work
World.content:
Chipolopolo interim Coach George Lwandamina is demanding hard work from players as Zambia begins preliminary preparations for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign that kicks off next month.

Zambia will face Algeria away in Algiers on match day one in the first week of September, before hosting Togo in match day two days later.

Speaking during the local camp in Lusaka on Friday, Lwandamina said national team places should not come easily.

“National team places should not come easily. If there is competition in a team, then you have a team. If players can fight for places, then you have a team. Players have to work extra harder,” he said.

Lwandamina has named a 28-member squad for the local camp ahead of the qualifiers.

The assemblage is a mix of young players who featured at the Mukuru Four Nations tournament in Botswana and part of the group that played Argentina in a friendly in Buenos Aires in March this year.

He said local players must sweat to earn the few slots in the final Chipolopolo squad that will be dominated by foreign-based players.

“This is an initial preparatory camp and after a week or two we will reconvene more especially with the locals. As you may be aware foreign based players can only come two weeks before the games so we have to train with the locals hoping one, two or three will make it into the final squad. Foreign based players are active and that is where most of the team will come from,” Lwandamina said.

Lwandamina left out players who have club commitments with Power Dynamos, Red Arrows and Zesco United.

Zambia is in Group I of the 2027 AFCON qualifiers alongside Algeria, Togo and Burundi.

FULL SQUAD

Goalkeepers

Mangani Banda (Green Eagles FC), Victor Chabu (Nchanga Rangers FC), Bradley Mweene (Nkwazi FC) and Christo Chitambala (Kabwe Warriors FC).

Defenders

Jonathan Kalimina (Kafue Celtic FC), Headson Paina (Green Eagles FC), Joseph Mulenga (Nchanga Rangers FC), Jackson Phiri (Konkola Blades FC), Frederick Mwimanzi and Tinkler Sinkala (both Zanaco FC), Yoram Chanda (Kabwe Warriors FC) and William Kamwanga (Mufulira Wanderers FC).

Midfielders

Kelvin Mwanza, Given Kalusa and Chanda Chileshe (all FC MUZA), Humphrey Bwembya (Kabwe Warriors FC), Elliot Kampukesa (Nchanga Rangers FC), Nduna Zulu (Nkana FC), Francis Banda, Dominic Kanda and Ian Sindaye (all Zanaco FC), Golden Mashata (Green Buffaloes FC), Patson Kwataine (Mufulira Wanderers FC) and Kelvin Chipelu (Forest Rangers FC).

Strikers

Bridger Ngandu (FC MUZA), Abel Nyirongo (Atletico Lusaka), Derrick Bulaya and Rickson Ng’ambi (both Green Eagles FC).
