World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: Azerbaijan’s ambassador to Costa Rica presents credentials to President (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Seymur Fataliyev, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Azerbaijan to Costa Rica, presented his credentials to Laura Fernández, President of the Republic of Costa Rica.

This was reported by the Azerbaijani Embassy in Costa Rica.

In addition, it was reported that the ambassador conveyed sincere greetings and best wishes from the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, to the President of Costa Rica. President Laura Fernández expressed her gratitude and asked that her sincere greetings be conveyed to the President of Azerbaijan.

During the meeting, the ambassador briefed President Laura Fernández on Azerbaijan’s growing role against the backdrop of recent geopolitical developments in the region and emerging new realities, as well as on the country’s economic potential and favorable investment climate. In addition, he highlighted important achievements in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

President Laura Fernández congratulated Azerbaijan on the progress made in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. She expressed her readiness to continue joint efforts aimed at further developing friendly relations and cooperation between Costa Rica and Azerbaijan during her presidential term. The President of Costa Rica wished the Azerbaijani ambassador success in his diplomatic work.

The ambassador also presented President Laura Fernández with a book published by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation titled “Azerbaijan: Captivated by the Charms of Nature.”

World.title: Uzbekistan’s Fergana region explores new industrial projects with Germany
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Uzbekistan’s Fergana region is exploring new opportunities for industrial cooperation with Germany, including the development of manufacturing, construction, healthcare, pharmaceuticals and information technology projects.

This was reflected in the statement by the Fergana Regional Administration, following a meeting between Governor Khayrullo Bozorov, Bakhrom Tulaganov, rector of the Tashkent University of Architecture and Civil Engineering, and Abduvakhob Dadamakhammmedov, head of Germany’s ABM Anlagenbau & Maschinentechnik GmbH in Central Asia.

According to the Regional Administration, the meeting focused on expanding interregional cooperation, establishing new partnerships and developing joint initiatives between Fergana and German businesses.

''The parties emphasized that effective cooperation requires identifying specific needs and opportunities, developing proposals that meet modern requirements, and implementing them through clearly defined plans,'' the Regional Administration says, citing the meeting.

Particular attention was given to the experience of ABM Anlagenbau & Maschinentechnik GmbH in supplying industrial enterprises with modern equipment, introducing technological solutions and improving production processes.

Based on the company’s expertise, the sides discussed potential areas for expanded cooperation with German partners, including industrial cooperation in Fergana, mechanical engineering, construction, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, information technology, livestock production and manufacturing.

The meeting also highlighted the importance of transforming potential areas of cooperation into concrete investment and industrial projects.

''Effective cooperation should be based on a thorough assessment of specific needs and opportunities, followed by the development and implementation of practical projects,'' the participants noted.

Following the meeting, the sides agreed to identify priority areas for cooperation and continue negotiations aimed at developing them into concrete projects.

World.title: Hazar Logistik sees rail links via Akina, Turghundi as key Afghan routes (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Turkmenistan's Hazar Logistics sees rail routes through Akina and Turghundi as the most promising links for expanding transport cooperation with Afghanistan.

The company made the assessment in an exclusive response to Trend's questions about the outcomes of its August 6 meeting with a Herat delegation and prospects for developing bilateral logistics routes.

"Hazar Logistik considers railway routes passing through the Akina and Turghundi border crossings, which connect Afghanistan with Turkmenistan's transport infrastructure, to be the most promising," the company said.

According to Hazar Logistik, these routes could connect Afghanistan with Turkmenistan's railway network, the International Seaport of Turkmenbashi and international transport corridors.

"Of particular importance are routes integrated with Turkmenistan's railway network, the International Seaport of Turkmenbashi and international transport corridors, creating additional opportunities for cargo delivery to the Caspian region, the Caucasus, Europe and other destinations," the company noted.

The company said potential cargo flows could include several categories of goods as trade ties between the two countries develop.

"With further development of trade and economic cooperation, potential cargo flows could include construction materials, oil and gas and industrial equipment, agricultural and food products, mineral fertilizers, petroleum products, containerized cargo and other goods," Hazar Logistik said.

Hazar Logistik also considers the Afghan direction promising for the further development of international logistics, although it did not provide specific cargo growth forecasts.

"Hazar Logistik considers the Afghan direction one of the promising areas for further development of international logistics," the company added.

According to the company, future cargo growth will depend on the development of foreign trade ties, joint infrastructure projects, market demand and the formation of sustainable logistics chains.

The company also highlighted Turkmenistan's potential as a transit link connecting Afghanistan and Central Asia with the Caspian region and international markets.

"Thanks to its favorable geographical location and consistent state policy aimed at developing international transport corridors, Turkmenistan has significant potential as an important transit link between Central Asia, Afghanistan, the Caspian region and international markets," the company said.

According to Hazar Logistik, the August 6 meeting with the Herat delegation resulted in an agreement to continue professional dialogue, exchange necessary information and assess potential areas of cooperation.

The company said the next stage would involve further consultations and work on organizational and technical aspects of possible joint projects, including logistics solutions, transport routes and cooperation mechanisms in accordance with international conventions and Turkmenistan's legislation.

Hazar Logistik is a Turkmen transport and logistics company providing container, rail, road, sea, air and multimodal transportation services. The company handles import, export and transit operations and provides cargo transportation services across Turkmenistan, the CIS and international destinations. Its services are covered by licenses for maritime transportation, transport and forwarding activities and road freight services, while its management system is certified under the ISO 9001:2015 international standard.

The company has branches and offices in Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, China, Türkiye, Georgia and the UAE, including offices in Poti and Istanbul. Its services include rail freight, customs clearance, container transportation, maritime shipping and multimodal logistics. Hazar Logistik is also included in the official register of customs brokers maintained by the Customs Service of Turkmenistan under registration code GD-0066.

World.title: UNCCD: Uzbekistan's water security key to sustaining environmental gains
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Uzbekistan is emerging as one of Central Asia's key examples of efforts to combat land degradation and restore ecosystems, but growing water shortages and climate pressures could complicate the country's progress.

This was reflected in the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification's (UNCCD) regional thematic report titled Central Asia: Region of Ancient Traditions and Modern Perspectives.

The report highlights Uzbekistan's environmental initiatives alongside broader challenges facing the region, including land degradation, shrinking water resources, soil salinization and growing pressure on the Amu Darya and Syr Darya river basins.

Uzbekistan has planted saxaul across 2 million hectares of the dried Aral Sea bed, helping stabilize the exposed seabed and reduce dust and sand movement. According to the report, actual dust retention from these efforts reached 35%-40%, significantly above the initial forecast of 15%-18%.

The country's "Yashil Makon" initiative is also targeting the planting of around 200 million seedlings annually, while the government aims to increase urban green coverage from 8% to 30% by 2030. Uzbekistan has also expanded water-saving agriculture, with drip irrigation covering about 1 million hectares.

Trend's analysis shows that Uzbekistan's environmental policy is increasingly moving from individual restoration projects toward a broader land-management strategy that combines reforestation, water conservation, legislation and community participation. The country's national land-degradation neutrality targets, approved in 2023, include restoring degraded land, expanding forest cover and introducing water-saving technologies.

The report notes that forested areas across Central Asia increased by 6.4% during the period assessed, with Uzbekistan recording one of the strongest increases at 39%. Tajikistan followed with a 23% increase.

Trend's calculations show that Uzbekistan's reported increase in forested areas was more than six times the regional average, underscoring the scale of the country's reforestation efforts. However, these gains are occurring alongside a significant deterioration in regional water resources. The area covered by water bodies across Central Asia declined by 18.5%, while the decline in Uzbekistan was approaching 50%, according to the report. This creates a particular challenge because newly planted trees in arid areas require irrigation during their first several years of growth.

Water availability could become the main constraint on Uzbekistan's environmental restoration efforts. The country is located downstream in the region's major river systems and depends heavily on water flows originating in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, while much of its agricultural land is concentrated in water-intensive irrigated areas. The economic dimension further highlights Uzbekistan's dependence on regional connectivity. According to macroeconomic data presented in the report, Uzbekistan's 2023 exports totaled $24.3 billion, while imports reached $38.1 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of about $13.7 billion. The country's GDP stood at approximately $102 billion.

At the same time, Uzbekistan maintained substantial trade links with its Central Asian neighbors. The data show that Uzbekistan exported about $4.4 billion worth of goods to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan in 2023. In the opposite direction, Uzbekistan imported approximately $2.8 billion from those four countries. Central Asian neighbors accounted for roughly 18.2% of Uzbekistan's total exports and about 7.3% of its total imports in 2023. Uzbekistan therefore recorded an estimated $1.6 billion trade surplus with the other four Central Asian economies, despite running a much larger overall trade deficit. Kazakhstan was the largest regional market for Uzbek goods, with imports from Uzbekistan reaching about $3.04 billion. Turkmenistan followed at approximately $950 million, while Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan imported around $284 million and $142 million, respectively.

These trade links reinforce the importance of regional cooperation on environmental and water issues. Uzbekistan's economic relationships with its neighbors are already substantial, while the country's agriculture, energy security and ecological restoration remain closely connected to transboundary resources. The report identifies a structural conflict between upstream energy needs and downstream irrigation demand. Reservoirs in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are increasingly operated to generate electricity during winter, while Uzbekistan and other downstream countries require greater water availability during the summer agricultural season.

This creates what the report describes as a regional "water compromise" problem: upstream countries need water for energy generation, while downstream economies depend on predictable summer flows for irrigation.

Uzbekistan also faces a persistent soil-salinization problem. Secondary salinization is particularly acute in the lower reaches of the Amu Darya, including Karakalpakstan and Khorezm, where irrigated agriculture has historically placed substantial pressure on soil and water resources. Climate change adds another layer of risk. Glacial coverage in the Aral Sea basin has declined by around 30% over the past 50 years, according to the report. Accelerated melting could temporarily increase river flows, but the resulting decline in glacier reserves could eventually reduce the region's long-term water supply.

In Trend's assessment, Uzbekistan's experience demonstrates both the potential and limits of environmental restoration in an increasingly water-stressed region. The country's large-scale saxaul planting, expansion of water-saving irrigation and growth in forested areas show that meaningful ecological recovery is possible. However, Uzbekistan's position as a major downstream economy means that sustaining those gains will increasingly depend on regional water cooperation as well as economic interdependence. Its substantial trade with neighboring countries provides an existing foundation for deeper regional coordination, while the growing pressure on shared water resources makes cooperation increasingly important for both environmental and economic stability.

For Uzbekistan, the environmental challenge is therefore not limited to restoring degraded land. Ensuring reliable access to water, reducing pressure on irrigated agriculture and coordinating water and energy policies across Central Asia will be critical to determining whether the country's restoration gains can be sustained through 2030 and beyond.

World.title: Bridge between two cultures: New horizons in Batumi (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. With the support of and within the framework of projects implemented by the State Committee on Work with the Diaspora of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the M.F. Akhundov Georgian-Azerbaijani Charity Society has begun operating in the Georgian city of Batumi.

The head of the society, Rovshan Namazov, stated that the projects implemented by the State Committee on Work with the Diaspora, the educational materials it has prepared, and the cultural centers it has established play an important role in strengthening the ties of Azerbaijanis living abroad with their historical Homeland. According to him, the newly established M.F. Akhundov Georgian-Azerbaijani Charity Society will also contribute to bringing together Azerbaijanis living in Batumi, preserving national and spiritual values, and strengthening national identity through language courses, cultural events, and projects and initiatives aimed at youth development.

Rovshan Namazov emphasized that the society's activities will not be limited solely to preserving the native language and national-cultural heritage. The organization will also support the active participation of Azerbaijanis living in Batumi in the city's socio-economic and public life, as well as their successful integration into Georgia's multicultural environment.

The society's activity program for the near future includes teaching Georgian and foreign languages alongside the native language, organizing exhibitions introducing Azerbaijan's history and culture, literary and artistic evenings, and events dedicated to national holidays. In addition, it envisages providing social and moral support to compatriots in need living in the region, as well as Azerbaijani students studying in Batumi.

It was noted that this initiative will contribute to the further development of the existing friendship and strategic partnership between Azerbaijan and Georgia in the cultural and humanitarian sphere. The activities of the M.F. Akhundov Georgian-Azerbaijani Charity Society will serve to expand cultural dialogue in the region and further strengthen the centuries-old bonds of friendship between the two nations.

World.title: Georgia’s housing market holds strong despite rising construction costs
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Georgia’s construction costs increased in June 2026, while the residential property market continues to show stable demand supported by domestic customers, urbanization and investment returns.

According to the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat), the Construction Cost Index (CCI) increased by 0.9% month-on-month in June and by 3.9% year-on-year.

The annual increase was mainly driven by higher costs of transportation, fuel and electricity, which rose by 16.6% and contributed 1.9 percentage points to the overall index growth. Average monthly nominal wages in the construction sector increased by 1.8% year-on-year, adding another 1.01%age point to the index. Compared with February 2022, the Construction Cost Index has increased by 29.3%.

The residential construction segment recorded stronger monthly growth than other categories, with its index rising 2.6% compared with May and 3.5% year-on-year. The civil construction segment increased 5.8% annually, while the non-residential segment declined 0.1% compared with June 2025.

Despite higher construction costs, Georgia’s residential property market continues to demonstrate stable fundamentals, Galt & Taggart, an investment banking arm of Lion Finance Group, told Trend in an exclusive comment. "Price growth has stabilized. Based on our analysis, primary market prices rose by 6.1% year-on-year in May. We expect price growth to remain within 5-7% year-on-year, supported by stable fundamental demand, backed by growing urbanization, declining household size, rising incomes and attractive investment returns," the company said.

According to Galt & Taggart, the current market cycle differs from the rapid price increases observed in previous years, with demand increasingly driven by structural factors rather than temporary external shocks. The company noted that local buyers remain the main source of residential demand in Tbilisi. Georgian buyers accounted for 76% of surveyed primary market sales in the capital in 2026, while Israeli buyers accounted for 11% and Russian buyers for 3%.

In Batumi, the buyer structure is more diversified, with Georgian buyers accounting for 37% of surveyed primary sales, followed by European buyers at 18%, Ukraine-Russia-Belarus buyers at 16% and Israeli buyers at 10%.

Galt & Taggart also highlighted the continued attractiveness of the rental market. Tbilisi’s gross rental yield stood at 8.4% in May 2026, broadly in line with its long-term average of around 8-9%, while average rents stabilized at around $10 per square meter.

Earlier, Geostat reported that Georgia’s Residential Property Price Index increased by 4.9% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, with prices reaching 63.8% above the 2020 average. Trend’s analysis shows that Georgia’s residential market is entering a more mature phase after the sharp price acceleration of 2022-2023. While construction costs continue to rise, the pace is significantly more moderate than during the previous period of rapid market adjustment.

The 3.9% annual increase in construction costs remains below the price growth rates recorded during the post-2022 demand surge, indicating that developers are operating in a more predictable cost environment. At the same time, the combination of higher construction costs and stable housing demand is supporting continued price growth, although at a more sustainable pace. Trend’s calculations show that Tbilisi’s new-build residential prices have increased by approximately 63.8% since 2020, equivalent to average annual growth of about 8.6%. The changing buyer structure is also significant. The limited share of Russian buyers in primary sales indicates that the market has moved beyond the migration-driven demand shock seen after 2022. Current demand is increasingly linked to domestic purchasing power, investment returns, and long-term urban development trends.

World.title: Adelaide lacrosse community turns out to support girl, 5, with leukaemia
World.content:
Within days of five-year-old Margot Whinnen being diagnosed and treated for acute myeloid leukaemia, a tight-knit sports community has rallied in support.

Margot was diagnosed with the blood cancer last Saturday after she had described painful symptoms, prompting her parents Jesse and Nicole to take her for tests.

"She was really bad, complaining of a stomach ache, she couldn't move, so we decided to take her in," said Mr Whinnen.

"The blood test came back with some surprising results so she got transferred to the Women's and Children's and then we found out it was acute myeloid leukaemia."

Margot immediately began chemotherapy at the Women's and Children's Hospital, where she remains.

Mr Whinnen said Margot will undertake four rounds of treatment and will likely remain in hospital for months.

" We've just got to deal with it and hopefully she pulls through with flying colours. "

Lacrosse community comes together

In support of the Whinnen family, the South Australian lacrosse community held a fundraising fete dubbed 'Stick It 2 Leukaemia' in Brighton on Saturday, with hundreds in attendance.

A GoFundMe page established to support the family has raised more than $63,000.

"[It's] pretty overwhelming, very emotional but amazing that the whole community has gotten behind Margot and behind our family. We really appreciate it from everyone," said Mr Whinnen.

Traci Mathwin, a director of Lacrosse South Australia, said support for the Whinnen family had come in from across the globe.

"I drove up here this morning and you expect people to be a part of it, but I didn't expect people to be this involved," Ms Mathwin said.

"The kids, probably some of them don't understand, but the fact that they get to support Margot and Jesse and Nicole and [their] boys, Logan and Miles, is fabulous, it means a lot.

"Our community is a really tight community, so when things like this happen, even worldwide, World Lacrosse is on board."

World.title: For years, one man spearheaded a Nigerian government agency that didn't exist
World.content:
On paper, the Nigerian Presidential Foreign Intervention Promotion Council (PFIPC) looked every bit like an official government agency.

It had funding, an office inside the Federal Secretariat in Abuja, which houses many government ministries, and a website bearing the government's stamp of authenticity. Few reasons existed to question its legitimacy.

Until it emerged that the agency did not officially exist.

The revelation has triggered wider scrutiny of government institutions, with a second organisation, the National Brands Development and Made in Nigeria Special Project Office (NBDMNSPO), now also under investigation.

Here is how both agencies managed to operate under the radar.

A budget of $1 million

For years, Prince Adeniyi Adeyemi Matthew walked Nigeria's government halls as the "Director-General" of the PFIPC.

The role of the agency was purportedly to attract foreign investment, aid and partnerships into Africa's most populous country.

It had what looked like a legitimate website, maintained a social media presence, and even won approval to hire more than 300 staff.

The Instagram account of the fictitious PFIPC is still active. (Instagram:_pfipc)

Adeyemi even met with government officials, including cabinet ministers, financial regulators, the head of Nigeria's anti-corruption agency and foreign diplomats.

So, after almost two years, what triggered the alarm bells?

Well, in 2025, officials from the Nigerian Investment Promotion Council wrote to the presidency to complain about Adeyemi's activities, noting that his agency appeared to function at "cross-purposes" with it.

Then a few months later, Femi Gbajabiamila, the president's chief of staff, wrote to police alleging that his signature, along with official seals and reference numbers, had been forged by Adeyemi.

"The fake documents, bearing falsified signatures, reference/folio numbers, and seals, have been used to claim leadership appointments to non-existent entities, with particular reference to the PFIPC," Gbajabiamila wrote.

Local reports said Adeyemi claimed he was given the PFIPC director-general appointment letter by Gbajabiamila, who has denied knowing him.

"Politicians and members of the public who are weaponising Adeyemi's claim against the chief of staff should refrain from swallowing his narrative hook, line and sinker," the presidency said in a statement defending Gbajabiamila.

In a July 1, 2026 statement, the Nigerian presidency also claimed Adeyemi misled the country's accountant-general's office into opening 34 bank accounts for the PFIPC, including with the Central Bank of Nigeria.

The fake agencies flew under Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's nose. (Reuters: Kin Cheung)

When the 2026 national budget was signed into law, the PFIPC was included with an allocation of 1.3 billion naira ($1.3 million).

However, according to the police and the accountant-general's office, no government money was transferred into any of the bank accounts.

Following the revelation, Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu directed the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) to investigate and submit a comprehensive report.

The report, published on August 8, found Adeyemi was never appointed by "any authority of government" and that he should be prosecuted.

It stressed that the investigation was still ongoing, particularly to identify other persons who may have participated in or facilitated the alleged scheme.

What about the other fake agency?

There is little information on the NBDMNSPO.

That is because its discovery as a fake agency was only recently announced by the ICPC.

However, the ICPC did reveal the NBDMNSPO was spearheaded by George Buchi Nwabueze, who allegedly operated with the assistance of suspected collaborators within the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (OSGF).

A photo that purports to be George Buchi Nwabueze. (Instagram: pmainpro)

It said the investigation found that Nwabueze used four variations of his name while running the illegal operation.

Musa Adamu Aliyu, the head of the ICPC, did not say whether Nwabueze had profited from the scheme before it was uncovered.

On the NBDMNSPO website's "vision and mission page", it says the agency's purpose is "Transforming The National From A Resource Dependent Nation Into A Vibrant Hub of Production Oriented Manufacturing Country".

What were they charged with?

Adeyemi was charged with eight offences, including forgery and impersonation.

After failing to appear at a hearing to face the charges, the Federal High Court issued a warrant for Adeyemi.

After weeks in hiding fearing his safety, he was arrested in Osun State in south-western Nigeria.

Adeyemi has maintained his innocence in interviews with local media.

Two of his accomplices have also been charged.

Meanwhile, authorities have issued an arrest warrant for Nwabueze while his collaborators MS Danjuma, Engr Nandungu Gagare and Richard Pheelangwa were suspended from the OSGF.

World.title: Delhi's electric tuktuk boom gets a hacking shock
World.content:
Few sights and sounds are as familiar in Delhi as colourful auto rickshaws and the rhythmic beat of their engines.

The same could be said of the Indian capital's notorious air pollution, fed in part by the three-wheelers' belching exhausts.

Indrajeet Sachdeva has been driving one for decades, earning a few hundred rupees a day.

Now, he says his career is at risk after Delhi's government announced a ban on new non-electric rickshaws from January 2027.

From April 2028, the ban will extend to new motorcycles and scooters as well, slowly replacing more than 6 million small vehicles registered in the city in a bid to clean its persistent smog.

"This policy is like bringing a mongoose to kill a snake. What will we do if the mongoose kills us?" Mr Sachdeva said.

More than 95,000 auto rickshaws are registered in the Delhi National Capital Territory. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Tuktuk no more

Since the 50s, rickshaws with two-stroke engines have become notorious for their iconic tuktuk sound and smoky exhausts, contributing to harmful smog in Delhi and other large Asian cities.

India's Supreme Court mandated Delhi's rickshaws switch to compressed natural gas (CNG) in 2001 to help clean the city's air, but the problem hasn't gone away.

In 2025, air quality tracking service IQAir ranked Delhi's urban area as the most polluted on Earth.

Delhi's toxic smog compared to smoking 50 cigarettes a day Delhi's notorious air pollution kills thousands. Can it be fixed?

"Estimates vary between one-third to 50 per cent [of Delhi's pollution] coming from transport," International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) India director Amit Bhatt said.

"We've found that CNG vehicles are not so clean when it comes to nitrogen oxide emissions, and nitrogen oxides lead to secondary particulate matter [in the air]."

Despite the persistent pollution, many rickshaw drivers still consider CNG a clean alternative to petrol and fear losing their income to another change.

"I have been driving an auto since 2002 and [an electric rickshaw] costs 250,000 to 300,000 rupees ($3,700-$4,400)," rickshaw driver Suraj Kumar Gupta said.

" If I buy in this age, I would be tired paying interest on the loan. Either the auto will get old or I will. "

Mr Sachdeva, who leads a welfare group for rickshaw drivers in the city, said they were planning a legal challenge before the restrictions in January.

Electric rickshaw revolution

Sunitha Anup is a researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation in India. (ABC News: Som Patidar)

Regardless of the challenge, they may soon be outnumbered by others who have already switched.

ICCT researcher Sunitha Anup said their analysis indicated around half of India's rickshaws were already electric, a far higher percentage than any other class of vehicle.

"For four-wheelers, it's around 4 per cent," she said.

Other South and South-East Asian countries have also embraced electric scooters, motorcycles and rickshaws far more than electric cars.

India's micro-EV boom has been partly supported by imported components that can be easily adapted for use by local manufacturers.

However, just days after Delhi's cabinet signed its new EV policy into law, the drivers of those affordable electric rickshaws were given a rude shock.

Battery hacking

In July, videos began to spread online showing electric rickshaws stopping dead on Delhi's streets.

The hack was simple and spread quickly: scammers would download a free battery management app, scan for passing vehicles with unsecured Bluetooth connections, then use the app to disable the battery remotely.

Loading Instagram content

Some would use this opportunity to extort money from the driver.

The Indian government responded quickly, ordering Google and Apple to remove some Chinese battery management apps from app stores.

Experts have warned that many of Delhi's electric rickshaws are still vulnerable.

"These [banned] apps are not the only apps; anybody can write such an app and share it," International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad director Sandeep Kumar Shukla said.

"We have these battery packs being imported and being fitted into vehicles without any cybersecurity compliance check.

" In fact, there is no guideline or compliance requirement [in India] against which it can be checked. "

Incoming surge

As organised and vocal as Delhi's rickshaw drivers may be, they are far outnumbered by the city's motorcycles and scooters.

With the ban on new non-electric two-wheeled vehicles starting in April 2028, the countdown is on to prepare the electrical grid for a surge in charging.

ICCT's Mr Bhatt said the smaller size of two- and three-wheeled EVs would make the transition easier for Delhi's infrastructure but admitted that access to chargers would be an obstacle for many.

Electric rickshaw drivers have reported technical issues at swappable battery charge points in Delhi. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

"Two-wheelers and three-wheelers do not require the massive public charging which a truck or a bus or even a car would require; a lot of charging will happen at home," Mr Bhatt said.

However, he conceded that after owning an EV himself for four years in Delhi, he still hadn't been permitted to install a charger at his home.

"My resident welfare association is saying, 'What if it catches fire because there is no [regulation or guidelines] on how to go about setting up this charging?'" he said.

This Delhi public charger listed four batteries as ready but then said none were available when a request was made. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Driver Indrajeet Sachdeva estimated 90 per cent of rickshaw owners did not have a space at home to install chargers.

At one of Delhi's public charging stations for swappable batteries, the ABC watched drivers waiting while the machine's display listed four batteries were ready.

When a battery was requested from the machine, a pop-up message said none were available.

Mr Sachdeva said issues like this meant the government needed to give the industry more time before going all-in on electrification.

Delhi's chief minister's office did not respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Teen hospitalised on NSW Central Coast after alleged stabbing
World.content:
A teenage boy has undergone surgery after he was allegedly stabbed at Terrigal on the NSW Central Coast on Friday night.

Emergency services were called to a home on Painters Lane about 9:45pm, with paramedics treating the 15-year-old for an alleged stab wound, before he was taken to Gosford Hospital in a critical condition.

Officers with Brisbane Water Police District set up a crime scene, with investigations focusing on two groups of teenagers that were reportedly in the area at the time.

"Those two groups met up in the Terrigal area; they appear to have gone to Painters Lane," Brisbane Water Police District, Detective Chief Inspector John Zdrilic said.

"The reason is unclear as to why they did that, and an incident has occurred which has resulted in the [alleged] stabbing of the 15-year-old male.

"The 15-year-old who was [allegedly] stabbed was there with two mates, and they met up with another group that could have numbered up to five."

Detective Chief Inspector Zdrilic said it is believed at this stage that there was no confrontation between the two groups in Painters Lane.

Brisbane Water Police District, Detective Chief Inspector John Zdrilic. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

"[Police are investigating] one, the reason as to why they've gone into Painters Lane and, two, whether there's a previous relationship between these two groups," he said.

"The boy approached a home at Painters Lane to seek help, with residents calling 000.

"It appeared to be a single stab wound to the left side, heavy bleeding. [An] ambulance attended fairly quickly and he was conveyed to Gosford [Hospital]."

Knife warning

Brisbane Water Police District has established a strike force to investigate what led to the alleged stabbing.

Detective Chief Inspector Zdrilic said a weapon has not been found, and investigators are yet to identify a person of interest.

"We're interested in speaking with members of that second group, to assist us with our inquiries," he said.

"Youths walking around the place with knives is not on. We constantly have operations to take knives off the streets.

" One knife out there is one too many, and if you are found in a public place without a lawful reason for a knife, we will take action. "

NSW Police has asked anyone with information, CCTV footage or dash-cam footage from the area to come forward.

World.title: Mundi Mundi offers music fans complimentary day amid improved weather
World.content:
Thousands had to be turned away from the Mundi Mundi Bash outback music festival in Broken Hill after record rainfall turned its campground into a field of mud this week.

But two relatively dry days — and welcome sunshine for the final day — has seen organisers open the gates for hangers-on to come into the festival free of charge.

The Mundi Mundi Bash has continued despite substantial rainfall on the festival site forcing organisers to turn some ticketholders away. (ABC News)

"The sun came out yesterday, it's out again today [and] any of those people who were turned away who are still hanging around Broken Hill, we're going to let them come in today," the event's founder and organiser Greg Donovan told ABC Weekend Breakfast.

Mr Donovan said the event's full program had been fulfilled, including performances from Jessica Mauboy, Troy Cassar Daly and the Teskey Brothers. The final day is set to feature The Whitlams, Baby Animals, John Butler and Jon Stevens.

Around 10,000 ticketholders were able to attend the event, despite many being locked out. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Safety first as region sees a third of its annual rainfall

The Mundi Mundi site saw around 75mm of rainfall over an 11-day period, according to Mr Donovan.

"To put that into context, the rain we've had just over this little period amounts to one-third of the annual rainfall for Broken Hill," he said.

The decision to restrict entry to the campsite was made after many vehicles became bogged in the mud as arrivals were checked in on Monday night.

Cars queue up to enter the flooded Mundi Mundi Bash campsite. (ABC News)

"We had another 2,000 coming the following day, there was just no way the campsite had the ability to take that many more people … 25 to 30 per cent of the campsite became unusable," said Mr Donovan.

He said around 10,000 were still able to see the festival. Around 15,000 people were originally ticketed to enter.

World.title: Wallaroos hammered in historic 100th Test by ruthless Black Ferns
World.content:
The Wallaroos' 100th Test match, and the Test debut of Australia's all-time leading rugby 7s try-scorer, has been soured by a dominant New Zealand performance in Auckland.

The Black Ferns maintained their unblemished record against the Wallaroos in Test rugby, with a 66-19 win at Mt Smart Stadium.

New Zealand came into Saturday's Test having not lost to Australia in all 30 Tests between the two nations, and a 10-try haul ensured that streak would continue.

The Wallaroos scored three tries, including a score from Waiaria Ellis who started at fly half for the first time.

Maddison Levi, Australia's all-time leading rugby 7s try scorer, made her Wallaroos debut with a 30-minute stint off the bench. Meanwhile, Emily Chancellor became the first woman to represent the Black Ferns and Wallaroos in Test rugby when she made her Australian debut off the bench.

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said her team was disappointed in the result, but was pleased the Australians continued fighting, managing to score two of the game's final three tries.

"New Zealand started off really fast, so we were on the back foot," she said.

"But you could see towards the end that we can get back, it's just a matter of starting well."

Highlights were few and far between for the Wallaroos as the Black Ferns dominated from the opening whistle.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' As the Wallaroos prepare for their 100th Test, past and present players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching this milestone.

A brilliant counter ruck inside Australian territory gave the home side possession, and the Black Ferns then methodically worked their way to the goal-line before fullback Braxton Sorensen-McGee scored on the right flank in the fourth minute.

The Black Ferns continued their early dominance. The Wallaroos were forced to scramble on their goal line to hold out a rampant home side, with New Zealand lock Maiakawanakaulani Roos held up over the line from a line-out maul.

That was just a reprieve for the Wallaroos, as the Black Ferns continued to attack, with prop Chryss Viliko charging over from close range for the second try.

The Black Ferns had a third try in the 24th minute, with lock Maama Mo'onia Vaipulu making a big line break up the middle of the field before passing to fly half Ruahei Demant, who scored under the posts.

New Zealand's one blemish in the first half was Vaipulu being sent to the sin bin, not lowering herself enough in a tackle and making head-on-head contact with Wallaroos' flanker Lily Bone.

Being down to 14 women did not seem to matter to the Black Ferns, who scored a fourth try when Liana Mikaele-Tu'u touched down in the 35th minute.

The Wallaroos were able to take momentum into half-time with their first try of the afternoon. A free kick against the Black Ferns from their own line-out, gave the Wallaroos the ball near the opposition goal-line. The visitors seized the opportunity, with left winger Desiree Miller scoring and then converting her own try.

Down 26-7 at half-time, any hope the Wallaroos had of making a famous comeback was doused quickly.

After being held up early in the first half, Roos finished off a nice passage of play to score New Zealand's fifth try just three minutes into the second half.

By the time Australia's Rugby 7's all-time leading try scorer Levi came on for her Wallaroos debut, the game was not a contest.

Tries to Ayesha Leti-I'iga in the 50th minute and reserve hooker Vici-Rose Green in the 56th minute piled on more misery for the Wallaroos.

The Black Ferns crossed the half-century mark with a try to Maia Joseph, then Shyrah Tuliau-Tua'a charged down a kick from Wallaroos fullback Faitala Moleka inside the Australian in-goal, and grounded the ball.

A lovely side-step from Wallaroos fly half Waiaria Ellis sliced open the Black Ferns defensive line for a try in the 67th minute.

That was the start of a bright spot for the Wallaroos, who produced a driving maul from close range, with reserve hooker Brittany Merlo scoring Australia's third try.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Bitter finals blow for Pendlebury, Blues move a step closer to dream Pies final
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury will miss Collingwood’s cutthroat wildcard final next week and could well have played his final match in black and white.

The Magpies revealed on Saturday that the VFL/AFL games-record holder had suffered a hamstring strain in the club’s loss to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Friday night, ruling him out for “two to three weeks”.

In a further blow to Collingwood, rugged defender Brayden Maynard strained the MCL in his left knee during a Saturday-morning training session and will also likely miss several weeks.

The Pendlebury injury will leave coach Craig McRae lamenting a decision to play his veteran leader in a match that ultimately had no bearing on their ladder position. Many felt he should have rested the former skipper.

“These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden,” Magpies head of football Charlie Gardiner said on Saturday afternoon.

“Scott experienced tightness in the back of his knee during last night’s game. Scans earlier today confirmed a hamstring strain, and we expect Scott to be sidelined for two to three weeks.

“Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade one MCL strain. This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury.

“These are unfortunate setbacks, especially at this time of year but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible.”

World.title: Labuschagne’s woes continue after Starc’s 22-ball masterclass
World.content:
Updated SportCricketTest cricket Labuschagne’s woes continue after Starc’s 22-ball masterclass Nick Wright Updated August 22, 2026 — 3:03pm ,first published August 22, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Marnus Labuschagne’s hopes of playing a key role in Australia’s looming series in South Africa has suffered another telling blow, despite his side taking complete control of the second Test after Mitchell Starc’s new-ball masterclass rolled Bangladesh for 64. It was in bizarre circumstances that the besieged No.3 was bowled for four, straying across and brushing an attempted leg glance onto his stumps off left-arm quick Shoriful Islam. The 32-year-old has endured a wretched three-and-a-half years, now averaging just 29.69 in Test cricket dating back to the start of 2023, his last century coming in July that year. Marnus Labuschagne’s wretched run of form continues. Getty Images Australian coach Andrew McDonald had warned Labuschagne “needs runs” if he is to retain his spot throughout a gruelling calendar which could include as many as 19 more Tests between now and July – including a three-match series in South Africa beginning in October.



Labuschagne’s dismissal came after Shoriful had also enticed Travis Head to chop onto his stumps for the third time in as many innings this series for 22, while the returning Matt Renshaw – his first appearance in the baggy green for more than three years – caught a leading edge attempting to guide Taskin Amed to the leg side, and was caught at third slip for eight. Loading Steve Smith (six*) and Cameron Green (one*) guided Australia to 3-50 at the tea break. Earlier, Starc’s 43-minute, 22-ball five-wicket haul triggering a drastic Bangladesh collapse in Mackay. Seething from a shock nine-wicket defeat in the opening clash of the two Test series, the 36-year-old Starc’s six-wicket haul began with the first ball of the historic clash at Great Barrier Reef Arena – the 28th time he has made inroads during his first over of an innings.



Mitch Starc has claimed a five-wicket haul in his first 22 balls in Mackay. Getty Images The left-arm quick’s delivery angled in at Shadman Islam’s leg stump, before swinging away to catch the outside edge, with Cameron Green latching onto the catch. Skipper Pat Cummins’ decision to bowl after winning the toss looked better by the over, as Starc struck first ball of his second over as well – Tanzid Hasan (0) unable to dig out a full ball outside off, and instead guiding it off the edge to Beau Webster in the slips. Starc was on a tear. His next ball, he trapped Najmul Hossain Shanton lbw, with the Bangladesh captain’s challenge ultimately deemed to be clipping leg stump based on the umpire’s call. The left-arm spearhead was in a mood to impress the crowd, drawing a low edge from Mominul Haque (nine) in his third over, with Green diving low to his left to claim an impressive catch.



Loading When a vicious Starc bouncer caught Litton Das high on the bat in his fourth over, only for Webster to drop a sitter in the slips, it appeared maybe Bangladesh had some fortune going their way. But that hope was eradicated next ball when Starc trapped him on the pads for a duck, and despite the appeal being turned down, replays confirmed the ball had pitched in line and was hitting to deliver Starc a five-wicket haul in 22 balls. It took nine overs from that point for another breakthrough, Cummins getting one to nip off the seam from off stump into middle to bowl Mushfiqur Rahim for five. After returning from lunch at 6-35, any hopes Bangladesh had of mustering a miracle were quickly snuffed out – Cummins quickly drawing Mehidy Hasan Miraz’s outside edge, caught by Webster, for 11, before Josh Hazlewood claimed his first wicket when Hasan Mahmud guided a leg glance straight to Nathan Lyon at leg gully for 10.



Matt Renshaw and Marnus Labuschagne in Mackay. Getty Images There was one moment of controversy which soon followed, as Taskin Islam skied an attempted slog, only to get in Hazlewood’s way as the towering seamer attempted to get into position to take the catch. The umpires deemed the batter had not intentionally obstructed Hazlewood. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Never let him settle’: Spin legend Mushie on Warne, Lyon and how Bangladesh humbled Australia But his reprieve was short-lived, as the very next over he went for a similar shot off Cummins, only to send it straight down Lyon’s throat. A lavish boundary over backward point off Shoriful helped Bangladesh avoid equalling their lowest-ever Test total of 43, set against the West Indies in 2018, with he and Taijul Islam sharing in a 25- run stand – the highest partnership of the innings – before Starc claimed his sixth scalp, finishing with 6-12, in dismissing the former caught behind by Alex Carey.



Trailing 1-0 in the series, the Australians stepped out in Mackay with the one change – Queensland’s Renshaw replacing Jake Weatherald to open the batting alongside Travis Head. Bangladesh made one change to their triumphant line-up, with left-arm quick Shoriful coming in for Ebadot Hossain. Second Test XIs Australia: Travis Head, Matthew Renshaw, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (capt), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood Bangladesh: Tanzid Hasan, Shadman Islam, Mominul Haque, Najmul Hossain Shanto (capt), Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das, Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Hasan Mahmud, Taskin Ahmed, Taijul Islam, Shoriful Islam

World.title: ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump
World.content:
Exclusive NationalComedy ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump Stephen Brook August 22, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diplomats never tell, but a new dark TV comedy created by the former Australian ambassador to France promises to be anything but discreet. Brendan Berne, our man in Paris from 2017 to 2020, has just filmed the pilot for a sitcom called Rank, inspired by his two decades of service with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Brendan Berne (left), pictured with French President Emmanuel Macron, is a former ambassador now focused on creative projects. Berne, 56, who resigned from DFAT in 2020 to move to Burgundy in France with his husband and to concentrate on creative projects, describes Rank as “The Thick of It updated for the age of Trump, Truss and Thunberg”. Networks and production houses were interested, but then the US president sued the BBC for defamation and, long story short, corporations shied away from a pointed comedy in the era of Donald Trump, Liz Truss’ short stint as UK prime minister and eco-warrior Greta Thunberg.



“Trump suing the BBC has scorched the earth for political satire, and the joke invigilators and sensitivity readers make transgressive comedy challenging. Five years on, someone laughed it’s been my Odyssey, but I’d say it’s more been the Plodyssey,” Berne says. “When the rights returned to me, I revisited my more provocative scripts, which resonated with investors, and we have just finished shooting the pilot.” As Australia’s ambassador, Berne helped to persuade French President Emmanuel Macron to visit Australia – a first. And in 2017, when Australia’s marriage equality legislation became law, he started a video on social media discussing stronger relations between Australia and France and ended it with him proposing to his Swiss-Australian partner of 11 years, Thomas Marti. Millions in France viewed it on social media, which led to Berne appearing on France’s top TV talk show. Rank is not Berne’s only project. He has helped to develop a cello concerto that tells the largely lost story of a 19th-century French cabin boy being adopted by an Aboriginal tribe on the Cape York Peninsula.



Melissa King, the director of artistic planning for the Sydney Symphony Orchestra (SSO), commissioned the work, by composer Matthew Hindson. It was developed with the support of the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies and is scheduled to premiere in NAIDOC Week 2028. The concerto will bring to life the largely untold story of 14-year-old Narcisse Pelletier, who was abandoned by his ship’s crew in Far North Queensland in 1858 and adopted by the Uutaalnganu people, with whom he lived for 17 years. The cast of Rank (from left): Phillip Honeywell, Bryan Williams, Felicity Bown, Jodyanne Fletcher Richardson, Dana Blacklake and Will Frazer. “This an important concerto for the SSO, as it brings the story of Narcisse and the Uutaalnganu to a wider audience, the first major cultural project dedicated to this incredible true story,” King says. Berne and French cellist Sebastien Hurtaud, who hails from the same place as Pelletier, travelled last September to the Cape York Peninsula and met members of the Uutaalnganu people, some of whom still had oral accounts of Pelletier passed down from the 19th century. While visiting, Hurtaud played part of the composition for locals.



“They still share stories of the para (white man) who they saved in 1858 and who became part of them. One young woman recounted to me the story of Narcisse killing a crocodile after it had taken a baby, earning the respect of his new community,” Berne says. Pelletier was later returned to France against his wishes, and his parents forced him to undertake an exorcism. Berne (right) and husband Thomas Marti in Paris. “As a former ambassador to France, I believed this forgotten chapter of the France-Australia relationship needed to be told, especially as the Indigenous people were the hero of the story,” Berne says. “I also hoped it might help salve some of the wounds in the immediate wake of the cancellation of the submarine program in a country where culture means a tremendous amount.”



The French embassy in Australia appointed Berne to the French-Australian Culture Exchange Foundation, which is chaired in Melbourne by Myriam Boisbouvier-Wylie. Related Article Foreign relations Trump, subs and the Iran war: Australia’s replacement for Rudd has arrived in DC Berne’s TV program had a circuitous route to existence. In 2022, it was ranked in the top three of a co-production pitching competition, Series Mania, an international TV industry festival staged annually in Lille. In developing the project, he worked with executive producer Glen Condie, the Emmy Award-nominated producer of Top End Wedding. Rank, billed as a comedy of diplomatic proportions, was written by Berne and should appeal to disillusioned Gen Xers. It is set in a fictional South Pacific country, where British diplomats decide to give asylum to a rogue state weapons scientist in a misguided attempt to celebrate women in science week. The team is then thrown into turmoil by the appearance of a bumbling British minister.



The program will be released in December and is available on rankthecomedy.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000 Wes Mountain August 22, 2026 — 1:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A two-bedroom Edwardian in Richmond, directly across from Bicentennial Park, sold for $1,385,000 at auction on Saturday – $65,000 above its reserve. The home at 20 Parkville Street sits in a row of red-brick terraces looking onto the park. It maintains original exterior features such as tessellated tile paths and stained-glass windows, and has an updated interior featuring high ceilings, open-plan living and new appliances. It had a price guide of $1.2 million to $1.32 million, and a reserve of $1.32 million. Jellis Craig Richmond agent and auctioneer Luke Schickerling said strong bidding opened at $1.2 million, the bottom of the guide, and went up quickly in $10,000 increments before hitting $1.32 million and being declared on the market.



Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne house prices How much it costs to live in Melbourne’s most desired school zones From there, three potential buyers continued to trade bids until the home sold to a young couple, who Schickerling said were new to the Richmond area. The vendors were renovators, who he said were now “onto the next adventure”. He said the property had performed well, and there were more people bidding than he would have expected just a few weeks ago, as the market was starting to warm up for spring – traditionally the peak period for auctions in Melbourne – and fewer properties were coming up for sale than expected. “We have the lowest stock levels I can recall in recent memory,” Schickerling said. The preserved Edwardian features at the front of the property conceal a modern, spacious interior. Jellis Craig Richmond



The property was one of 598 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. In Brunswick, a warehouse conversion apartment – in the same building known to be the home of Nina Proudman in the TV series Offspring – sold for $1,126,000 at auction, soaring $126,000 above its $1 million reserve. The light-filled two-bedroom apartment at 210/1-3 Dods Street, complete with quirky egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, expansive open-plan living, dining and storage areas, and a north-facing view to Brunswick’s churches and rooftops, had a price guide of $950,000 to $1 million. Nelson Alexander Brunswick agent Janine Ballantyne said auctioneer James Pilliner opened bidding at $970,000, before four bidders pushed it easily past the $1 million mark in $10,000 increments.



From there, the bidders winnowed down to three to take the price up to $1.1 million, and then down to two as the increments grew smaller and the auction came to a close. The buyer was a professional moving into the area. The egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, askew in its own box within the apartment’s expansive interior, was just one characterful element of the warehouse conversion. Nelson Alexander Brunswick The vendor had decided to upsize within Brunswick after 21 years in the stylish apartment. Ballantyne said the result was indicative of the market. “[It’s] price-sensitive, but if people can see value, they will engage,” she said. “It doesn’t feel as though we are going to have the usual levels of spring stock, whether that puts pressure on prices or not remains to be seen.”
