World.title: ‘It’s like we’re being robbed’: The relentless march of data centres
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dublin: The sun is setting over the rolling fields near a small town in Ireland as Sorcha O’Neill and Dolores Moore point towards a large stretch of farmland that is meant to be bulldozed to make way for a row of data centres. We are standing at the edge of their suburb in Naas, a centuries-old town in County Kildare, at an old fence covered in blackberry bushes. Within weeks, they fear, their council will approve the next step in building the data factories of the internet age. “We were never informed about this,” says O’Neill, a former local councillor who understands the planning system. Only four weeks earlier, she tells me, she was checking plans for a more distant data centre when she noticed the paperwork for the farmland in an area known as Jigginstown. Sorcha O’Neill stands near a Microsoft data centre at Castle Grange Business Park in Ireland. She and her neighbours are worried about a similar project being built near their homes in Naas, in County Kildare. David Crowe Her heart sank. “That’s right next door.” Now the two neighbours have joined the agonising debate in Ireland about the scale of these new projects. The country already has about 72 data centres and is forecast to have dozens more in only a few years because it is so attractive for developers. It has skilled workers, low company tax rates, a cool climate and good land. Most importantly, it has the location. The facilities here, close to the high-speed lines that connect Europe to America, can quickly crunch data for artificial intelligence applications being used by businesses and consumers in the world’s wealthiest nations. Already, these facilities use one-fifth of the electricity from the nation’s grid. Soon it will be one-third. That makes Ireland a test case in the march of the data centres.



O’Neill and Moore discovered too late that Kildare County Council had zoned the land next to their homes for data centre use by the owner, Microsoft. That decision, made without fanfare several years ago, now makes it very difficult for them to challenge the outcome and ensure the land is zoned only for agriculture, as it was for years. Moore, a former catering worker, has been in this community since 1995. “I moved here from Dublin to make a better life for my children,” she says. “And my kids loved it here.” Now she worries about the construction noise from the project and the changes when the data centres are built. O’Neill, a tech worker, talks about the scale of the project when we drive around the perimeter of the farmland, passing horse studs and an old canal. “Who’s going to want to buy to live next to a data centre?” she asks. The rolling fields in Waterford could soon be hosting enormous data centres. Nobody in this community knows how big the data centres may be because those plans are yet to be unveiled. For many, the goal is to stop the plans at a council meeting on September 9, before the developers take the next step. A short drive away, just off the motorway into Dublin, stands a sign of things to come. The Grange Castle Business Park hosts tech giants including Amazon, Google and Microsoft. It is also home to a vast Pfizer facility that makes medicines for global markets – a high-tech contrast to the old pubs and traditional music found in Dublin’s city centre. O’Neill stops outside a long row of white buildings at Site 075. There are no logos on the fence, but this is Microsoft’s address. And it is a future O’Neill does not want in her backyard.



Demand for data is soaring as people use more AI. The Grange Castle data centre complex is Microsoft’s largest outside the United States, consuming 1.3 million megawatt hours of electricity last year, according to its latest environmental report. To put that in perspective, the Microsoft data centre in Sydney consumed only 7704 megawatt hours. Related Article Data centres ‘Difficult to reconcile’: The Australian council moving to ban data centres Microsoft is building a new gas-fired power station to support the Irish site and take some of the load off the national electricity grid. It is also vowing to minimise water use. Each year, the Castle Grange facility uses the equivalent of seven Olympic swimming pools – very low compared to the 392 used by the company’s data centre in Phoenix, Arizona. (The Sydney facility used three last year.) As demand grows, Microsoft needs more space. That is why it is working on the Jigginstown project. The precinct is 54.55 hectares – bigger than the Royal Botanic Gardens in Melbourne (38 hectares) and in Sydney (30 hectares). The company says 37 hectares will be set aside for new parklands, including a boardwalk and a walking track. This is not enough to mollify local residents – especially when O’Neill sees the size of the buildings at Grange Castle. The challenge for Ireland, however, is that it wants more growth in the tech industries that set up there during the nation’s “Celtic Tiger” economic revival in the 1990s, helping to lift living standards. Swimming against the tide



Critics say the data centres use too much power and water without creating enough jobs or paying enough economic dividends to local communities. But they are wrong on all counts, according to Ronan Kelly, the chief executive of Digital Infrastructure Ireland, an industry group that represents companies that build and operate these facilities. “The world is in a wave of investment in the data centre space at the moment, which is underpinned by the wave of investment in the AI sector in general, and that won’t last forever,” he says. “When this wave of investment in the AI space stops, the data centres that have capacity will capture the workloads for the next 20, 30 or 40 years. With that will come the taxation from the revenues that flow through them. With that will come the high-skilled jobs to continue to develop and adapt those facilities for emerging workloads.” Loading Ireland has a natural advantage with data centre location, positioned as it is between the US and Europe. Latency, measured in the milliseconds it takes to get a response from an AI app or an online service, is its strength. A facility in Ireland can deliver faster speeds for multiple applications talking to each other across continents, and Kelly believes this will be vital for “agentic AI”, where the apps are increasingly autonomous. Australia, located at the end of the world’s data lines, is unlikely to be able to offer this kind of low latency. For Kelly and the data centre companies he represents, there is a limited time for Ireland to ride this economic wave. He rejects the argument that the projects are vast spaces without workers, pointing to the jobs that are created to build and operate them. This includes the creation of specialist Irish companies that develop power and cooling systems for projects in and outside the country.



The Irish government has data to back these claims, courtesy of a report it commissioned from KPMG, received in June, which estimated that Irish-owned high-tech construction generated €2.1 billion ($3.4 billion) in exports in the data centre business in 2024. Related Article Explainer

Data centres Underwater, in space and in your city: Behind the data centre boom From 2010 to 2014, it found, the sector created about 17,000 jobs directly. This comprised 9356 additional construction jobs and 7636 operational jobs. Even if the building boom eased over time, KPMG said, the tax benefits would continue to flow from this workforce. Over five years to 2030, it estimated this would be worth €1.36 billion to the government. When KPMG looked at the broadest possible benefits of digital infrastructure, it claimed this part of the economy supported 876,000 jobs and €14.6 billion in annual employment-related tax in 2024 alone. Stopping this growth, says Kelly when we meet in Dublin, means letting other countries gain the jobs instead. “If you look at the backdrop of the world today, where they talk about AI, it is going to have a significant impact on the number of jobs that are out there,” he says. “Sending capacity overseas is really dangerous. You need to look 10, 20 or 50 years out to consider all the implications of this. Any short-term decisions taken today can have really damaging long-term implications.” Feeding the AI beast

World.title: The Swans are nothing without the W: Why I’ll be at the SCG on Sunday
World.content:
NationalAFL off-field behaviour Opinion The Swans are nothing without the W: Why I’ll be at the SCG on Sunday

Victoria Rawlings August 22, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s been a hard week to be a Swans supporter, especially as a woman. The horror of headlines on Monday and Tuesday about some of our most revered players has led to a reckoning of who we are and what we can support. While police investigations are ongoing, the details that are emerging are both damning and distressing. Victoria Rawlings is a former AFLW field umpire and passionate Swans supporter. Stefanie Zingsheim As a researcher in gendered violence, and a passionate Swans supporter, this has been a particularly challenging experience. Like many supporters, I have long seen the Swans as leaders in social justice and progressive issues in the AFL. They are the Pride Round club, and this year took a stand against another club’s inaction and hypocrisy around homophobia. They create a home ground experience that is incredibly inclusive and oriented to welcome all. From this baseline, the best word to define my feelings this week has been betrayal. In many ways, I was foolish enough to think the Swans were different. But really, I should have paid more attention to my own two-decade experience as an AFL player, administrator, umpire and fan. The signs of exclusion and hostility were there as a girl; there was no pathway for me to play football, so it never even appeared on my radar. We were framed as incapable, too delicate, not interested, or not active enough to have leagues warranted for us. Many current and past AFLW players continue to share this narrative.



The signs were there when I finally played in the Sydney Women’s Australian Football League, as it was then known, a group of teams from around Sydney that played a league that was run by women, for women. Even then, it was hard to find space and time for training that didn’t clash with the favoured men’s teams. At Sydney University, we trained on a grass hockey square, despite our games being played at large oval grounds. This, I was told, was a huge improvement from just a couple of years prior, where volunteers had to bring temporary Auskick posts to set up games on “cow paddock” fields each weekend. Victoria Rawlings umpiring a game of AFL. Stefanie Zingsheim They were there when I worked in a club administrator job in Sydney. They were keen to have a “ladies’ day”, not for the players of the adjacent women’s club, but for the wives and girlfriends of the men’s players. As I pitched the idea of fundraising for a charity that focused on violence against women, I was told that it was a bit grim, and we should go for the more palatable concern of breast cancer. The message? Men’s violence against women exists elsewhere, and is not our concern. They were there as I umpired for around 10 years, where both personally and structurally, I was subjected to elements that make girls and women understand that they are, and always will be, outsiders. My research on the experience of female umpires in Australian football showed that this was not an individual experience, but a systemic issue, and one that the AFL has been slow to address. While I’m not suggesting that these experiences are commensurate or comparable to the harms of sexual assault, they speak to a broader positioning of women as lesser, as peripheral, and of not warranting equal respect in football spaces. Coupled with “jokes” or “banter” that are difficult to act against, these are the seeds that grow into incidents of sexual violence. We might see the eventual outcomes as unintelligible, but they have been fostered through countless interactions that diminish the value and humanity of women.



Of course there have been incredible moments of hope and triumph – the establishment and expansion of the AFLW, the well-attended games at Henson Park, the increasing visibility and pay of these athletes and those who participate in the league. However, the challenges are ongoing. This battle has had dramatic costs this week, with women again understanding the ways that sexism, objectification, and misogyny operate away from public eyes. Our thoughts are with those women as they navigate what is likely to be a horrific experience at protecting their privacy and their mental and emotional health. Related Article Opinion

AFL off-field behaviour Men run the AFL and it is time they fixed its dark underbelly Angela Pippos Contributor As Angela Pippos and Kate McCarthy argued earlier in the week, this horror is compounded by the incredibly jarring use of passive language around sexual assault, like “players found themselves in this situation” from Matthew Pavlich, the CEO of the Swans. It is unacceptable that any statement on sexual violence does not centre the women who have been harmed. And it is unacceptable that we are not attentive to the women players and staff in this club who will have had the rug pulled out from under them again as they see and hear about disrespectful, objectifying and dehumanising behaviours from their colleagues. Like so many this week I have been doing some soul-searching about whether to attend Sunday’s match. I was always, of course, going to attend the AFLW game. This is our time to show that the Swans are nothing without W. But I am also, with great apprehension, seeking to open myself up to supporting the remainder of the men’s Swans squad as they take the field later in the afternoon.



The five players allegedly involved in this case have been stood down, and that is the only correct step that the club could take to signal their institutional obligations and commitments to rightfully furious and disappointed fans. Coach Dean Cox and Captain Callum Mills fronted the media on Friday, and the latter started with an apology “to the AFLW players, our female staff, and the women in our lives, our partners, mothers, sisters, and all women in the community”. His words, though likely carefully crafted, seemed genuinely heartfelt, as he expressed that he was “deeply shocked and disappointed to be here”, and that as a playing group they fully supported the club’s suspension of the players involved. These words matter. And it’s the club’s approach to saying them that have convinced me that it’s possible to both carry disappointment, rage, and betrayal, but also to show up with some care and openness for the other players on the team. Perhaps we can show them that we, too, are part of their team. Women and girls have managed to sustain our relationship with football through many hostilities, and it’s through our commitment to this love of the game that we are seeing the painstakingly slow work of cultural change. By our voices being loud in membership, play, administration, and officiating, perhaps we can hang on to this game that we love, and perhaps one day, it will love us back. Victoria Rawlings is an associate professor in the Sydney School of Education and Social Work. She conducts research about gender, sexuality, and schooling, and is a former AFLW and NEAFL field umpire. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Alleged sexual assault victim from Swans late-night party plans civil action
World.content:
A woman who alleges she was the victim of a sexual assault during a late-night party with five Sydney Swans players in a Melbourne hotel room has hired a lawyer to prepare civil legal action. Law firm Slater and Gordon confirmed on Saturday morning that it had been engaged to investigate a potential civil claim on behalf of the woman, and lawyer Jackson Pannam said the woman was “trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience”. The Pullman East Melbourne hotel, where the Swans players stayed on Sunday night. Simon Schluter He said his client called the police “immediately after what had happened” in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. “She’s provided a statement and she’s continuing to assist the police with their investigation,” Pannam said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Nobody knows if any of these five will play for the Swans again “Whatever the outcome of the criminal investigation, we intend to explore other avenues for our clients to seek justice, including through civil remedies. We will be putting all of the relevant parties on notice in due course.” Pannam told reporters the woman’s complaint to police was about “alleged sexual assaults”. A police spokesperson, in a statement on Saturday morning, said Sexual Crimes Squad detectives continued “to investigate a report of a sexual assault”. “The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established and a number of people have been spoken to,” the spokesperson said.



“As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken.” This masthead has previously reported that star player Isaac Heeney is at the centre of the police inquiry. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine Five Swans players – Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were stood down for the rest of the season for breaching the club’s standards. On Friday, a lawyer representing the other two women who were present at the hotel on Monday described what occurred as “demeaning, abhorrent and simply not moral or acceptable”.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL off-field behaviour Swans hotel drama deepens as former star placed inside late-night party “These women were subjected to the most disgusting actions and behaviour I have ever heard about in my 28 years as a lawyer,” Carbone Lawyers head of personal injury and litigation John Karantzis told 3AW. Karantzis also claimed there were “even a few leaders in that room” along with the five Swans players. Pannam described those comments as unhelpful, and said the woman he represented wanted privacy. “I’m not in the business of ranking the types of cases that I’ve been involved in,” he said.



“Certainly, I don’t think that’s helpful.” The Swans have denied there were any other club officials or staff members in the hotel room. “The Sydney Swans supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today’s statement regarding the investigation,” the club said on Saturday. Loading “The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation.



“The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage.”



Pannam, when asked who his client intended to launch legal action against, said: “A claim for compensation can be made against anyone who has caused or contributed to someone suffering injury, harm, damage. It’s very early days, and we are considering our options. “We’ll be writing to the relevant parties in due course with a view to putting them on notice of what our intentions are.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Bitter finals blow for Pendlebury, Blues move a step closer to dream Pies final
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury will miss Collingwood’s cutthroat wildcard final next week and could well have played his final match in black and white.

The Magpies revealed on Saturday that the VFL/AFL games-record holder had suffered a hamstring strain in the club’s loss to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Friday night, ruling him out for “two to three weeks”.

In a further blow to Collingwood, rugged defender Brayden Maynard strained the MCL in his left knee during a Saturday-morning training session and will also likely miss several weeks.

The Pendlebury injury will leave coach Craig McRae lamenting a decision to play his veteran leader in a match that ultimately had no bearing on their ladder position. Many felt he should have rested the former skipper.

“These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden,” Magpies head of football Charlie Gardiner said on Saturday afternoon.

“Scott experienced tightness in the back of his knee during last night’s game. Scans earlier today confirmed a hamstring strain, and we expect Scott to be sidelined for two to three weeks.

“Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade one MCL strain. This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury.

“These are unfortunate setbacks, especially at this time of year but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible.”

World.title: Labuschagne’s woes continue after Starc’s 22-ball masterclass
World.content:
Updated SportCricketTest cricket Labuschagne’s woes continue after Starc’s 22-ball masterclass Nick Wright Updated August 22, 2026 — 3:03pm ,first published August 22, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Marnus Labuschagne’s hopes of playing a key role in Australia’s looming series in South Africa has suffered another telling blow, despite his side taking complete control of the second Test after Mitchell Starc’s new-ball masterclass rolled Bangladesh for 64. It was in bizarre circumstances that the besieged No.3 was bowled for four, straying across and brushing an attempted leg glance onto his stumps off left-arm quick Shoriful Islam. The 32-year-old has endured a wretched three-and-a-half years, now averaging just 29.69 in Test cricket dating back to the start of 2023, his last century coming in July that year. Marnus Labuschagne’s wretched run of form continues. Getty Images Australian coach Andrew McDonald had warned Labuschagne “needs runs” if he is to retain his spot throughout a gruelling calendar which could include as many as 19 more Tests between now and July – including a three-match series in South Africa beginning in October.



Labuschagne’s dismissal came after Shoriful had also enticed Travis Head to chop onto his stumps for the third time in as many innings this series for 22, while the returning Matt Renshaw – his first appearance in the baggy green for more than three years – caught a leading edge attempting to guide Taskin Amed to the leg side, and was caught at third slip for eight. Loading Steve Smith (six*) and Cameron Green (one*) guided Australia to 3-50 at the tea break. Earlier, Starc’s 43-minute, 22-ball five-wicket haul triggering a drastic Bangladesh collapse in Mackay. Seething from a shock nine-wicket defeat in the opening clash of the two Test series, the 36-year-old Starc’s six-wicket haul began with the first ball of the historic clash at Great Barrier Reef Arena – the 28th time he has made inroads during his first over of an innings.



Mitch Starc has claimed a five-wicket haul in his first 22 balls in Mackay. Getty Images The left-arm quick’s delivery angled in at Shadman Islam’s leg stump, before swinging away to catch the outside edge, with Cameron Green latching onto the catch. Skipper Pat Cummins’ decision to bowl after winning the toss looked better by the over, as Starc struck first ball of his second over as well – Tanzid Hasan (0) unable to dig out a full ball outside off, and instead guiding it off the edge to Beau Webster in the slips. Starc was on a tear. His next ball, he trapped Najmul Hossain Shanton lbw, with the Bangladesh captain’s challenge ultimately deemed to be clipping leg stump based on the umpire’s call. The left-arm spearhead was in a mood to impress the crowd, drawing a low edge from Mominul Haque (nine) in his third over, with Green diving low to his left to claim an impressive catch.



Loading When a vicious Starc bouncer caught Litton Das high on the bat in his fourth over, only for Webster to drop a sitter in the slips, it appeared maybe Bangladesh had some fortune going their way. But that hope was eradicated next ball when Starc trapped him on the pads for a duck, and despite the appeal being turned down, replays confirmed the ball had pitched in line and was hitting to deliver Starc a five-wicket haul in 22 balls. It took nine overs from that point for another breakthrough, Cummins getting one to nip off the seam from off stump into middle to bowl Mushfiqur Rahim for five. After returning from lunch at 6-35, any hopes Bangladesh had of mustering a miracle were quickly snuffed out – Cummins quickly drawing Mehidy Hasan Miraz’s outside edge, caught by Webster, for 11, before Josh Hazlewood claimed his first wicket when Hasan Mahmud guided a leg glance straight to Nathan Lyon at leg gully for 10.



Matt Renshaw and Marnus Labuschagne in Mackay. Getty Images There was one moment of controversy which soon followed, as Taskin Islam skied an attempted slog, only to get in Hazlewood’s way as the towering seamer attempted to get into position to take the catch. The umpires deemed the batter had not intentionally obstructed Hazlewood. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Never let him settle’: Spin legend Mushie on Warne, Lyon and how Bangladesh humbled Australia But his reprieve was short-lived, as the very next over he went for a similar shot off Cummins, only to send it straight down Lyon’s throat. A lavish boundary over backward point off Shoriful helped Bangladesh avoid equalling their lowest-ever Test total of 43, set against the West Indies in 2018, with he and Taijul Islam sharing in a 25- run stand – the highest partnership of the innings – before Starc claimed his sixth scalp, finishing with 6-12, in dismissing the former caught behind by Alex Carey.



Trailing 1-0 in the series, the Australians stepped out in Mackay with the one change – Queensland’s Renshaw replacing Jake Weatherald to open the batting alongside Travis Head. Bangladesh made one change to their triumphant line-up, with left-arm quick Shoriful coming in for Ebadot Hossain. Second Test XIs Australia: Travis Head, Matthew Renshaw, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Pat Cummins (capt), Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood Bangladesh: Tanzid Hasan, Shadman Islam, Mominul Haque, Najmul Hossain Shanto (capt), Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das, Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Hasan Mahmud, Taskin Ahmed, Taijul Islam, Shoriful Islam

World.title: ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump
World.content:
Exclusive NationalComedy ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump Stephen Brook August 22, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diplomats never tell, but a new dark TV comedy created by the former Australian ambassador to France promises to be anything but discreet. Brendan Berne, our man in Paris from 2017 to 2020, has just filmed the pilot for a sitcom called Rank, inspired by his two decades of service with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Brendan Berne (left), pictured with French President Emmanuel Macron, is a former ambassador now focused on creative projects. Berne, 56, who resigned from DFAT in 2020 to move to Burgundy in France with his husband and to concentrate on creative projects, describes Rank as “The Thick of It updated for the age of Trump, Truss and Thunberg”. Networks and production houses were interested, but then the US president sued the BBC for defamation and, long story short, corporations shied away from a pointed comedy in the era of Donald Trump, Liz Truss’ short stint as UK prime minister and eco-warrior Greta Thunberg.



“Trump suing the BBC has scorched the earth for political satire, and the joke invigilators and sensitivity readers make transgressive comedy challenging. Five years on, someone laughed it’s been my Odyssey, but I’d say it’s more been the Plodyssey,” Berne says. “When the rights returned to me, I revisited my more provocative scripts, which resonated with investors, and we have just finished shooting the pilot.” As Australia’s ambassador, Berne helped to persuade French President Emmanuel Macron to visit Australia – a first. And in 2017, when Australia’s marriage equality legislation became law, he started a video on social media discussing stronger relations between Australia and France and ended it with him proposing to his Swiss-Australian partner of 11 years, Thomas Marti. Millions in France viewed it on social media, which led to Berne appearing on France’s top TV talk show. Rank is not Berne’s only project. He has helped to develop a cello concerto that tells the largely lost story of a 19th-century French cabin boy being adopted by an Aboriginal tribe on the Cape York Peninsula.



Melissa King, the director of artistic planning for the Sydney Symphony Orchestra (SSO), commissioned the work, by composer Matthew Hindson. It was developed with the support of the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies and is scheduled to premiere in NAIDOC Week 2028. The concerto will bring to life the largely untold story of 14-year-old Narcisse Pelletier, who was abandoned by his ship’s crew in Far North Queensland in 1858 and adopted by the Uutaalnganu people, with whom he lived for 17 years. The cast of Rank (from left): Phillip Honeywell, Bryan Williams, Felicity Bown, Jodyanne Fletcher Richardson, Dana Blacklake and Will Frazer. “This an important concerto for the SSO, as it brings the story of Narcisse and the Uutaalnganu to a wider audience, the first major cultural project dedicated to this incredible true story,” King says. Berne and French cellist Sebastien Hurtaud, who hails from the same place as Pelletier, travelled last September to the Cape York Peninsula and met members of the Uutaalnganu people, some of whom still had oral accounts of Pelletier passed down from the 19th century. While visiting, Hurtaud played part of the composition for locals.



“They still share stories of the para (white man) who they saved in 1858 and who became part of them. One young woman recounted to me the story of Narcisse killing a crocodile after it had taken a baby, earning the respect of his new community,” Berne says. Pelletier was later returned to France against his wishes, and his parents forced him to undertake an exorcism. Berne (right) and husband Thomas Marti in Paris. “As a former ambassador to France, I believed this forgotten chapter of the France-Australia relationship needed to be told, especially as the Indigenous people were the hero of the story,” Berne says. “I also hoped it might help salve some of the wounds in the immediate wake of the cancellation of the submarine program in a country where culture means a tremendous amount.”



The French embassy in Australia appointed Berne to the French-Australian Culture Exchange Foundation, which is chaired in Melbourne by Myriam Boisbouvier-Wylie. Related Article Foreign relations Trump, subs and the Iran war: Australia’s replacement for Rudd has arrived in DC Berne’s TV program had a circuitous route to existence. In 2022, it was ranked in the top three of a co-production pitching competition, Series Mania, an international TV industry festival staged annually in Lille. In developing the project, he worked with executive producer Glen Condie, the Emmy Award-nominated producer of Top End Wedding. Rank, billed as a comedy of diplomatic proportions, was written by Berne and should appeal to disillusioned Gen Xers. It is set in a fictional South Pacific country, where British diplomats decide to give asylum to a rogue state weapons scientist in a misguided attempt to celebrate women in science week. The team is then thrown into turmoil by the appearance of a bumbling British minister.



The program will be released in December and is available on rankthecomedy.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000 Wes Mountain August 22, 2026 — 1:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A two-bedroom Edwardian in Richmond, directly across from Bicentennial Park, sold for $1,385,000 at auction on Saturday – $65,000 above its reserve. The home at 20 Parkville Street sits in a row of red-brick terraces looking onto the park. It maintains original exterior features such as tessellated tile paths and stained-glass windows, and has an updated interior featuring high ceilings, open-plan living and new appliances. It had a price guide of $1.2 million to $1.32 million, and a reserve of $1.32 million. Jellis Craig Richmond agent and auctioneer Luke Schickerling said strong bidding opened at $1.2 million, the bottom of the guide, and went up quickly in $10,000 increments before hitting $1.32 million and being declared on the market.



Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne house prices How much it costs to live in Melbourne’s most desired school zones From there, three potential buyers continued to trade bids until the home sold to a young couple, who Schickerling said were new to the Richmond area. The vendors were renovators, who he said were now “onto the next adventure”. He said the property had performed well, and there were more people bidding than he would have expected just a few weeks ago, as the market was starting to warm up for spring – traditionally the peak period for auctions in Melbourne – and fewer properties were coming up for sale than expected. “We have the lowest stock levels I can recall in recent memory,” Schickerling said. The preserved Edwardian features at the front of the property conceal a modern, spacious interior. Jellis Craig Richmond



The property was one of 598 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. In Brunswick, a warehouse conversion apartment – in the same building known to be the home of Nina Proudman in the TV series Offspring – sold for $1,126,000 at auction, soaring $126,000 above its $1 million reserve. The light-filled two-bedroom apartment at 210/1-3 Dods Street, complete with quirky egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, expansive open-plan living, dining and storage areas, and a north-facing view to Brunswick’s churches and rooftops, had a price guide of $950,000 to $1 million. Nelson Alexander Brunswick agent Janine Ballantyne said auctioneer James Pilliner opened bidding at $970,000, before four bidders pushed it easily past the $1 million mark in $10,000 increments.



From there, the bidders winnowed down to three to take the price up to $1.1 million, and then down to two as the increments grew smaller and the auction came to a close. The buyer was a professional moving into the area. The egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, askew in its own box within the apartment’s expansive interior, was just one characterful element of the warehouse conversion. Nelson Alexander Brunswick The vendor had decided to upsize within Brunswick after 21 years in the stylish apartment. Ballantyne said the result was indicative of the market. “[It’s] price-sensitive, but if people can see value, they will engage,” she said. “It doesn’t feel as though we are going to have the usual levels of spring stock, whether that puts pressure on prices or not remains to be seen.”
